The HIGHEST CIVILIAN award of India is:

(A) Padma Shri
(B) Bharat Ratna
(C) Padma Vibhushan

cards.back:

(C) Amartya Sen

cards.front:
Who were the first three recipients of the Bharat Ratna in 1954?

(A) Jawaharlal Nehru, Mahatma Gandhi, Sardar Patel
(B) C. Rajagopalachari, Dr. S. Radhakrishnan, C. V. Raman
(C) Rajendra Prasad, Lal Bahadur Shastri, B. R. Ambedkar
(D) Subhas Chandra Bose, Mother Teresa, Morarji Desai
cards.back:
(B) C. Rajagopalachari, Dr. S. Radhakrishnan, C. V. Raman

Awards & Honours — The Bharat Ratna was instituted on 2 January 1954 by President Dr. Rajendra Prasad. The FIRST three awardees (1954) were: (1) C. Rajagopalachari — last Governor-General of India; (2) Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan — philosopher, later 2nd President; (3) Sir C. V. Raman — physicist, 1930 Nobel. Mahatma Gandhi never received the Bharat Ratna despite multiple nominations. Nehru received it in 1955 (in office — by himself, controversial). Sardar Patel was posthumously awarded in 1991. Dr. Ambedkar received it posthumously in 1990. NO BR between 1992-2008 due to an SC case challenging its 'medal' status (resolved by a 1995 judgment).

cards.front:
The Jnanpith Award, India's highest literary award, is given by whom and for writing in which languages?

(A) Sahitya Akademi; only English
(B) Bharatiya Jnanpith Trust; 22 scheduled languages + English
(C) Ministry of Culture; Hindi only
(D) Indian Council for Cultural Relations; any Indian language
cards.back:
(B) Bharatiya Jnanpith Trust; 22 scheduled languages + English

Awards & Honours — The Jnanpith Award is instituted by the Bharatiya Jnanpith Trust (established 1944 by the Sahu Jain family), given annually since 1965 for literary work in any of the 22 Scheduled Languages + English. Prize: ₹11 lakh + bronze Saraswati statue + citation. First recipient: G. Sankara Kurup (Malayalam, 1965). First woman: Ashapoorna Devi (Bengali, 1976). First in English: Amitav Ghosh (2018). Odia didn't have a Jnanpith winner till 1973 (Gopinath Mohanty). Hindi has most winners. Distinct from Sahitya Akademi awards (which are by genre in each language each year). Saraswati Samman is another major literary award (KK Birla Foundation since 1991).

cards.front:
The Dadasaheb Phalke Award for lifetime achievement in Indian cinema is named after whom?

(A) The first Indian film actor
(B) The 'Father of Indian Cinema'
(C) The founder of Filmfare Awards
(D) The first Indian to win an Oscar
cards.back:
(B) The 'Father of Indian Cinema'

Awards & Honours — Dhundiraj Govind Phalke (1870-1944), known as 'Dadasaheb' Phalke, is regarded as the Father of Indian Cinema. He directed India's FIRST feature film RAJA HARISHCHANDRA (1913, silent, black-and-white) — the actual release was on 3 May 1913 at Coronation Cinematograph, Mumbai. He made 95 films and 27 shorts. The Dadasaheb Phalke Award was instituted in 1969 (his birth centenary year); first recipient: Devika Rani. Prize: Swarna Kamal (Golden Lotus), ₹10 lakh, shawl. National Film Awards are separately given. India's national cinema day: 3 May. who made India's first feature film 'Raja Harishchandra' (1913).

cards.front:
Which Indian-origin scientist won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 for his work on the structure and function of the ribosome?

(A) Hargobind Khorana
(B) Venkatraman Ramakrishnan
(C) Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
(D) Abhijit Banerjee
cards.back:
(B) Venkatraman Ramakrishnan

Awards & Honours — Venkatraman 'Venki' Ramakrishnan (born 1952, Chidambaram, Tamil Nadu; US/UK citizen) won the 2009 Chemistry Nobel (shared with Thomas A. Steitz and Ada E. Yonath) 'for studies of the structure and function of the ribosome'. Served as President of the Royal Society, UK (2015-20). Khorana won Medicine 1968 (genetic code); Chandrasekhar won Physics 1983 (stellar structure — Chandrasekhar limit); Banerjee won Economics 2019 (poverty experiments, with Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer). Tagore (Literature 1913), Raman (Physics 1930), Mother Teresa (Peace 1979), Sen (Economics 1998), Satyarthi (Peace 2014) complete the list of Indian-linked Nobels.

cards.front:
The Magsaysay Award is often called the 'Asian Nobel Prize'. It is named after a former President of which country?

(A) Thailand
(B) Philippines
(C) Indonesia
(D) South Korea
cards.back:
(B) Philippines

Awards & Honours — Named after Ramon Magsaysay, the 7th President of the Philippines (1953-57), who died in an air crash 1957. The Award was instituted in 1957 by the Rockefeller Brothers Fund to honour his memory. Given since 1958 in categories like government service, public service, community leadership, journalism/literature/creative arts, international understanding, emergent leadership. Indian recipients include: Vinoba Bhave (1958, first Indian), Mother Teresa (1962, pre-Nobel), Satyajit Ray (1967), Ela Bhatt, Baba Amte, Mahasweta Devi, Kiran Bedi, Arvind Kejriwal, TM Krishna, Bezwada Wilson, Anshu Gupta, Ravish Kumar (2019 last Indian so far). The Emergent Leadership category was discontinued in 2020; 2020-21 awards skipped due to COVID.

cards.front:
The Param Vir Chakra (PVC) is India's highest military gallantry award. Who was the FIRST recipient, posthumously awarded?

(A) Major Somnath Sharma
(B) Havildar Abdul Hamid
(C) Subedar Joginder Singh
(D) Captain Vikram Batra
cards.back:
(A) Major Somnath Sharma

Awards & Honours — The Param Vir Chakra (PVC) was instituted on 26 January 1950, retrospectively effective from 15 August 1947. The first PVC was awarded POSTHUMOUSLY to Major Somnath Sharma (4th Battalion, Kumaon Regiment) for his leadership in the Battle of Badgam (3 November 1947) during the First Kashmir War. Only 21 PVCs have been awarded (14 posthumous). Other notable recipients: Major Shaitan Singh (Rezang La 1962), Lance Naik Albert Ekka (1971), Second Lt Arun Khetarpal (1971), Capt Vikram Batra (Kargil 1999), Capt Manoj Pandey (Kargil 1999). India's second-highest military honour is Maha Vir Chakra (MVC), third is Vir Chakra. In PEACETIME, the corresponding highest is Ashoka Chakra.

The Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna (India's highest sporting honour) was originally known as what, and is given by which ministry?

(A) Arjuna Award; Ministry of Culture
(B) Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna; Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports
(C) Dronacharya Award; Ministry of Home Affairs
(D) National Sports Award; Ministry of Education
cards.back:
(B) Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna; Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports

Awards & Honours — Originally the 'Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna' (instituted 1991-92), RENAMED in August 2021 to 'MAJOR DHYAN CHAND KHEL RATNA AWARD' (after the legendary hockey player and 3-time Olympic gold medalist, 1928/1932/1936). First Khel Ratna awardee: Viswanathan Anand (1991-92). Given by the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports. National Sports Awards hierarchy: (1) Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna (top, for outstanding performance over 4 years); (2) Arjuna Award (consistent excellence for 4 years); (3) Dronacharya Award (for coaches); (4) Dhyan Chand Award (for lifetime contribution — different from Khel Ratna). cards.front:
BHARAT RATNA, India's HIGHEST CIVILIAN AWARD, was instituted in:

(A) 26 Jan 1950
(B) 2 JANUARY 1954
(C) 15 August 1947
(D) 14 April 1891
cards.back:
(B) 2 JANUARY 1954

Awards & Honours — BHARAT RATNA — India's HIGHEST CIVILIAN AWARD. INSTITUTED on 2 JANUARY 1954 by President Rajendra Prasad. Originally awarded for 'exceptional service of the highest order in any field of human endeavour' — arts, literature, sciences, public services. EXPANDED 2011 (Rule amendment) to explicitly include SPORTS + any field of human endeavour. DESIGN: PIPAL LEAF (SACRED FIG, Bodhi tree-leaf) shape; BRONZE; inscription 'BHARAT RATNA' in Hindi + 'SUN' in the centre, + embossed platinum sun; 'SATYAMEV JAYATE' in Hindi on reverse. Worn around neck on WHITE ribbon. NOT a formal 'title' (Art 18 of Constitution prohibits titles) — recipients cannot use it as prefix/suffix to their name (though commonly referred to as 'Bharat Ratna X'). ELIGIBILITY: PM recommends to PRESIDENT. NO formal recommendation needed (unlike Padma). MAX 3 PER YEAR conventionally (not a strict rule); years with no award are common. POSTHUMOUS allowed SINCE 1955 (Lal Bahadur Shastri first posthumous). INCLUDES cash benefit? NO — only certificate + medallion. Railway passes + VIP protocol benefits. RECIPIENTS till 2024: 53 individuals. FIRST 3 (1954): (1) Dr. SARVEPALLI RADHAKRISHNAN — philosopher + 2nd President. (2) C. RAJAGOPALACHARI — 'Rajaji', first Indian Governor-General, freedom fighter, statesman. (3) Dr. CHANDRASEKHARA VENKATA RAMAN — Nobel laureate Physicist (Raman Effect). NOTABLE RECIPIENTS (select): (4) DR BHAGWAN DAS (1955). (5) MOKSHAGUNDAM VISVESVARAYA (1955, engineer). (6) PANDIT GOVIND BALLABH PANT (1957). (7) PANDIT JAWAHARLAL NEHRU (1955, while PM — self-recommendation controversial). (8) DR RAJENDRA PRASAD (1962, as President). (9) MOTHER TERESA (1980, Nobel Peace laureate). (10) INDIRA GANDHI (1971, as PM). (11) M.G. RAMACHANDRAN (1988, TN CM + actor). (12) Dr. B.R. AMBEDKAR (1990 posthumous). (13) NELSON MANDELA (1990 — 2nd non-Indian after Abdul Ghaffar Khan 1987). (14) RAJIV GANDHI (1991 posthumous). (15) Sardar VALLABHBHAI PATEL (1991 posthumous). (16) Maulana ABUL KALAM AZAD (1992 posthumous). (17) J.R.D. TATA (1992). (18) SATYAJIT RAY (1992, filmmaker). (19) A.P.J. ABDUL KALAM (1997 — before becoming President). (20) AMARTYA SEN (1999, Nobel Economics). (21) RAVI SHANKAR (1999, sitar maestro). (22) LATA MANGESHKAR (2001, 'Nightingale of India'). (23) BHIMSEN JOSHI (2008, Hindustani vocalist). (24) Prof. C.N.R. RAO (2014, chemist). (25) SACHIN TENDULKAR (2014 — FIRST sportsperson + youngest at 40). (26) ATAL BIHARI VAJPAYEE (2015). (27) MADAN MOHAN MALAVIYA (2015 posthumous). (28) PRANAB MUKHERJEE (2019, ex-President). (29) NANAJI DESHMUKH (2019 posthumous). (30) Dr BHUPEN HAZARIKA (2019 posthumous). (31) P.V. NARASIMHA RAO (2024 posthumous). (32) CHAUDHARY CHARAN SINGH (2024 posthumous). (33) M.S. SWAMINATHAN (2024 posthumous, Green Revolution father). (34) L.K. ADVANI (2024, BJP veteran, still living — among rare). (35) KARPOORI THAKUR (2024 posthumous, Bihar socialist CM). LATEST year had RECORD 5 awards (unusual). NON-INDIAN recipients: KHAN ABDUL GHAFFAR KHAN 'Frontier Gandhi' (Pakistan, 1987) + NELSON MANDELA (1990). The FIRST Bharat Ratna recipient was:

(A) Jawaharlal Nehru
(B) Dr SARVEPALLI RADHAKRISHNAN (1954) — philosopher-statesman; 2nd President of India (1962-67); Teachers' Day 5 Sep = his birthday
(C) Mahatma Gandhi (posthumous)
(D) B.R. Ambedkar (posthumous)
cards.back:
(B) Dr SARVEPALLI RADHAKRISHNAN (1954) — philosopher-statesman; 2nd President of India (1962-67); Teachers' Day 5 Sep = his birthday

Awards & Honours — Dr. SARVEPALLI RADHAKRISHNAN (5 Sep 1888 – 17 Apr 1975) — first recipient of Bharat Ratna (1954, along with CV Raman + Rajagopalachari). Indian philosopher, statesman, second PRESIDENT of India. BIRTH: Tiruttani, Madras Presidency (now TN); died Madras 1975. EDUCATION: Christian College Madras (MA Philosophy 1906-09 — influenced by missionary critique of Hinduism, responded to it). TEACHING: Assistant professor Madras Presidency College 1909; moved to Mysore University + Calcutta University; Spalding Professor of Eastern Religions + Ethics at Oxford (1936-52) — first Indian in that chair. VICE CHANCELLOR of Andhra University (1931-36) + BHU (1939-48) + Chairman of University Education Commission (1948-49). Won great RESPECT in academic world. PHILOSOPHICAL WORKS: (1) 'THE PHILOSOPHY OF RABINDRANATH TAGORE' (1918). (2) 'THE REIGN OF RELIGION IN CONTEMPORARY PHILOSOPHY' (1920). (3) 'INDIAN PHILOSOPHY' (2 vols 1923-27). (4) 'THE HINDU VIEW OF LIFE' (1927 — Oxford Upton lectures). (5) 'AN IDEALIST VIEW OF LIFE' (1932 — Hibbert Lectures). (6) 'EASTERN RELIGIONS + WESTERN THOUGHT' (1939). (7) Translations: Bhagavad Gita (1948), Upanishads, Dhammapada, Brahmasutras. Championed modernised Advaita Vedanta. KEY IDEAS: Hinduism is tolerant + universal; Self-realization through intuition; religion + science complementary; emphasis on 'religious experience' over dogma; India as 'living laboratory' of religions. TRIBUTE by BERTRAND RUSSELL: 'It is an honour for philosophy that Radhakrishnan should have been Vice-President of India'. POLITICAL CAREER: (1) AMBASSADOR to USSR (1949-52) — Nehru's appointment despite not being politician; developed rapport with Stalin; praised Soviet anti-caste policies. (2) VICE-PRESIDENT of India (1952-62) + Chairman of Rajya Sabha. (3) PRESIDENT of INDIA (13 May 1962 – 13 May 1967) — SUCCEEDED Dr Rajendra Prasad. Second President. Oversaw 1962 Sino-Indian War + 1965 Indo-Pak War. Delivered celebrated Republic Day addresses. HONOURS: (1) BHARAT RATNA 1954 (first batch). (2) KNIGHTHOOD from British 1931 (never formally used title). (3) 27+ honorary doctorates. (4) Order of Merit (UK) 1963. TEACHERS' DAY on 5 September = his birthday — declared in 1962 when students asked to celebrate his birthday + he replied 'Instead of celebrating my birthday, it would be my proud privilege if September 5 is observed as Teachers' Day'. DIED 17 April 1975 in Madras. RADHAKRISHNAN legacy: ideal scholar-statesman; bridged Indian + Western thought; presented Hinduism to the West as a rational religion. FAMOUS quote: 'Teachers should be the best minds of the country'. Wrote philosophically + with grace; his 1929 Hibbert Lecture 'An Idealist View of Life' is considered a classic.

cards.front:
The HIERARCHY of Indian CIVILIAN AWARDS (highest to lowest) is:

(A) Padma Shri → Padma Bhushan → Padma Vibhushan → Bharat Ratna
(B) BHARAT RATNA → PADMA VIBHUSHAN → PADMA BHUSHAN → PADMA SHRI
(C) Arjuna Award → Dronacharya → Khel Ratna → Bharat Ratna
(D) Param Vir Chakra → Ashok Chakra → Vir Chakra
cards.back:
(B) BHARAT RATNA → PADMA VIBHUSHAN → PADMA BHUSHAN → PADMA SHRI

Awards & Honours — INDIA's CIVILIAN AWARD HIERARCHY (highest to lowest, per Order of Precedence): (1) BHARAT RATNA (1954) — HIGHEST. 'Ornate pipal leaf'. 'Exceptional service of highest order'. (2) PADMA VIBHUSHAN (1954) — 2nd highest. 'Exceptional + distinguished service' in any field. 'Lotus' design. (3) PADMA BHUSHAN (1954) — 3rd highest. 'Distinguished service of a high order'. (4) PADMA SHRI (1954) — 4th highest. 'Distinguished service' in any field. COLLECTIVELY, the three Padma awards = 'PADMA AWARDS'. All instituted 2 Jan 1954 (along with Bharat Ratna, by President Rajendra Prasad). AWARD PROCESS: (1) Any CITIZEN can NOMINATE any deserving person via online PadmaAwards.gov.in portal or Rashtrapati Bhavan. (2) Nominations scrutinised by PADMA AWARDS COMMITTEE (constituted annually under Home Ministry; chaired by Cabinet Secretary; members = Home Secretary + Secretary to President + 4-6 eminent persons). (3) Committee recommends to PM + PRESIDENT. (4) President APPROVES. (5) ANNOUNCED on REPUBLIC DAY EVE (25 Jan); presented at RASHTRAPATI BHAVAN Durbar Hall in March-April by PRESIDENT. ANNUAL NUMBERS: max ~120 Padma Awards (incl. Vibhushan + Bhushan + Shri) per year. Padma Vibhushan: 5-7 typically; Bhushan: 20-30; Shri: 80-100. No posthumous Padma for persons who died >3 years prior (SPECIAL cases can be exceptions). Cannot be refused publicly without renouncing — e.g., BAUL SINGER SUBODHCHANDRA NAYAK, PATRIOT PROF. C.N.R. RAO's son, SITARA DEVI (declined 2002 Padma Bhushan — felt she deserved Bharat Ratna or higher), historian ROMILA THAPAR (refused Padma Bhushan 1992, 2005). UNIQUE FEATURES: Padma awards are NOT TITLES (per Art 18) — cannot prefix names. No monetary benefit. BENEFITS: prestige + some ceremonial rights + state protocol. CASH prizes come only with some specific fields (e.g., Jnanpith — literature). MILITARY GALLANTRY AWARDS — separate hierarchy: (1) PARAM VIR CHAKRA (PVC) — highest wartime. (2) MAHA VIR CHAKRA (MVC). (3) VIR CHAKRA (VrC). PEACETIME: (1) ASHOK CHAKRA (AC) — highest peacetime. (2) KIRTI CHAKRA (KC). (3) SHAURYA CHAKRA (SC). FORCE-specific: (4) PARAM VISHISHT SEVA MEDAL (PVSM) — distinguished service. (5) AVSM (Ati Vishisht Seva Medal). (6) VSM (Vishisht Seva Medal). PRESIDENT'S POLICE MEDAL + Police Medal for Gallantry + Distinguished Service. SPORTS AWARDS: (1) MAJOR DHYAN CHAND KHEL RATNA (ex-Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna) — highest sport award; renamed 2021. (2) ARJUNA AWARD. (3) DRONACHARYA AWARD (coaches). (4) DHYAN CHAND AWARD (lifetime contribution). LITERARY: (1) JNANPITH AWARD — highest Indian literary award (est. 1961 by Sahu Shanti Prasad Jain Bharatiya Jnanpith foundation); 1.1M + bronze Saraswati. (2) SAHITYA AKADEMI AWARD (annual, per language, 24 languages). FILM: DADASAHEB PHALKE AWARD (highest film, since 1969, for lifetime contribution — given at National Film Awards). (DPA): Devika Rani (1969 first), recent Waheeda Rehman (2023). NATIONAL FILM AWARDS — annual; established 1954.

The FIRST sportsperson to receive BHARAT RATNA (2014) was:

(A) Major Dhyan Chand
(B) SACHIN TENDULKAR
(C) Kapil Dev
(D) Sunil Gavaskar
cards.back:
(B) SACHIN TENDULKAR

Awards & Honours — SACHIN RAMESH TENDULKAR (b. 24 April 1973) — 'GOD OF CRICKET'; 'Little Master'; arguably CRICKET's GREATEST BATSMAN. FIRST SPORTSPERSON to receive BHARAT RATNA — announced 16 NOVEMBER 2013 (the very day he RETIRED from international cricket after his 200th Test at Wankhede). Medal received 4 February 2014 from President Pranab Mukherjee. At 40 years = YOUNGEST Bharat Ratna recipient ever. Prior minimum age for civilian honours was often higher. The rule was AMENDED 2011 to include sports (previously sports had separate awards — Khel Ratna). CRICKET RECORDS: (1) Most INTERNATIONAL runs ever — 34,357 (across 664 matches; Tests + ODIs + T20s). (2) ONLY player with 100 INTERNATIONAL CENTURIES (51 Tests + 49 ODIs). (3) Most TEST runs — 15,921 in 200 Tests (record held till Virat Kohli's overtaking likely future). (4) Most ODI runs — 18,426 in 463 ODIs. (5) ONLY cricketer to score DOUBLE CENTURY in ODI — 200* vs South Africa at Gwalior, 24 Feb 2010. (6) Debut at 16 YEARS (15 Nov 1989 at Karachi vs Pakistan — youngest Indian Test debutant at 16 yrs 205 days). (7) First batsman to 10,000 + 12,000 + 14,000 + 15,000 Test runs. (8) Played in 6 WORLD CUPS (1992, 1996, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2011) — most by any cricketer. (9) WON 2011 WORLD CUP ('I have carried the nation for 21 years; today, the team carried me' — quote from teammates). FINAL Test match 14-16 Nov 2013 at Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai. Emotional farewell speech. TEAM INDIA won 2011 ICC World Cup at same Wankhede. OTHER HONOURS: Arjuna Award 1994, Padma Shri 1999, Khel Ratna 1997-98, Padma Vibhushan 2008, BHARAT RATNA 2014. Inducted into ICC Hall of Fame 2019. Rajya Sabha MP (2012-18, NOMINATED). OTHER SPORTING BHARAT RATNA: None (Sachin remains the ONLY sportsperson with BR as of 2025). 'GOD OF CRICKET' nickname by Matthew Hayden; Sir Don Bradman called Sachin 'the closest modern batsman to himself' (invited to his 90th birthday 1998). CHARITABLE: Sachin Tendulkar Foundation; Apnalaya (slum children); Wanted Dead or Alive for educating poor children. FAMOUS QUOTES: 'Cricket is my first love'; 'Play with a straight bat'; 'Chase your dreams'. MAJOR DHYAN CHAND — 'HOCKEY WIZARD' (1905-79) — 3 Olympic gold medals (1928, 1932, 1936); scored 400+ international goals. Awarded PADMA BHUSHAN 1956 (before Khel Ratna existed). Demands to posthumously award him Bharat Ratna still ongoing — birthday 29 Aug = NATIONAL SPORTS DAY since 2012; Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna renamed MAJOR DHYAN CHAND KHEL RATNA in Aug 2021. OTHER ICONIC Indian sportspersons: Kapil Dev (1983 WC captain), Sunil Gavaskar (first to 10,000 Test runs), Mahendra Singh Dhoni (3 ICC trophies captain — T20 2007, ODI 2011, CT 2013), Virat Kohli (modern great), Abhinav Bindra (first individual Olympic gold 2008 shooting), Neeraj Chopra (javelin gold Tokyo 2020, Paris silver 2024), P.V. Sindhu (badminton, Rio 2016 silver, Tokyo 2020 bronze), P.T. Usha, Milkha Singh, Viswanathan Anand (5x world chess champion 2000-13), Mary Kom (6x world boxing champ), Sania Mirza, Saina Nehwal, Bhaichung Bhutia (football), Leander Paes, Mahesh Bhupathi, Karnam Malleswari (weightlifting first woman Olympic medal 2000), Vijender Singh, Rani Rampal (hockey captain). 'God of Cricket'; 100 international centuries; announced 16 Nov 2013 (day of retirement); age 40 = YOUNGEST BR recipient.

(B) JNANPITH AWARD

Awards & Honours — JNANPITH AWARD — India's HIGHEST literary honour; one of the largest + most prestigious in world. INSTITUTED 1961 by BHARATIYA JNANPITH foundation (established 1944 by the JAIN BUSINESS FAMILY — Sahu Shanti Prasad Jain + Rama Jain). Only for literature in languages listed in 8TH SCHEDULE of Constitution + ENGLISH (added 2013). Awarded ANNUALLY (though some gaps). CURRENT MONETARY VALUE: ₹11 LAKH CASH + Vagdevi (Saraswati) bronze idol + citation. PROCESS: nominated + selected by JNANPITH SELECTION BOARD (chaired in past by poets + scholars of stature — currently by Pratibha Ray). FIRST RECIPIENT: G. SHANKARA KURUP (1965) — for 'Odakkuzhal' (Malayalam, 1950). 2nd: Tarashankar Bandyopadhyay (1966, Bengali). Notable RECIPIENTS: (a) RAMDHARI SINGH 'DINKAR' (1972, Hindi 'Urvashi'). (b) UR ANANTHAMURTHY (1994, Kannada). (c) MAHASWETA DEVI (1996, Bengali). (d) GIRISH KARNAD (1998, Kannada). (e) GURDIAL SINGH (1999, Punjabi). (f) INDIRA GOSWAMI (2000, Assamese). (g) RAJENDRA SHAH (2001, Gujarati). (h) JAYAKANTHAN (2002, Tamil). (i) VINDA KARANDIKAR (2003, Marathi). (j) K. AYYAPPA PANIKER (2004, Malayalam). (k) KUNWAR NARAYAN (2005, Hindi). cards.front:
INDIA's highest PEACETIME GALLANTRY AWARD is:

(A) Kirti Chakra
(B) ASHOK CHAKRA
(C) Shaurya Chakra
(D) Vir Chakra
cards.back:
(B) ASHOK CHAKRA

Awards & Honours — ASHOK CHAKRA — India's HIGHEST PEACETIME MILITARY GALLANTRY AWARD. Equivalent in peacetime to PARAM VIR CHAKRA (wartime). INSTITUTED 4 January 1952 as 'Ashoka Chakra Class I'; renamed 'Ashok Chakra' 1967. AWARDED for 'most conspicuous bravery or some act of daring or pre-eminent valour or self-sacrifice' OTHERWISE than in FACE of the ENEMY (i.e., not wartime front-line). Covers counter-terrorism, counter-insurgency operations, internal security, rescue/disaster operations. DESIGN: circular gold medallion with Ashoka Chakra engraved; green ribbon with 2 orange vertical stripes. AWARD PROCESS: recommended by unit commander → MHA's military awards committee → President approves. Often POSTHUMOUS. AWARDED: ~96 times till 2024; mostly POSTHUMOUS. NOTABLE RECIPIENTS: (1) NAIK NARBAHADUR THAPA (1952) — FIRST recipient; for rescuing drowning colleagues. (2) MAJOR D. SREERAM KUMAR (1965). (3) LT Col. N.J. NAIR (1988, Sri Lanka IPKF). (4) Captain MAHENDRA NATH MULLA (1971 — posthumous; drowned with INS Khukri rather than abandon crew). (5) MAJOR SANDEEP UNNIKRISHNAN (2008, NSG commando; died combating 26/11 Mumbai attack; posthumous; 'Ullasa + fearless' commander). (6) MAJOR MOHIT SHARMA (2009 posthumous, Kashmir CT ops). (7) HAVILDAR BACHITTAR SINGH (1952). (8) HAVILDAR HANGPAN DADA (2016 posthumous, Kashmir CT). (9) MAJOR PADMAPANI ACHARYA (earlier MVC; part of Kargil posthumous). (10) COLONEL SANTOSH BABU (2020 posthumous, GALWAN VALLEY clash 15-16 June 2020, commanded 16 Bihar; India's first combat death with China since 1975). (11) MAJOR BHOOPATI (EARLIER). (12) Flt Lt Shipra Majumdar (first woman AC?). (13) Various NSG + SPG + CRPF commandos. (14) LANCE HAV MOHAN NATH GOSWAMI (2016 posthumous). LATEST: Havildar (Sub retd.) Sanjay Kumar + Chief Constable Swapandeep Bannerjee (2024). ASHOK CHAKRA is followed by: (2) KIRTI CHAKRA (2nd highest peacetime). (3) SHAURYA CHAKRA (3rd highest peacetime). All 3 awarded for gallantry in non-war situations — counter-terrorism, insurgency, rescue. WARTIME gallantry (in face of enemy): (1) PARAM VIR CHAKRA (PVC, highest) — 21 awardees. (2) MAHA VIR CHAKRA (MVC). (3) VIR CHAKRA (VrC). INSTITUTED 26 Jan 1950; retrospective to 15 Aug 1947 (for Kashmir War). OTHER gallantry/service awards: Sena Medal (Army), Nao Sena Medal (Navy), Vayu Sena Medal (Air Force), Yudh Seva Medal, Sarvottam Yudh Seva, Uttam Yudh Seva. DISTINGUISHED SERVICE: Param Vishisht Seva Medal (PVSM), Ati Vishisht Seva Medal (AVSM), Vishisht Seva Medal (VSM). POLICE: President's Police Medal (PPM), Police Medal for Gallantry (PMG), Police Medal for Distinguished Service (PMD). PRESIDENT'S COLOURS — highest unit award; conferred on select regiments + squadrons. STATE POLICE specific awards. FIRE SERVICE / HOME GUARDS / CIVIL DEFENCE medals. BSF + CRPF + ITBP + CISF + Assam Rifles each have their own gallantry medals. equivalent to Param Vir Chakra (wartime); awarded for valour in non-war operations (counter-terrorism, counter-insurgency, peace).

cards.front:
The DADASAHEB PHALKE AWARD, India's highest FILM honour, was instituted in 1969. It is named after:

(A) First Indian Oscar winner
(B) DHUNDIRAJ GOVIND PHALKE (1870-1944)
(C) First Bollywood producer
(D) Satyajit Ray
cards.back:
(B) DHUNDIRAJ GOVIND PHALKE (1870-1944)

Awards & Honours — DADASAHEB PHALKE AWARD — India's highest FILM honour; presented annually at the NATIONAL FILM AWARDS ceremony by PRESIDENT. Instituted 1969 by Government of India to commemorate DHUNDIRAJ GOVIND PHALKE's contribution to Indian Cinema. AWARDED for 'outstanding contribution to the growth + development of Indian cinema' — LIFETIME achievement basis. DADASAHEB PHALKE (30 Apr 1870 – 16 Feb 1944) — 'FATHER OF INDIAN CINEMA' / 'PITAMAHA of Indian cinema'. Born Maharashtra (Trimbak, Nashik). Raised in Brahmin family; cultural background (sculpture, photography). Attended J.J. School of Art Mumbai; trained in photography + LITHOGRAPHY. SET UP printing press; various ventures. Deeply moved by 'LIFE OF CHRIST' film (1910 Christmas Bombay screening); decided to make first Indian feature. Sold house + borrowed money; bought camera + film equipment from Britain. MADE 'RAJA HARISHCHANDRA' (1913) — INDIA's FIRST FULL-LENGTH FEATURE FILM (silent, 40 minutes). Shot on black + white; cast of all-MALE actors (including for female roles — women actors not yet accepted in mainstream; earlier cinema acts could only use men for female roles per convention). Released 3 May 1913 at Coronation Cinematograph Bombay (first commercial screening 21 April 1913 at Olympia Theatre; public 3 May). First 'swadeshi' film. Launched HINDUSTAN FILM COMPANY at Nashik — produced 27 films in next 15 years (all silent era). Notable: Mohini Bhasmasur (1913), Satyavan Savitri, Lanka Dahan (1917 — massive hit), Shri Krishna Janma, Kaliya Mardan (1919). Phalke went BANKRUPT; died poverty 1944. AWARD RECIPIENTS (select, cash ₹10 lakh + Swarna Kamal gold lotus medallion + shawl): (1) DEVIKA RANI (1969) — FIRST recipient; 'First Lady of Indian Cinema'. (2) Birendranath Sircar (1970). (3) PRITHVIRAJ KAPOOR posthumous (1971). (4) Pankaj Mullick (1972). (5) Sulochana Devi (1973). (6) B.N. Reddi (1974). (7) Dhiren Ganguly (1975). (8) K. Subrahmanyam (1980). (9) DIRECTOR/FILMMAKERS: Satyajit Ray (1984), V. Shantaram (1985), Hrishikesh Mukherjee (1999), B.R. Chopra (2001), Adoor Gopalakrishnan (2004), MRINAL SEN (2005), Tapan Sinha (2006), K. Balachander (2010), Soumitra Chatterjee (2012), RAMOJI RAO (2009). (10) ACTORS: ASHOK KUMAR (1988), Raj Kapoor (1987), DILIP KUMAR (1994), DEV ANAND (2002), SHYAM BENEGAL (2019), K. Viswanath (2016), SHATRUGHAN SINHA (2013), AMITABH BACHCHAN (2018). (11) MUSIC: NAUSHAD (1982), LATA MANGESHKAR (1989), ASHA BHOSLE (2000), A.R. RAHMAN — never Phalke (got Oscar + Bharat Ratna not Phalke). (12) COMPOSERS: SHANKAR-JAIKISHAN, MANNA DEY, MAHENDRA KAPOOR. (13) RECENT: REKHA (2023 at 2021 Ceremony), WAHEEDA REHMAN (2023 at 2023 ceremony — October), MITHUN CHAKRABORTY (2024, 70th NFA announced Aug 2024). NATIONAL FILM AWARDS est. 1954; Swarna + Rajat Kamals. FIRST PHALKE WINNER: DEVIKA RANI (1908-94) — actress-producer; founded Bombay Talkies; wife of Himanshu Rai + later S. Svetoslav Roerich. 'FATHER OF INDIAN CINEMA'; made India's first full-length feature 'Raja Harishchandra' (1913, silent).

cards.front:
India's NOBEL PRIZE laureates include (only Indian citizens):

(A) Only Tagore
(B) RABINDRANATH TAGORE (Lit 1913), C.V. RAMAN (Phy 1930), MOTHER TERESA (Peace 1979), AMARTYA SEN (Eco 1998), KAILASH SATYARTHI
(C) Over 20 laureates
(D) None
cards.back:
(B) RABINDRANATH TAGORE (Lit 1913), C.V. RAMAN (Phy 1930), MOTHER TERESA (Peace 1979), AMARTYA SEN (Eco 1998), KAILASH SATYARTHI

Awards & Honours — NOBEL LAUREATES of INDIAN ORIGIN — INDIAN CITIZENS AT TIME OF AWARD (5): (1) RABINDRANATH TAGORE (1861-1941) — LITERATURE 1913 — for 'GITANJALI' ('Song Offerings'); FIRST non-European Nobel in Literature; FIRST Asian Nobel in any field. Translated his Bengali poems into English himself + W.B. Yeats. Composed national anthems of India (Jana Gana Mana) + Bangladesh (Amar Sonar Bangla). Founded Santiniketan/Visva-Bharati. Renounced knighthood 1919 after Jallianwala. (2) Sir C.V. RAMAN (1888-1970) — PHYSICS 1930 — for DISCOVERY of RAMAN EFFECT (inelastic scattering of light); discovered 28 Feb 1928; Indian scientist in Calcutta at IACS. Later founded Raman Research Institute Bengaluru. 28 Feb = National Science Day. FIRST Asian Nobel in science. (3) MOTHER TERESA (1910-97) — PEACE 1979 — for humanitarian work with Missionaries of Charity (founded 1950 in Calcutta); Indian citizen since 1951 (naturalised); Albanian-born. Received Bharat Ratna 1980. Canonised as SAINT TERESA OF CALCUTTA 2016 by Pope Francis. (4) AMARTYA SEN (b. 1933) — ECONOMICS (formal: Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel) 1998 — for WELFARE ECONOMICS, capability approach, social choice theory, poverty measurement (Sen index), gender studies, human development. Bengali; Cambridge + Harvard professor. 'MOTHER OF CAPABILITY APPROACH'. Books: 'Poverty + Famines', 'Development as Freedom', 'The Idea of Justice', 'The Argumentative Indian'. Indian citizen. (5) KAILASH SATYARTHI (b. 1954) — PEACE 2014 (SHARED with Malala Yousafzai of Pakistan) — for struggle against child labour + for child rights; founded BBA (Bachpan Bachao Andolan) 1980; rescued 100,000+ children from bonded labour / trafficking; Global March Against Child Labour. INDIAN-ORIGIN LAUREATES with FOREIGN CITIZENSHIP at time of award: (a) HAR GOBIND KHORANA (1922-2011) — Medicine 1968 (with Nirenberg + Holley) — interpretation of genetic code + protein synthesis; Indian-American (born Punjab, Wisconsin-MIT later). (b) SUBRAHMANYAN CHANDRASEKHAR (1910-95) — Physics 1983 — Chandrasekhar limit (stellar evolution); Indian-American (MI-Bombay-Chicago). NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory named after him. Nephew of CV Raman. (c) V.S. NAIPAUL (1932-2018) — Literature 2001 — Trinidadian-born British; Indian origin. Novels on post-colonial identity. (d) VENKATRAMAN RAMAKRISHNAN (b. 1952) — Chemistry 2009 — ribosome structure; Indian-born American (Chidambaram TN → Ohio → Cambridge UK). Was president of Royal Society 2015-20. (e) ABHIJIT BANERJEE (b. 1961) — Economics 2019 (with Esther Duflo + Michael Kremer) — experimental approach to alleviating global poverty; Randomised Control Trials (RCTs); MIT prof, US citizen, Indian-origin, wife Duflo is co-awardee (2nd woman + youngest Eco Nobel). MANY OTHER Indian origin contributions: (a) PRANAB BARDHAN, JAGDISH BHAGWATI, GITA GOPINATH (IMF), RAGHURAM RAJAN — major economists, not Nobel (yet). (b) GOPI HINDURAO, C.N.R. RAO (world-class chemist, Bharat Ratna 2014) — world contributions. India UNDER-REPRESENTED in Nobels given its population + scientific potential — active discussion in policy + science circles. 5 native-born Nobel laureates as Indian citizens.

cards.front:
The RAMON MAGSAYSAY AWARD, often called 'ASIA's NOBEL PRIZE', is awarded by:

(A) Indian Government
(B) RAMON MAGSAYSAY AWARD FOUNDATION, Manila
(C) UN Asia-Pacific Office
(D) ASEAN
cards.back:
(B) RAMON MAGSAYSAY AWARD FOUNDATION, Manila

Awards & Honours — RAMON MAGSAYSAY AWARD — 'Asia's NOBEL PRIZE'. ESTABLISHED April 1957 by RAMON MAGSAYSAY AWARD FOUNDATION (Manila) in memory of late Philippine President RAMON MAGSAYSAY (1907-1957, killed in plane crash at age 49; known as 'Champion of the Masses', anti-Huk insurgency leader, simple + populist; 3rd President of Philippines 1953-57). cards.front:
Rule for BHARAT RATNA — maximum number of recipients per year (conventionally):

(A) 10
(B) 3 (though not strictly binding)
(C) Unlimited
(D) 50
cards.back:
(B) 3 (though not strictly binding)

Awards & Honours — BHARAT RATNA — PER-YEAR LIMIT: 3 per year (conventionally, per original notification 1954). Sometimes this convention is relaxed: (a) 2024 had 5 AWARDEES (post-facto for various years' delayed decisions). 4 on 9 Feb 2024 + 1 more (MS Swaminathan + Narasimha Rao + Charan Singh + Karpoori Thakur on 23 Jan 2024 had been announced). Advani announced 3 February. (b) 1999 had 4 awardees (JRD Tata, Satyajit Ray, M. Vishvesvaraya were earlier — this was unusual). TOTAL RECIPIENTS till 2024: 53 persons. 2024 alone: FIVE recipients announced. YEARS WITH NO BHARAT RATNA — several years (e.g., 1956, 1959, 1960, 1964, 1967-70, 1972-74, 1976-79, 1981-82, 1984-86, 1989, 1993, 1996, 2000-2007 except 2001, 2009, 2010-13, 2017, 2020-22). Awards clustered in certain years. POSTHUMOUS — recently almost all have been posthumous — 9 of last 12 (2015-2024). OLDEST AT RECEIVING: D. DEVARAJ URS (1976)? MS SUBBULAKSHMI was 82; PRANAB MUKHERJEE was 83. YOUNGEST AT RECEIVING: Sachin Tendulkar at 40 (2014); Indira Gandhi at 54 (1971); Rajiv Gandhi at 47 (1991 posthumous). INDIAN PRESIDENTS who received Bharat Ratna (in chronological order): RAJENDRA PRASAD (1962, post-presidency 1950-62), S. RADHAKRISHNAN (1954, pre- + during VP-days), Dr ZAKIR HUSSAIN (1963, before becoming President 1967-69), V.V. GIRI (1975, post), INDIRA GANDHI (1971, during PM), A.P.J. ABDUL KALAM (1997, before becoming Pres 2002-07), PRANAB MUKHERJEE (2019, post-presidency 2012-17). Future PM or PRES ASPIRANTS wait. PM/CM RECIPIENTS: Nehru (1955, while PM), Indira Gandhi (1971 while PM), MGR (1988, TN CM), Rajiv Gandhi (1991 posthumous), Atal Bihari Vajpayee (2015), Narasimha Rao (2024 posthumous), Charan Singh (2024 posthumous), Karpoori Thakur (2024 posthumous). ALL PMs/PRES received if still alive post-retirement? NO — Manmohan Singh, Deve Gowda, Gujral, Chandra Shekhar, V.P. Singh etc. did not. Controversial. CONTROVERSIES / DEMANDS: (1) Jawaharlal Nehru gave himself Bharat Ratna 1955 (as PM recommending to President; widely criticised; many feel he should have waited or it should be given posthumously). Indira similarly 1971. Both controversies. (2) CHAUDHARY DEVI LAL refused Bharat Ratna. SUBHAS CHANDRA BOSE was OFFERED posthumous 1992 Bharat Ratna; family REFUSED unless proof of his death (still maintaining doubts); Government WITHDREW the offer. (3) DEMANDS for posthumous Bharat Ratna to: Major Dhyan Chand (hockey), Ram Manohar Lohia, Kanshi Ram, Mulayam, E. Sreedharan, Maharshi Dayanand, Subrahmanya Bharathi (declined), Rajiv Gandhi (got), Veer Savarkar (demand + opposition), Guru Gobind Singh etc. (4) 2024's FIVE awardees seen as POLITICAL gesture preceding Lok Sabha elections by critics (Advani BJP, Charan Singh Jats, Karpoori Thakur OBCs, Rao Telangana, Swaminathan farmers). BHARAT RATNA rules: (a) recommendation by PM to Pres. (b) Cannot be used as title (Art 18). (c) No cash. (d) Certificate + Medal. (e) Posthumous OK. (f) 3 max convention. ORDER of PRECEDENCE: rank 7a (high official protocol). Rao, Charan Singh, Swaminathan, Advani, Karpoori Thakur. many years have NONE or 1-2 awardees; 2024 was unusual with 5 recipients.

(A) Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
(B) C. V. Raman
(C) Homi Bhabha
(D) Satyendra Nath Bose
cards.back:

Awards & Honours — Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering the Raman effect — inelastic scattering of light by molecules. 28 February (the day of his announcement, 1928) is India's National Science Day. S. Chandrasekhar (Raman's nephew, a naturalised US citizen) won Physics 1983 for work on stellar structure. S. N. Bose gave his name to bosons but never received a Nobel. Homi Bhabha led India's atomic programme but was never a laureate either.

(A) 1 October
(B) 10 December
(C) 10 November
(D) 21 October
cards.back:
(B) 10 December

Awards & Honours — Alfred Nobel died on 10 December 1896. The Nobel awards are formally presented every year on 10 December in Stockholm (all prizes except Peace) and Oslo (Peace Prize). Nobel himself invented dynamite; the prizes were set up in his will. The Prize in Economic Sciences (in memory of Alfred Nobel) was added in 1969 by the Swedish central bank — strictly speaking it is not one of Nobel's own five prizes.

Har Gobind Khorana won the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on:

(A) Blood-group classification
(B) The genetic code
(C) Vaccines
(D) Antibiotics
cards.back:
(B) The genetic code

Awards & Honours — Har Gobind Khorana (Indian-American) shared the 1968 Nobel with Robert Holley and Marshall Nirenberg for deciphering the genetic code — how DNA triplets (codons) specify the 20 amino acids of proteins. cards.front:
The NOBEL PRIZE was instituted in the WILL of Swedish industrialist ALFRED NOBEL, inventor of:

(A) Gunpowder
(B) DYNAMITE
(C) The telephone
(D) The diesel engine
cards.back:
(B) DYNAMITE

Awards & Honours — ALFRED BERNHARD NOBEL (1833-1896) — Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman; best known for INVENTING DYNAMITE (patented 1867) — a safer formulation of NITROGLYCERIN (a violently unstable liquid explosive discovered by Italian Sobrero, 1847) absorbed onto DIATOMACEOUS EARTH (kieselguhr), making it stable enough to transport + use in construction, mining, tunnelling, demolition. BUSINESS: founded BOFORS (armaments firm, Sweden) + 90 factories in 20 countries; developed ballistite (smokeless powder). Personal tragedy: his brother Emil was killed in a nitroglycerin explosion at Nobel's factory (1864), which spurred him to make it safer. WILL: Drafted on 27 November 1895, a year before his death. When he died in San Remo, Italy, 10 December 1896 (age 63), no direct heirs; 94% of his assets were directed to fund FIVE PRIZES for those who had ‘conferred the greatest benefit on mankind’. Why? Legend: In 1888, his brother Ludvig died; a French newspaper erroneously wrote an obituary of Alfred titled ‘Le marchand de la mort est mort’ (‘The merchant of death is dead’), criticising him for his inventions. Shocked at how he would be remembered, he determined to reshape his legacy — hence the PEACE prize and the others. THE ORIGINAL FIVE NOBEL PRIZES (first awarded 1901): (1) PHYSICS — awarded by Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences; (2) CHEMISTRY — same; (3) PHYSIOLOGY OR MEDICINE — Karolinska Institute; (4) LITERATURE — Swedish Academy; (5) PEACE — Norwegian Nobel Committee (at the time Sweden + Norway were in union; after 1905 separation, Norway retained this role per Nobel's will). SIXTH PRIZE — NOBEL MEMORIAL PRIZE IN ECONOMIC SCIENCES, instituted 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank (Swedish Central Bank) in memory of Nobel, on its 300th anniversary; FIRST AWARDED 1969 (to Ragnar Frisch + Jan Tinbergen). TECHNICALLY not a Nobel Prize per se but administered identically. PRIZE CEREMONY: annually on 10 DECEMBER (Nobel's death anniversary) — Peace Prize in OSLO, others in STOCKHOLM. Each laureate receives a gold medal + diploma + cash award (currently ~11 million Swedish Kronor, ~$1 million). Max 3 laureates per prize per year. Prize can NOT be awarded posthumously (rule since 1974), EXCEPT if laureate dies between announcement + ceremony; ONE exception (Ralph Steinman, Medicine 2011 — died 3 days before announcement, committee didn't know, decision stood). patented 1867; a safe-to-handle formulation of nitroglycerin absorbed on diatomaceous earth; Nobel's will (1895) set aside his fortune (~$265 mn in 2024 $) to endow the Prizes.

cards.front:
The FIRST INDIAN to win a NOBEL PRIZE was:

(A) Mahatma Gandhi (nominated 5 times, never won)
(B) RABINDRANATH TAGORE — NOBEL PRIZE IN LITERATURE 1913, for his work ‘GITANJALI’ (Song Offerings) — also the first NON-EUROPEAN to win this prize
(C) C.V. Raman (Physics 1930)
(D) Mother Teresa (Peace 1979)
cards.back:
(B) RABINDRANATH TAGORE — NOBEL PRIZE IN LITERATURE 1913, for his work ‘GITANJALI’ (Song Offerings) — also the first NON-EUROPEAN to win this prize

Awards & Honours — RABINDRANATH TAGORE (1861-1941) — Bengali polymath; poet, philosopher, musician, painter, educationist, novelist, playwright, social reformer. WON the NOBEL PRIZE IN LITERATURE 1913 — ‘because of his profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse, by which, with consummate skill, he has made his poetic thought, expressed in his own English words, a part of the literature of the West’. FIRST INDIAN + FIRST NON-EUROPEAN + FIRST ASIAN to win the Nobel Prize. Awarded for his work ‘GITANJALI’ (Song Offerings) — English translation (by himself) of his Bengali devotional poems, published 1910-12 in Bengali, 1912 in English with an introduction by W.B. YEATS. OTHER ACHIEVEMENTS of Tagore: (1) Founded SHANTINIKETAN (1901, in Bolpur, Birbhum district, West Bengal) — experimental school emphasizing open-air learning, synthesis of East-West; grew into VISHVA-BHARATI UNIVERSITY (1921, central university since 1951). (2) Composed INDIA'S NATIONAL ANTHEM ‘JANA GANA MANA’ (first sung 1911, Calcutta Congress session; adopted 24 Jan 1950). (3) Composed BANGLADESH'S NATIONAL ANTHEM ‘AMAR SHONAR BANGLA’ (1905, during Bengal partition protest; adopted 1971). (4) Influenced SRI LANKA'S national anthem ‘Sri Lanka Matha’ (written by his student Ananda Samarakoon). (5) RETURNED KNIGHTHOOD (‘Sir’, given by British 1915) in 1919 to PROTEST the JALLIANWALA BAGH MASSACRE. (6) Travelled extensively — friendship with Einstein (famous dialogue on science + mysticism), Yeats, Ezra Pound, Gandhi (called Tagore ‘Gurudev’). (7) KEY WORKS: Poetry — Gitanjali, Gitimalya, Balaka, Puravi, Sanchaita. Novels — Chokher Bali, Gora, Ghare Baire (The Home and The World — film by Satyajit Ray 1984), Chaturanga, Shesher Kobita. Drama — Dak Ghar, Raja, Muktadhara, Rakta Karabi. Short stories — Kabuliwallah, Postmaster. Essays — Sadhana, Creative Unity, Personality. (8) RABINDRA SANGEET — 2,000+ songs; a distinct musical tradition. (9) PAINTER — began at 60, over 2,000 works, modernist style. (10) JAMINI ROY, NANDALAL BOSE were among his students. INDIAN / INDIAN-ORIGIN NOBEL LAUREATES to date (chronological): (1) TAGORE — Literature 1913; (2) C.V. RAMAN — Physics 1930 (Raman effect, scattering of light — only Indian Physics Nobel); (3) HARGOBIND KHORANA — Medicine 1968 (genetic code/RNA synthesis — Indian-born, US citizen); (4) MOTHER TERESA — Peace 1979 (humanitarian work in Kolkata — born in Albania, Indian citizen); (5) SUBRAHMANYAN CHANDRASEKHAR — Physics 1983 (stellar structure, Chandrasekhar limit — nephew of CV Raman, Indian-born US citizen); (6) AMARTYA SEN — Economics 1998 (welfare economics, famines — born Bengal, mostly UK); (7) V. RAMAKRISHNAN — Chemistry 2009 (ribosome structure — born TN, US+UK citizen); (8) KAILASH SATYARTHI — Peace 2014 (with Malala Yousafzai, children's rights, Bachpan Bachao Andolan); (9) ABHIJIT VINAYAK BANERJEE — Economics 2019 (with Esther Duflo + Michael Kremer, poverty alleviation experimental approach — Indian-American). So, TWO resident-Indian-citizen Nobels: C.V. Raman, Kailash Satyarthi; others were Indian-born naturalised citizens of other countries.

cards.front:
C.V. RAMAN won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for:

(A) Discovery of X-rays
(B) Theory of relativity
(C) DISCOVERY of the RAMAN EFFECT
(D) Splitting of the atom
cards.back:
(C) DISCOVERY of the RAMAN EFFECT

Awards & Honours — SIR CHANDRASEKHARA VENKATA RAMAN (1888-1970) — Indian physicist; born Tiruchirappalli, TN; FIRST ASIAN + first NON-WHITE to win Nobel Prize in a SCIENCE discipline. NOBEL PRIZE IN PHYSICS 1930 — ‘for his work on the SCATTERING OF LIGHT and for the discovery of the effect named after him’. THE RAMAN EFFECT — discovered on 28 FEBRUARY 1928 at Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS), Calcutta/Kolkata. DAY celebrated as NATIONAL SCIENCE DAY in India. DESCRIPTION: when monochromatic light passes through a transparent medium (gas, liquid, or solid), a TINY FRACTION (~1 in a million photons) of the scattered light has a DIFFERENT WAVELENGTH from the incident light — due to INELASTIC scattering in which the photon exchanges energy with the molecule's VIBRATIONAL or ROTATIONAL modes. The shifted wavelengths (Stokes + anti-Stokes lines) form the ‘RAMAN SPECTRUM’, unique to each molecule — like a molecular FINGERPRINT. Applications: (1) CHEMICAL ANALYSIS — identify substances non-destructively; (2) MATERIALS SCIENCE — graphene, semiconductor quality; (3) PHARMACEUTICALS — purity, counterfeit detection; (4) ART CONSERVATION — pigment identification; (5) SECURITY SCREENING — detect explosives/narcotics; (6) EARTH + PLANETARY SCIENCES — MARS rovers (Perseverance has SHERLOC instrument using Raman); (7) MEDICAL DIAGNOSTICS — tumour identification. CONTEXT OF DISCOVERY: Raman, returning by ship from London in 1921, was intrigued by the BLUE OF THE MEDITERRANEAN; Lord Rayleigh's explanation of blue sky (Rayleigh scattering) didn't fully satisfy him regarding the sea — a different kind of scattering seemed involved. Back in Calcutta, he + K.S. Krishnan worked with meticulous spectroscopy on various liquids (benzene, etc.) and isolated the shifted lines in scattered light. Used merely a MERCURY ARC LAMP + PRISM + SPECTROSCOPE — a triumph of Indian indigenous science with modest equipment. Simultaneously + independently, Soviet scientists LANDSBERG + MANDELSTAM discovered the same in 1928 in crystals, but Raman's publication was earlier (31 March 1928, Nature journal). HONORS: Knighthood (Sir, 1929); BHARAT RATNA (1954 — the FIRST awarded, along with Rajaji + Radhakrishnan); Lenin Peace Prize (1957). FOUNDED: Indian Academy of Sciences (Bengaluru, 1934); Raman Research Institute (Bengaluru, 1948). STUDENTS: S. CHANDRASEKHAR (nephew, Nobel 1983 — stellar structure, black holes), HOMI BHABHA (father of Indian atomic programme, though not a direct PhD student — met at Raman's institute). KEY LESSON: Raman rejected JOB OFFERS from UK/US; chose to do cutting-edge physics IN INDIA + with Indian institutional support — a symbol of Indian scientific self-reliance. the inelastic scattering of light by molecules, which reveals molecular vibrational modes; discovered 28 February 1928; announced in ‘Nature’ + ‘Indian Journal of Physics’.

cards.front:
The NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 2014 was shared by Kailash Satyarthi and:

(A) Greta Thunberg
(B) MALALA YOUSAFZAI
(C) Mother Teresa
(D) Aung San Suu Kyi
cards.back:
(B) MALALA YOUSAFZAI

Awards & Honours — NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 2014 — jointly awarded to KAILASH SATYARTHI (Indian, b. 11 Jan 1954, Vidisha, MP) and MALALA YOUSAFZAI (Pakistani, b. 12 July 1997, Mingora, Swat Valley) — ‘for their struggle against the suppression of children and young people and for the right of all children to education’. Malala (at 17) became the YOUNGEST-EVER NOBEL LAUREATE in any category. This joint award of an Indian + Pakistani — Hindu + Muslim — was SYMBOLIC, urging peace across the subcontinent. KAILASH SATYARTHI: (1) Founded BACHPAN BACHAO ANDOLAN (BBA, ‘Save the Childhood Movement’) in 1980, rescuing children from bonded labour + trafficking in India; liberated >85,000 children. (2) Initiated GLOBAL MARCH AGAINST CHILD LABOUR (1998) — 80,000-km march across 103 countries — led to ILO Convention 182 on WORST FORMS OF CHILD LABOUR (1999, most rapidly ratified convention in ILO history). (3) RugMark (now GoodWeave) — certification of child-labour-free carpets. (4) Padma Shri awarded 2025 (not before; he had refused earlier honours while children were still in bondage, per one account). Several other Indian honours. (5) Post-Nobel: expanded to 100 Million for 100 Million Campaign (youth global action for marginalised children); Laureates & Leaders for Children; led Fair Share for Children Fund. MALALA YOUSAFZAI: (1) Daughter of education activist Ziauddin; blogged anonymously for BBC Urdu from age 11 about Taliban's ban on girls' schools in Swat valley. (2) Survived an assassination attempt by Taliban: on 9 OCT 2012, a Taliban gunman boarded her school bus and shot her in the head at close range. Airlifted first to Peshawar, then Birmingham UK for brain surgery. Miraculously survived + became a global symbol. (3) ‘I AM MALALA’ (2013, autobiography co-authored with Christina Lamb) — international bestseller, translated to many languages. (4) Founded MALALA FUND for girls' education worldwide. (5) Graduated from OXFORD (Lady Margaret Hall, PPE, 2020). (6) 2013 Sakharov Prize; 2013 Pakistani youth peace prize; UN honorary Messenger of Peace. MALALA DAY — 12 July (her birthday), declared by UN since 2013. OTHER famous PEACE NOBEL LAUREATES: Henri Dunant (1901, 1st — Red Cross founder), Theodore Roosevelt (1906, Russo-Japan peace), Albert Schweitzer (1952), Martin Luther King Jr (1964), Willy Brandt (1971, Ostpolitik), Dalai Lama (1989), Nelson Mandela + F.W. de Klerk (1993), Yitzhak Rabin + Shimon Peres + Yasser Arafat (1994, Oslo Accords), Aung San Suu Kyi (1991 — later controversial over Rohingya), Barack Obama (2009 — controversial), Muhammad Yunus + Grameen Bank (2006, microfinance), Mother Teresa (1979 — 1st India-based), AL Gore + IPCC (2007, climate). 2024: NIHON HIDANKYO (Japanese atomic bomb survivors org). 2025: MARIA CORINA MACHADO (Venezuelan opposition leader). Pakistani activist for girls' education; at 17, the YOUNGEST EVER Nobel Laureate; shot by the Taliban in 2012 for advocating girls' schooling.

cards.front:
AMARTYA SEN won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences 1998 for his contributions to:

(A) Monetary theory
(B) WELFARE ECONOMICS
(C) Game theory
(D) Behavioural finance
cards.back:
(B) WELFARE ECONOMICS

Awards & Honours — AMARTYA KUMAR SEN (b. 3 Nov 1933, Santiniketan, West Bengal) — Indian economist-philosopher. NOBEL PRIZE IN ECONOMIC SCIENCES 1998 ‘for his contributions to WELFARE ECONOMICS’ — specifically (1) SOCIAL CHOICE THEORY (axiomatic analysis of collective decision-making), (2) POVERTY + INEQUALITY INDICES (Sen index for poverty), (3) CAPABILITY APPROACH (human well-being measured by what people can DO and BE — capabilities — not just income), (4) analysis of famines demolishing myths. Sen was the FIRST ASIAN Nobel laureate in Economics. KEY CONTRIBUTIONS: (1) ‘POVERTY AND FAMINES: AN ESSAY ON ENTITLEMENT AND DEPRIVATION’ (1981) — LANDMARK book showing that famines are NOT caused solely by drops in food availability. The 1943 BENGAL FAMINE killed ~3 million Indians even though food output was HIGHER than in non-famine years; the problem was collapse of ENTITLEMENTS of certain groups (fishermen, weavers, peasant labourers) — inability to command food due to inflation, lack of work, administrative failures. FAMINE in a democracy — Sen argued — doesn't happen because free press + elections force action; ‘no famine has ever occurred in a functioning democracy’ (with free press). (2) ‘SOCIAL CHOICE THEORY’ — built on Kenneth Arrow's impossibility theorem; Sen's 1970 book ‘COLLECTIVE CHOICE AND SOCIAL WELFARE’ (expanded edition 2017). Developed Sen-Debreu criterion, Arrow-Sen theorem. (3) CAPABILITY APPROACH — co-developed with Martha Nussbaum; emphasises freedom to achieve well-being rather than utility/income alone; influenced HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI, UNDP 1990) that Sen co-designed with PAKISTANI ECONOMIST MAHBUB UL HAQ. HDI has 3 components: (a) Life expectancy, (b) Education (mean + expected years of schooling), (c) GNI per capita. (4) ‘THE ARGUMENTATIVE INDIAN’ (2005), ‘IDEA OF JUSTICE’ (2009) — philosophical books; argues for pluralistic tradition in India; departs from Rawls's justice-as-fairness in favour of comparative justice. LIFE: Born in Santiniketan founded by his grandfather's friend TAGORE; name ‘Amartya’ given by Tagore himself. Witness to 1943 Bengal famine as a child — shaped his life's work. Schooling at Shantiniketan's Patha Bhavana; BA Presidency College Calcutta; PhD from Trinity College, Cambridge. Taught at Delhi School of Economics, Trinity College Cambridge (Master 1998-2004), All Souls Oxford, LSE, Harvard. Currently Thomas W. Lamont University Professor, Harvard. AWARDS: BHARAT RATNA (1999); Padma Vibhushan; Padma Bhushan; National Humanities Medal (US 2011). Three wives including historian Emma Rothschild. CRITIQUES on policy: argued against Bangladesh-India-Pakistan spending too much on military; supported UPA's MGNREGA + Right to Food Act. PROBIR CHAKRAVARTY, JEAN DRÈZE (Belgian-Indian, long-time collaborator) — joint books: INDIA: ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND SOCIAL OPPORTUNITY (1995), AN UNCERTAIN GLORY: INDIA AND ITS CONTRADICTIONS (2013). NOBEL PRIZE IN ECONOMIC SCIENCES 1998 ‘for his contributions to WELFARE ECONOMICS’ — specifically (1) SOCIAL CHOICE THEORY (axiomatic analysis of collective decision-making), (2) POVERTY + INEQUALITY INDICES (Sen index for poverty), (3) CAPABILITY APPROACH (human well-being measured by what people can DO and BE — capabilities — not just income), (4) analysis of famines demolishing myths. Sen was the FIRST ASIAN Nobel laureate in Economics. KEY CONTRIBUTIONS: (1) ‘POVERTY AND FAMINES: AN ESSAY ON ENTITLEMENT AND DEPRIVATION’ (1981) — LANDMARK book showing that famines are NOT caused solely by drops in food availability. cards.front:
MOTHER TERESA was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in:

(A) 1975
(B) 1979
(C) 1983
(D) 1997 (year of her death)
cards.back:
(B) 1979

Awards & Honours — MOTHER TERESA (1910-1997) — born ANJEZË GONXHE BOJAXHIU in SKOPJE, NORTH MACEDONIA (then Ottoman Empire, later Yugoslavia); of ALBANIAN ethnicity. Entered the LORETO sisters (Irish Catholic order) at 18, arrived in DARJEELING 1929, took final vows 1937 as ‘Sister Teresa’ (after Thérèse of Lisieux). Taught at St. Mary's school, Kolkata (1931-48), rising to principal. 1946 CALL WITHIN A CALL: on train journey Kolkata to Darjeeling (10 Sept, celebrated annually as INSPIRATION DAY), she felt a divine calling to leave her convent and serve the poorest of the poor. Permission granted 1948 by Vatican. Trained as nurse in Patna (with Medical Mission Sisters); returned to Kolkata, began serving destitute in slums of Motijheel. 1950 — FOUNDED MISSIONARIES OF CHARITY (Kolkata), initially 12 members, now 5,500+ sisters in 139 countries. Iconic WHITE SARI with three BLUE STRIPES became order's uniform. Adopted INDIAN CITIZENSHIP in 1948. Opened NIRMAL HRIDAY (Home for the Dying Destitutes) at Kalighat 1952, NIRMALA SHISHU BHAVAN (children), SHANTI NAGAR (leprosarium, Asansol), SHISHU BHAVAN, Titagarh leprosy centre, homes for AIDS patients, orphans globally. AWARDS: (1) PADMA SHRI 1962; (2) Jawaharlal Nehru Award for International Understanding 1969; (3) POPE John XXIII Peace Prize 1971; (4) BHARAT RATNA 1980 (first NATURALISED INDIAN citizen to receive it); (5) NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 1979 (gave her prize money to the poor; refused the ceremonial Nobel banquet + asked them to donate the banquet cost to the poor, $192,000 raised). (6) PRESIDENTIAL MEDAL OF FREEDOM (USA, 1985); (7) HONORARY CITIZENSHIP of USA (1996, only 6 persons ever). BEATIFIED 2003 by Pope John Paul II — ‘BLESSED TERESA OF CALCUTTA’. CANONIZED (made Saint) 4 September 2016 by Pope Francis — ‘SAINT TERESA OF CALCUTTA’. Her FEAST DAY: 5 September (death date). DEATH: 5 September 1997, Kolkata, aged 87. State funeral; her body lies in the Motherhouse of Missionaries of Charity, 54A Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Road, Kolkata — a pilgrimage site. CRITICS: (a) Christopher Hitchens's book ‘The Missionary Position’ (1995) alleged inadequate medical care, religious proselytisation, questionable finances; (b) Questions raised about conditions in her homes. Supporters counter: she served the DESTITUTE REJECTED even by hospitals; aim was COMFORT, not sophisticated care; financial transparency improved post-Nobel. PUBLISHED: No autobiography; her letters (posthumously, ‘Come Be My Light’, 2007) revealed she experienced decades of SPIRITUAL DARKNESS (‘dark night of the soul’) while outwardly smiling + serving — a testament to faith despite doubt. QUOTES: ‘NOT ALL OF US CAN DO GREAT THINGS. BUT WE CAN DO SMALL THINGS WITH GREAT LOVE’; ‘BE FAITHFUL IN SMALL THINGS BECAUSE IT IS IN THEM THAT YOUR STRENGTH LIES’. ‘for her work undertaken in the struggle to overcome poverty and distress, which also constitutes a threat to peace’; founded MISSIONARIES OF CHARITY (1950, Kolkata).

cards.front:
The SCIENTIST who has won the Nobel Prize in both PHYSICS and CHEMISTRY is:

(A) Albert Einstein
(B) Marie Curie
(C) Max Planck
(D) Richard Feynman
cards.back:
(B) Marie Curie

Awards & Honours — MARIE CURIE (1867-1934) — Polish-born French physicist-chemist; born MARIA SKŁODOWSKA in Warsaw. HOLDS UNIQUE RECORDS: (1) FIRST WOMAN to win a Nobel Prize; (2) ONLY PERSON to win Nobel Prizes in TWO DIFFERENT SCIENCES (Physics + Chemistry); (3) FIRST FAMILY with multiple Nobels (husband Pierre, daughter Irène Joliot-Curie + Frédéric Joliot-Curie also won). NOBEL 1 — PHYSICS 1903 (shared with husband PIERRE CURIE + HENRI BECQUEREL) ‘in recognition of the extraordinary services they have rendered by their joint researches on the RADIATION phenomena discovered by Professor Henri Becquerel’. The term ‘RADIOACTIVITY’ was coined by Marie Curie. NOBEL 2 — CHEMISTRY 1911 ‘in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements RADIUM and POLONIUM, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element’. POLONIUM (discovered 1898) — named after POLAND, her homeland (a patriotic statement: Poland was partitioned at the time, not independent). RADIUM (discovered 1898). Curies PROCESSED TONNES of PITCHBLENDE (uranium ore) from a Bohemian mine to isolate a few DECIGRAMS of radium — in a dilapidated shed, using buckets of chemicals + stirring with an iron rod, often with bare hands. Unaware of radiation hazards (science was new), both Curies suffered from long-term radiation exposure; Marie died of APLASTIC ANAEMIA from radiation 1934. Her laboratory notebooks are STILL radioactive today, kept in lead-lined boxes. PIERRE CURIE (1859-1906) — French physicist; also known for discovering PIEZOELECTRICITY with his brother Jacques. Died tragically in 1906: slipped on wet road in Paris + crushed by horse-drawn wagon, age 46. WWI CONTRIBUTION: Marie Curie designed MOBILE RADIOLOGICAL UNITS (‘PETITES CURIES’) — 20 units for battlefield X-ray imaging, saved thousands of Allied soldiers' lives; trained 150 women operators. CURIE FAMILY HEIRLOOM: 5 Nobel Prizes across 3 generations: Marie + Pierre (Physics 1903), Marie (Chemistry 1911), daughter IRÈNE JOLIOT-CURIE + son-in-law FRÉDÉRIC JOLIOT (Chemistry 1935 — artificial radioactivity), + Henry Labouisse (Marie's son-in-law/grandson-in-law, received Peace Nobel 1965 on behalf of UNICEF). RESEARCH INSTITUTIONS: INSTITUT CURIE, Paris — still a leading cancer research centre. OTHERS who won 2 Nobels in SCIENCE: (1) JOHN BARDEEN (Physics 1956 + 1972; transistor + superconductivity — BCS theory). (2) LINUS PAULING (Chemistry 1954 for chemical bonding + Peace 1962 for nuclear test ban — ONLY person with 2 UNSHARED Nobels in different categories). (3) FREDERICK SANGER (Chemistry 1958 + 1980; protein sequencing + DNA sequencing — Sanger sequencing). (4) KARL BARRY SHARPLESS (Chemistry 2001 + 2022; chirally catalysed + click chemistry). That's 5 individuals with 2 Nobels; only Curie did it across different science fields. ORGANISATIONS: ICRC (Red Cross) — 3 Peace Nobels (1917, 1944, 1963); UNHCR — 2 (1954, 1981). Physics 1903 (radioactivity, with husband Pierre + Henri Becquerel) and Chemistry 1911 (for discovery of polonium + radium); FIRST WOMAN + FIRST PERSON to win 2 Nobels in SCIENCE.

cards.front:
EINSTEIN won the NOBEL PRIZE IN PHYSICS 1921 for:

(A) Special Theory of Relativity (E = mc²)
(B) General Theory of Relativity
(C) His services to THEORETICAL PHYSICS, especially for his DISCOVERY of the LAW OF THE PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT
(D) Brownian motion
cards.back:
(C) His services to THEORETICAL PHYSICS, especially for his DISCOVERY of the LAW OF THE PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT

Awards & Honours — ALBERT EINSTEIN (1879-1955) — German-Swiss-American physicist; perhaps the most iconic scientist of the 20th century. NOBEL PRIZE IN PHYSICS 1921 (awarded in 1922, as 1921 was initially withheld) — citation: ‘for his services to theoretical physics, and especially for his discovery of the LAW OF THE PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT’. Notably, the award DID NOT explicitly cite the THEORY OF RELATIVITY — because at the time, relativity was still CONTROVERSIAL + not yet definitively verified (GTR's prediction of light bending by Sun was only confirmed in the 1919 eclipse expedition; some still doubted). The photoelectric effect result (1905) was by then well-established. PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT — emission of ELECTRONS from a metal surface when light is shone on it. Before Einstein, this was unexplained: (1) classical wave theory predicted that the ENERGY of ejected electrons should depend on light INTENSITY (brighter → more energy); experiments showed energy depends on FREQUENCY (colour), not intensity; (2) there was a THRESHOLD FREQUENCY below which NO electrons were emitted, regardless of how bright; (3) electrons were emitted INSTANTANEOUSLY when light hit, even at very low intensities. EINSTEIN'S EXPLANATION (1905): light is not a continuous wave but consists of discrete PACKETS (QUANTA) of energy, which he called LICHTQUANT (light quanta; later renamed PHOTONS by G.N. Lewis, 1926). Each photon carries energy E = hν (Planck's constant × frequency). An electron absorbs ONE photon; if hν ≥ work function (threshold energy) of the metal, electron is ejected with kinetic energy KE = hν − Φ. Einstein's equation beautifully explained all 3 puzzles. Built on PLANCK's 1900 quantum hypothesis (for black body radiation) but explicitly stated light ITSELF is quantised. Confirmed by ROBERT MILLIKAN's experiments 1914-16 (Millikan won Nobel 1923 partly for this, + oil-drop electron charge). IMPACT: this paper + the CURIE/RUTHERFORD/BOHR work founded QUANTUM MECHANICS. Einstein remained conflicted — his paper started quantum, yet he was UNCOMFORTABLE with quantum randomness; famous quote: ‘GOD DOES NOT PLAY DICE WITH THE UNIVERSE’. Debated Niels Bohr about interpretations for decades (Copenhagen interpretation vs Einstein's hidden-variables). Bell's theorem (1964) + Aspect's experiments (1982, Nobel 2022) eventually supported Bohr's side. EINSTEIN'S 1905 ‘MIRACLE YEAR’ (ANNUS MIRABILIS) — while a PATENT CLERK in Bern, age 26, Einstein published FOUR REVOLUTIONARY PAPERS: (1) Photoelectric effect — cited for Nobel; (2) BROWNIAN MOTION — confirmed atomic-molecular theory of matter, provided method to count atoms (Avogadro's number); (3) SPECIAL RELATIVITY — time dilation, length contraction, relativity of simultaneity; (4) Mass-energy equivalence E = mc². All in one year, all from a patent clerk's desk, in his spare time. 1915 — published GENERAL RELATIVITY (gravity = spacetime curvature); confirmed by 1919 eclipse (Eddington expedition) — instantly made Einstein a global celebrity. OTHER CONTRIBUTIONS: Bose-Einstein statistics (with Satyendra Nath Bose, Indian physicist); condensed matter; cosmological constant (‘biggest blunder’, now revived for dark energy); EPR paradox (quantum entanglement). Later life: EMIGRATED to USA 1933 after Nazi rise; joined Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton; 1939 letter to FDR led to Manhattan Project (though Einstein himself didn't work on bomb); post-war advocate of nuclear disarmament + world govt; declined offer to be 2nd President of Israel (1952). Died 1955, aged 76, Princeton. which established the quantum/particle nature of light (photons).

cards.front:
The NOBEL PRIZE CEREMONY is held annually on DEC 10 (Nobel's death anniversary) in which TWO cities?

(A) Helsinki + Copenhagen
(B) STOCKHOLM (Sweden) for all prizes + OSLO (Norway) for the Peace Prize
(C) Stockholm + Copenhagen
(D) Stockholm + Helsinki
cards.back:
(B) STOCKHOLM (Sweden) for all prizes + OSLO (Norway) for the Peace Prize

Awards & Honours — NOBEL PRIZE CEREMONIES held annually on 10 DECEMBER (anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death, 1896) — IN TWO CITIES: (1) STOCKHOLM (Sweden) — for Physics, Chemistry, Physiology/Medicine, Literature, Economic Sciences (5 prizes); at STOCKHOLM CONCERT HALL (Konserthuset), followed by banquet at STOCKHOLM CITY HALL (Stadshuset) — 1,300 guests in the Blue Hall, served by servers in traditional livery. (2) OSLO (Norway) — for PEACE PRIZE only; at OSLO CITY HALL (Rådhus); attended by Norwegian Royal Family + PM + Storting. WHY TWO CITIES? At the time of Nobel's will (1895), Sweden and Norway were in a POLITICAL UNION (under the Swedish King, 1814-1905). Nobel specified that the PEACE PRIZE committee would be appointed by the NORWEGIAN STORTING (parliament), while the others by Swedish institutions — perhaps reflecting his belief that Norway was less militaristic + more peaceful, or perhaps to share the recognition across the union. After Norway's INDEPENDENCE in 1905, the arrangement continued, cementing this geographic split. FORMAL CEREMONY includes: (1) Laureates wear white tie + tails (men) or full-length evening gowns (women); (2) Presentation by Swedish/Norwegian Royal Family (currently King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden presents; Crown Prince Haakon of Norway for Peace); (3) Each laureate receives (a) a GOLD MEDAL (23-carat, weighs 175g, diameter 66 mm, depicting Nobel's profile on obverse with different scene on reverse for each prize), (b) a DIPLOMA (personalised artwork by Swedish artists), (c) a CASH AWARD. The CASH PRIZE (as of 2024): 11 million Swedish Kronor (~$1 million / ~₹8.3 crore) per prize category. If shared among multiple laureates, they split it. Not indexed to inflation routinely; adjusted by the Nobel Foundation based on returns on Nobel's bequest investments. Each laureate also delivers a NOBEL LECTURE (~45 min) in the days before/after the ceremony at a respective Swedish/Norwegian institution. Awards are ANNOUNCED in OCTOBER — typically Physiology/Medicine first (Monday), Physics (Tuesday), Chemistry (Wednesday), Literature (Thursday), Peace (Friday), Economic Sciences (next Monday). Announcements attract global media coverage. NOBEL FOUNDATION, Stockholm, manages the endowment (worth SEK ~5.5 billion in 2023). AWARDING INSTITUTIONS per will: (a) Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences — PHYSICS + CHEMISTRY + ECONOMIC SCIENCES (latter added 1968); (b) Karolinska Institute's Nobel Assembly — MEDICINE/PHYSIOLOGY; (c) Swedish Academy — LITERATURE; (d) Norwegian Nobel Committee (5 members appointed by Storting) — PEACE. NOMINATIONS: submitted by qualified persons (past laureates, professors, academy members, heads of state for Peace, etc.). Nomination process opens in Sept, closes Jan 31. NOMINATIONS kept SECRET for 50 YEARS. Candidate cannot nominate themselves. 2024 Nobel winners included: Peace to NIHON HIDANKYO; Physics to Hopfield+Hinton (AI); Chemistry to Baker+Hassabis+Jumper (AlphaFold+protein design); Medicine to Victor Ambros + Gary Ruvkun (microRNA); Literature to HAN KANG (first Korean woman); Economics to Daron Acemoglu + Simon Johnson + James Robinson (institutions + prosperity). a division specified in Alfred Nobel's will reflecting Sweden-Norway union at the time.

After Norway's INDEPENDENCE in 1905, the arrangement continued, cementing this geographic split. FORMAL CEREMONY includes: (1) Laureates wear white tie + tails (men) or full-length evening gowns (women); (2) Presentation by Swedish/Norwegian Royal Family (currently King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden presents; Crown Prince Haakon of Norway for Peace); (3) Each laureate receives (a) a GOLD MEDAL (23-carat, weighs 175g, diameter 66 mm, depicting Nobel's profile on obverse with different scene on reverse for each prize), (b) a DIPLOMA (personalised artwork by Swedish artists), (c) a CASH AWARD. The CASH PRIZE (as of 2024): 11 million Swedish Kronor (~$1 million / ~₹8.3 crore) per prize category. If shared among multiple laureates, they split it. Not indexed to inflation routinely; adjusted by the Nobel Foundation based on returns on Nobel's bequest investments. Each laureate also delivers a NOBEL LECTURE (~45 min) in the days before/after the ceremony at a respective Swedish/Norwegian institution. Awards are ANNOUNCED in OCTOBER — typically Physiology/Medicine first (Monday), Physics (Tuesday), Chemistry (Wednesday), Literature (Thursday), Peace (Friday), Economic Sciences (next Monday). Announcements attract global media coverage. NOBEL FOUNDATION, Stockholm, manages the endowment (worth SEK ~5.5 billion in 2023). AWARDING INSTITUTIONS per will: (a) Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences — PHYSICS + CHEMISTRY + ECONOMIC SCIENCES (latter added 1968); (b) Karolinska Institute's Nobel Assembly — MEDICINE/PHYSIOLOGY; (c) Swedish Academy — LITERATURE; (d) Norwegian Nobel Committee (5 members appointed by Storting) — PEACE. NOMINATIONS: submitted by qualified persons (past laureates, professors, academy members, heads of state for Peace, etc.). Nomination process opens in Sept, closes Jan 31. NOMINATIONS kept SECRET for 50 YEARS. Candidate cannot nominate themselves. 2024 Nobel winners included: Peace to NIHON HIDANKYO; Physics to Hopfield+Hinton (AI); Chemistry to Baker+Hassabis+Jumper (AlphaFold+protein design); Medicine to Victor Ambros + Gary Ruvkun (microRNA); Literature to HAN KANG (first Korean woman); Economics to Daron Acemoglu + Simon Johnson + James Robinson (institutions + prosperity). a division specified in Alfred Nobel's will reflecting Sweden-Norway union at the time.

cards.back:
(C) MALALA YOUSAFZAI — at age 17 years, 218 days, won NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 2014 (shared with Kailash Satyarthi)

Awards & Honours — MALALA YOUSAFZAI (b. 12 July 1997) — age 17 years, 218 days when awarded NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 2014 (jointly with Kailash Satyarthi, announced 10 Oct 2014; ceremony 10 Dec 2014, Oslo). YOUNGEST NOBEL LAUREATE EVER in any category. Previous record for youngest ANY category: (1) WILLIAM LAWRENCE BRAGG — won Physics Nobel 1915 at age 25 (jointly with his father W.H. Bragg, for X-ray crystallography of crystals — Bragg's law: nλ = 2d·sinθ). Youngest Physics laureate. (2) MAIRÉAD CORRIGAN — Peace Nobel 1976 at age 32 (Northern Ireland Peace). (3) TAWAKKOL KARMAN — Peace Nobel 2011 at age 32 (Yemeni activist, Arab Spring). Malala broke all these. YOUNGEST in other categories: (1) PHYSICS — Lawrence Bragg (25, 1915); (2) MEDICINE — Frederick Banting (32, 1923, insulin); (3) CHEMISTRY — Frédéric Joliot-Curie (35, 1935); (4) LITERATURE — RUDYARD KIPLING (41, 1907 — author of ‘Jungle Book’, ‘Kim’; Indian-born Englishman, first English-language laureate); (5) ECONOMIC SCIENCES — Esther Duflo (46, 2019 — second woman to win Economics Nobel, French-American, wife of Abhijit Banerjee); (6) PEACE — Malala (17, 2014). OLDEST NOBEL LAUREATE: JOHN GOODENOUGH — Chemistry 2019 at age 97 (lithium-ion battery), shared with Stanley Whittingham + Akira Yoshino. Goodenough died 2023 at 100. Before him: LEONID HURWICZ (Economics 2007, at 90). ARTHUR ASHKIN (Physics 2018, at 96, optical tweezers). DORIS LESSING (Literature 2007, at 88). OLDEST Physics: John B. Goodenough. HIGHLIGHTED RECORDS in Nobel history: (a) MOST NOBELS in one family: CURIE FAMILY (5 Nobels) — Marie (Physics 1903 + Chemistry 1911), Pierre (Physics 1903), Irène Joliot-Curie (Chemistry 1935 with husband Frédéric Joliot). (b) FATHER-SON: Lawrence Bragg + Henry Bragg (Physics 1915); Niels Bohr (Physics 1922) + Aage Bohr (Physics 1975); Hans von Euler-Chelpin (Chemistry 1929) + Ulf von Euler (Medicine 1970); Manne Siegbahn (Physics 1924) + Kai Siegbahn (Physics 1981); Arthur Kornberg (Medicine 1959) + Roger Kornberg (Chemistry 2006). (c) HUSBAND-WIFE: Marie + Pierre Curie, Gerty + Carl Cori (Medicine 1947), Irène + Frédéric Joliot-Curie, May-Britt + Edvard Moser (Medicine 2014 — spatial navigation), Esther Duflo + Abhijit Banerjee (Economics 2019). (d) POSTHUMOUS: Dag Hammarskjöld (Peace 1961, UN Secretary-General killed in plane crash), Erik Axel Karlfeldt (Literature 1931), Ralph Steinman (Medicine 2011 — died 3 days before). Since 1974, rule changed: no new posthumous awards EXCEPT if laureate dies between announcement + ceremony. (e) REFUSED: JEAN-PAUL SARTRE (Literature 1964, declined — disliked official honours), LE DUC THO (Peace 1973, declined — Vietnam War ongoing). (f) HITLER's Germany forced 3 German laureates to refuse in the 1930s. (g) NO PRIZE awarded during WWI + WWII for some categories. (h) ORGANISATIONS that won Peace: ICRC (3x), UNHCR (2x), IAEA (2005), IPCC (2007, with Al Gore), OPCW (2013), EU (2012). (i) Prize CAN BE SHARED by up to 3 individuals or organizations.

(B) 1954

cards.back:

Awards & Honours — Bharat Ratna instituted on 2 January 1954 by President Rajendra Prasad. First three recipients (1954) — Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, C. Rajagopalachari, C.V. Raman. Suspended once during 1977-80 (Janata Party era). Awarded for 'exceptional service or performance of the highest order in any field of human endeavour' — initially restricted to arts/literature/science/public service; expanded in 2011 to ANY field. cards.front:
The FIVE RINGS of the Olympic symbol represent:

(A) The 5 main Olympic sports
(B) The FIVE INHABITED CONTINENTS of the world
(C) The 5 Olympic values
(D) The 5 modern Olympic Games chronological eras
cards.back:
(B) The FIVE INHABITED CONTINENTS of the world

Sports & Olympics — OLYMPIC SYMBOL (5 interlocking rings) — designed in 1913 by PIERRE DE COUBERTIN (father of the modern Olympic movement) on the OLYMPIC FLAG. RINGS = FIVE inhabited CONTINENTS (in the old 5-continent model that merges Europe and combines North+South America, excluding Antarctica): AFRICA, AMERICAS, ASIA, EUROPE, OCEANIA. COLOURS = Blue, Yellow, Black, Green, Red on WHITE background. Chosen because AT LEAST ONE of these six colours appears on every NATIONAL FLAG in the world at that time. OLYMPIC MOTTO: ‘CITIUS, ALTIUS, FORTIUS — COMMUNITER’ (‘Faster, Higher, Stronger — Together’). ‘Communiter’ added in 2021 (previously just Citius-Altius-Fortius since 1894, coined by Father Henri Didon, adopted by Coubertin). OLYMPIC CREED: ‘The most important thing in the Olympic Games is not to win but to take part, just as the most important thing in life is not the triumph but the struggle’. OLYMPIC TORCH: ritual dates back to 1936 Berlin; flame kindled at Olympia, Greece from sun's rays; relayed to host city. OLYMPIC OATH: taken by an athlete of the host country. INTERNATIONAL OLYMPIC COMMITTEE (IOC) — formed 1894 in Paris by Coubertin; HQ LAUSANNE, Switzerland. First modern Olympics: ATHENS 1896. colours Blue-Yellow-Black-Green-Red were chosen so that AT LEAST ONE appears on every national flag of the world; Africa, Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania.

OLYMPIC CREED: ‘The most important thing in the Olympic Games is not to win but to take part, just as the most important thing in life is not the triumph but the struggle’. OLYMPIC TORCH: ritual dates back to 1936 Berlin; flame kindled at Olympia, Greece from sun's rays; relayed to host city. OLYMPIC OATH: taken by an athlete of the host country. INTERNATIONAL OLYMPIC COMMITTEE (IOC) — formed 1894 in Paris by Coubertin; HQ LAUSANNE, Switzerland. First modern Olympics: ATHENS 1896. colours Blue-Yellow-Black-Green-Red were chosen so that AT LEAST ONE appears on every national flag of the world; Africa, Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania.

EVENT: MEN'S JAVELIN THROW. Winning throw: 87.58 m on his 2nd attempt. This was ONLY INDIA's 2nd individual Olympic gold (first was Abhinav Bindra 2008 shooting). 23 years old at time of win. Previously: (1) 2016 World U20 (Junior) champion — 86.48 m (still a world junior record); (2) Commonwealth Games 2018 & 2022 GOLD; (3) Asian Games 2018 & 2022 GOLD; (4) Diamond League champion 2022, runner-up in others; (5) World Championships 2022 SILVER, 2023 GOLD (Budapest — India’s first World Athletics Championships gold); (6) PARIS 2024 OLYMPICS: SILVER (89.45 m — Arshad Nadeem of Pakistan took gold with 92.97 m, an Olympic record). Sports & Olympics — KARNAM MALLESWARI (b. 1 June 1975, Voosavanipeta village, Srikakulam district, ANDHRA PRADESH) — FIRST INDIAN WOMAN to win an OLYMPIC MEDAL. (C) Shooting

cards.back:
(B) FIELD HOCKEY

Sports & Olympics — INDIAN FIELD HOCKEY at OLYMPICS — GOLDEN ERA 1928-1980; won 8 GOLDS, 1 SILVER (1960 Rome, lost to Pakistan 0-1), 3 BRONZES (1968, 1972, 2020 Tokyo, 2024 Paris — actually 2 bronzes in this modern era). GOLD YEARS: (1) 1928 AMSTERDAM — Dhyan Chand scoring spree; beat Netherlands 3-0; (2) 1932 LOS ANGELES — beat USA 24-1, Japan 11-1; (3) 1936 BERLIN — beat Germany (Nazi regime) 8-1 in final, Dhyan Chand scored 3; Hitler supposedly offered him Wehrmacht rank — he refused; (4) 1948 LONDON — first as independent India, beat UK 4-0; captain Kishan Lal; (5) 1952 HELSINKI — beat Netherlands 6-1; Balbir Singh Sr hat-trick; (6) 1956 MELBOURNE — Dhyan Chand retired by now; captain Balbir Singh Sr; (7) 1964 TOKYO — beat Pakistan 1-0; (8) 1980 MOSCOW — beat Spain 4-3; captain Vasudevan Bhaskaran. After 1980, hockey standards globally changed (astro-turf introduced 1970s = faster game; India slower to adapt); no medal till 2020 TOKYO BRONZE (beat Germany 5-4, ending 41-yr medal drought — captain Manpreet Singh, coach Graham Reid). 2024 PARIS — BRONZE again (beat Spain 2-1; captain Harmanpreet Singh). WOMEN’S TEAM: no Olympic medal yet (4th place Tokyo 2020). DHYAN CHAND (‘The Wizard’) = greatest Indian hockey player; National Sports Day 29 Aug (his birthday); Khel Ratna renamed ‘Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna’ 2021. 8 OLYMPIC GOLDS (1928, 1932, 1936, 1948, 1952, 1956, 1964, 1980); 11 total medals counting bronzes/silvers.

cards.front:
The HEADQUARTERS of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) is at:

(A) Paris, France
(B) Athens, Greece
(C) LAUSANNE, SWITZERLAND
(D) Geneva, Switzerland
cards.back:
(C) LAUSANNE, SWITZERLAND

Sports & Olympics — INTERNATIONAL OLYMPIC COMMITTEE (IOC) — the supreme authority of the OLYMPIC MOVEMENT. FOUNDED: 23 JUNE 1894 in PARIS by PIERRE DE COUBERTIN + DEMETRIOS VIKELAS (first President). HEADQUARTERS: LAUSANNE, Switzerland (moved from Paris in 1915 during WWI). MEMBER STRUCTURE: up to 115 active IOC members + honorary members. CURRENT PRESIDENT (as of 2026): KIRSTY COVENTRY (Zimbabwean, ex-swimmer, former IOC member, elected 2025 to succeed Thomas Bach; she is the first female + first African IOC President). Past Presidents: Coubertin (1896-1925), Avery Brundage (1952-72), Juan Antonio Samaranch (1980-2001), Jacques Rogge (2001-2013), Thomas Bach (2013-2025), Kirsty Coventry (2025-). THE OLYMPIC MUSEUM is in Lausanne (opened 1993). 23 JUNE = OLYMPIC DAY (anniversary of IOC founding). THREE PILLARS of Olympic Movement: IOC + International Federations (IFs, one per sport) + National Olympic Committees (NOCs, one per country — India’s is IOA, Indian Olympic Association, founded 1927). Olympic CHARTER — the governing document. OTHER KEY SPORTS HQ: FIFA (Zurich), ICC (Dubai), FINA (Lausanne), World Athletics (Monaco), BWF (Kuala Lumpur). since 1915, along the shore of Lake Geneva; hosts The Olympic Museum.
