cards.front:
The ancient Olympic Games of GREECE were held in honour of:

(A) Apollo
(B) ZEUS
(C) Hera
(D) Poseidon
cards.back:
(B) ZEUS

Sports & Olympics — ANCIENT OLYMPIC GAMES — religious+athletic festival held in honour of ZEUS (king of Greek gods) at OLYMPIA (not Mount Olympus!; Olympia is in the western Peloponnese, ancient region of Elis). Founded traditionally in 776 BCE (first recorded Olympiad); held every 4 YEARS for over 1,169 years until abolished by Roman Emperor THEODOSIUS I in 393 CE as a pagan festival (after Christianity became state religion). OLYMPIAD = 4-year interval; used as the primary Greek timekeeping method. FIRST-EVENT: STADION (short foot race ~192 m); winner: KOROIBOS of Elis (cook). Events expanded: wrestling, boxing, pentathlon, equestrian (horse, chariot), pankration. ATHLETES competed nude (gymnos, hence gymnasium) and were Greek-speaking FREE men (no slaves, no women until later). PRIZE: olive wreath (kotinos) — no cash. OLYMPIC TRUCE (ekecheiria): fighting suspended so athletes could travel safely. HERAEA — separate games for women in honour of Hera. MODERN REVIVAL: PIERRE DE COUBERTIN (French educator) championed revival; after lectures at Sorbonne 1892; congress of 1894 formed IOC; FIRST MODERN OLYMPICS held at ATHENS in 1896 (April 6-15). 13 countries, 280 athletes, 43 events; host Greece topped with 10 golds; USA second. First gold medallist of modern era: JAMES CONNOLLY (USA, Triple Jump). Since then, Olympic Games held every 4 years (exceptions: World Wars — 1916, 1940, 1944 cancelled; Tokyo 2020 postponed to 2021 due to COVID). father of Greek gods; held every 4 years at OLYMPIA (in Elis, western Peloponnese) from 776 BCE to 393 CE.

cards.front:
The PARA-OLYMPICS / PARALYMPIC GAMES are held for:

(A) Athletes below 18 years old (junior athletes)
(B) ATHLETES with PHYSICAL / VISUAL / INTELLECTUAL IMPAIRMENTS
(C) Veteran/senior athletes
(D) Athletes from tropical countries only
cards.back:
(B) ATHLETES with PHYSICAL / VISUAL / INTELLECTUAL IMPAIRMENTS

Sports & Olympics — PARALYMPIC GAMES — major international multi-sport event for athletes with a range of DISABILITIES including impaired muscle power, limb deficiencies, vision impairment, intellectual impairments. NAME: ‘PARA’ = Greek ‘beside/alongside’ → games held alongside Olympics in same city. FOUNDED by Sir LUDWIG GUTTMANN (neurologist who treated spinal-cord patients at Stoke Mandeville hospital, UK) — organised the 1948 Stoke Mandeville Games for WWII veterans. 1960 ROME — first official Paralympic Games (held 6 days after Olympic closing); 400 athletes, 23 countries. Since 1988 SEOUL, Paralympics have been held in the SAME HOST CITY as the Olympics (and since 2012 London, using the same venues). Winter Paralympics began 1976 (Örnsköldsvik, Sweden). GOVERNING BODY: INTERNATIONAL PARALYMPIC COMMITTEE (IPC) — formed 1989, HQ BONN (Germany). Athletes are CLASSIFIED by impairment type & degree (e.g., T11 totally blind, T12 low vision, T13 best vision, etc.). PARALYMPIC MOTTO: ‘SPIRIT IN MOTION’. PARALYMPIC SYMBOL: 3 agitos (curved shapes — Latin ‘I move’); red, blue, green. INDIA AT PARALYMPICS — 29 all-time medals till PARIS 2024 (which alone gave India 29 medals incl. 7 GOLDS — best-ever; shooting & athletics dominant; AVANI LEKHARA defended 10m air rifle SH1 gold). Famous Indian para-athletes: DEVENDRA JHAJHARIA (javelin F46 — first Indian para-athlete to win TWO golds — Athens 2004 + Rio 2016), MARIYAPPAN THANGAVELU (high jump T63 gold Rio 2016), SUMIT ANTIL (javelin F64 gold Tokyo 2020 + Paris 2024), MANISH NARWAL, PRAVEEN KUMAR. SPECIAL OLYMPICS (separate, for intellectual disabilities) and DEAFLYMPICS are DIFFERENT events. held right after the Summer/Winter Olympics in the same host city; governed by the IPC (International Paralympic Committee, Bonn).

Who authored the 'ARTHASHASTRA' — an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, political economy, and military strategy?

(A) Valmiki
(B) Kautilya / Chanakya / Vishnugupta
(C) Panini
(D) Aryabhata
cards.back:

Art, Culture & Heritage — ARTHASHASTRA — ancient Indian treatise on economics, statecraft, military strategy. Traditionally attributed to KAUTILYA (also known as Chanakya or Vishnugupta) — the legendary Brahmin advisor of Chandragupta Maurya (4th c. BCE). 15 books covering: finance, administration, foreign relations (Mandala theory of 'circles of states'), law, military strategy, spying, diplomacy. Rediscovered in 1905 by R. SHAMASASTRY (Mysore Govt Oriental Library). Compared to Machiavelli's 'The Prince' (1513) but 1800 years older + much broader. Other CLASSIC ancient Indian texts: (1) RAMAYANA by VALMIKI (~500 BCE - 100 BCE); (2) MAHABHARATA by VYASA / VEDA VYASA (100,000 couplets — world's longest epic, incl Bhagavad Gita); (3) ASHTADHYAYI by PANINI (4th c. BCE — Sanskrit grammar, ~4000 rules — first analytical language description in human history); (4) ARYABHATIYA by ARYABHATA (499 CE — astronomy, mathematics); (5) NATYA SHASTRA by BHARATA MUNI (on performing arts); (6) CHARAKA SAMHITA (medicine, by CHARAKA); SUSHRUTA SAMHITA (surgery); (7) KAMA SUTRA by VATSYAYANA.

Art, Culture & Heritage — 'DISCOVERY OF INDIA' (written 1944, published 1946) — by JAWAHARLAL NEHRU while imprisoned at AHMEDNAGAR FORT prison during Quit India (Aug 1942-June 1945). An ambitious historical + philosophical study of India's civilisation. Television adaptation: 'BHARAT EK KHOJ' (1988) — directed by SHYAM BENEGAL for Doordarshan, 53 episodes covering 5000 years of Indian history. Nehru's other books (almost all written in jails): (1) 'AN AUTOBIOGRAPHY' / 'Toward Freedom' (1936, Naini jail + Dehradun jail); (2) 'GLIMPSES OF WORLD HISTORY' (1934, 196 letters to daughter Indira from various jails 1930-33); (3) 'LETTERS FROM A FATHER TO HIS DAUGHTER' (1929-31, letters to 10-year-old Indira on natural history); (4) 'INDIA AND THE WORLD' (1936); (5) 'EIGHTEEN MONTHS IN INDIA' (1938). Nehru spent ~9 YEARS in British jails over 9 stints. Other prison-written works: GANDHI's 'Hind Swaraj' (1909, ship voyage, not jail), Tilak's 'Gita Rahasya' (Mandalay jail 1908-14), Savarkar's 'The Indian War of Independence 1857' (written 1908 while in England; smuggled), Gandhi's 'My Experiments with Truth' / 'Satya Ke Mere Prayog' (1927-29, serialised in Navjivan + Young India).

cards.front:
The 'ORIGIN OF SPECIES' — which introduced the theory of evolution by natural selection — was published in 1859 by:

(A) Gregor Mendel
(B) Charles Darwin
(C) Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
(D) Alfred Russel Wallace
cards.back:
(B) Charles Darwin

Art, Culture & Heritage — 'ON THE ORIGIN OF SPECIES BY MEANS OF NATURAL SELECTION' — published 24 November 1859 by CHARLES DARWIN (1809-1882). Presented the theory of EVOLUTION by NATURAL SELECTION — individuals with favourable heritable variations have higher reproductive success; over generations, this changes populations. Based on observations during the 5-year voyage of HMS BEAGLE (1831-36, esp. Galapagos finches). Rushed to publication when Alfred Russel WALLACE independently arrived at the same conclusion from SE Asia — both presented a joint paper in July 1858 at Linnean Society before Darwin's book. Controversial at the time due to religious implications. Darwin's later 'THE DESCENT OF MAN' (1871) applied evolution to humans. OTHER REVOLUTIONARY BOOKS: NEWTON's 'PRINCIPIA' (1687) — mathematical laws of motion + gravitation; COPERNICUS's 'DE REVOLUTIONIBUS' (1543) — heliocentric solar system; KARL MARX + ENGELS — 'COMMUNIST MANIFESTO' (1848), 'DAS KAPITAL' (1867-94); ADAM SMITH — 'WEALTH OF NATIONS' (1776, economics); KEYNES — 'General Theory' (1936); FREUD — 'Interpretation of Dreams' (1899); EINSTEIN — special relativity papers (1905 'Annus Mirabilis'). MENDEL's pea genetics (1866, contemporary with Darwin) were ignored for 35 years.

(A) Salman Rushdie

cards.back:
(B) Arundhati Roy

Art, Culture & Heritage — 'THE GOD OF SMALL THINGS' (1997) — by ARUNDHATI ROY (Suzanna Arundhati Roy, born 1961). Her debut novel — won the BOOKER PRIZE (1997) — first Indian woman, first Indian resident (Rushdie was UK-based). Semi-autobiographical, set in Kerala; explored forbidden love, caste, trauma. (2) ARUNDHATI ROY — 1997. (3) KIRAN DESAI — 'THE INHERITANCE OF LOSS' (2006) — daughter of Anita Desai (herself shortlisted multiple times). (4) ARAVIND ADIGA — 'THE WHITE TIGER' (2008). OTHER notable Indian English authors: VIKRAM SETH (Suitable Boy), AMITAV GHOSH (Ibis Trilogy, Shadow Lines — JNANPITH 2018, 1st English winner), JHUMPA LAHIRI (Pulitzer 2000 for 'Interpreter of Maladies'), ROHINTON MISTRY, CHITRA BANERJEE, RK NARAYAN (Malgudi Days), MULK RAJ ANAND (Coolie, Untouchable), RAJA RAO (Kanthapura).

cards.front:
Tagore's 'GITANJALI' (1910 Bengali; 1912 English) won him the Nobel Prize in 1913. Which other country's NATIONAL ANTHEM was also written by Tagore?

(A) Sri Lanka
(B) BANGLADESH
(C) Myanmar
(D) Nepal
cards.back:
(B) BANGLADESH

Art, Culture & Heritage — RABINDRANATH TAGORE (1861-1941) wrote the national anthems of TWO countries: (1) INDIA — 'JANA GANA MANA' (Bengali, 1911; adopted 24 Jan 1950); (2) BANGLADESH — 'AMAR SHONAR BANGLA' ('My Golden Bengal') — originally written in 1905 in protest against British plans for Bengal Partition; adopted by Bangladesh on independence (1971) as its national anthem. SRI LANKA's national anthem 'SRI LANKA MATHA' was written by Ananda Samarakoon (a Tagore student at Shantiniketan — so Tagore's INFLUENCE extends there too, though he didn't write it). Tagore also composed the Bengali 'RABINDRA SANGEET' — ~2,230 songs. Founded VISHVA-BHARATI University at SHANTINIKETAN (now a CENTRAL UNIVERSITY, UNESCO WHS 2023). Knighted 1915; RENOUNCED Knighthood 30 May 1919 in protest against Jallianwala Bagh massacre. Wrote in multiple genres: novels (Chokher Bali, Gora, Ghare Baire), short stories (Kabuliwala, Postmaster), poetry, essays, plays. GANDHI called him 'GURUDEV'; Tagore called Gandhi 'MAHATMA'. First non-European Nobel laureate in Literature. 'Amar Shonar Bangla', 1905.

(A) Jawaharlal Nehru
(B) Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
(C) Sardar Patel
(D) Mahatma Gandhi
cards.back:
(B) Maulana Abul Kalam Azad

Art, Culture & Heritage — 'INDIA WINS FREEDOM' (1959, published in full 1988 after contested 30-year embargo on sensitive portions) — by MAULANA ABUL KALAM AZAD (1888-1958) — Independent India's FIRST EDUCATION MINISTER, senior INC leader, scholar, freedom fighter. cards.front:
KALIDASA — the legendary Sanskrit poet-playwright of the Gupta era — wrote several famous works. Which of the following is NOT by Kalidasa?

(A) Abhijnanashakuntalam (play)
(B) Meghadutam (poem)
(C) Kumarasambhavam (poem)
(D) Mudrarakshasa
cards.back:
(D) Mudrarakshasa

Art, Culture & Heritage — MUDRARAKSHASA ('The Signet Ring of Rakshasa') was written by VISHAKHADATTA (not Kalidasa) — a political drama based on Chanakya + Chandragupta Maurya's rise to power. KALIDASA — flourished in the Gupta era (~4th-5th c. CE, probably in the court of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya at Ujjain). Works attributed to him: PLAYS (NATAKAS): (1) ABHIJNANASHAKUNTALAM (The Recognition of Shakuntala) — masterpiece; Goethe praised it; first Sanskrit play translated to English (1789) by William Jones; (2) VIKRAMORVASHIYAM (Vikrama and Urvashi); (3) MALAVIKAGNIMITRAM (Malavika and Agnimitra — first, possibly earliest play). POEMS (KAVYAS): (1) MEGHADUTAM (The Cloud Messenger) — lyrical poem, a yaksha sends message to his wife via a cloud; (2) KUMARASAMBHAVAM (Birth of Kumara/Kartikeya); (3) RAGHUVAMSHAM (Dynasty of Raghu/Rama's ancestors); (4) RITUSAMHARAM (Pageant of Seasons). Called the 'SHAKESPEARE OF INDIA'. 'NAVARATNA' (Nine Gems) of Chandragupta II's court (later tradition). OTHER SANSKRIT LITERARY GIANTS: BHASA (earlier, 'Swapnavasavadatta'), SHUDRAKA ('Mrichchhakatika' — the Little Clay Cart), BHAVABHUTI ('Uttararamacharita'), BANABHATTA ('Harshacharita' + 'Kadambari'), JAYADEVA ('Gita Govinda').

cards.back:

cards.front:
'The Origin of Species' (1859), which proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection, was written by:

(A) Gregor Mendel
(B) Charles Darwin
(C) Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
(D) Thomas Huxley
cards.back:
(B) Charles Darwin

Art, Culture & Heritage — Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection' (1859) revolutionised biology. He later wrote 'The Descent of Man' (1871) on human evolution. Lamarck had proposed an earlier (and largely incorrect) theory of inheritance of acquired characteristics. Gregor Mendel worked out the laws of heredity separately through his pea-plant experiments (1866). T. H. Huxley was Darwin's leading public defender ('Darwin's bulldog').

The traditional count is 8 (OR 9 if you include Chhau which SNA added in 2010). MNEMONIC ('BK²M²OSK'): BHARATANATYAM (TN), KATHAK (UP/N. India), KATHAKALI (Kerala), KUCHIPUDI (AP), MANIPURI (Manipur), MOHINIYATTAM (Kerala), ODISSI (Odisha), SATTRIYA (Assam). KEY CRITERIA for 'classical': based on NATYASHASTRA (treatise by BHARATA MUNI, ~2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE); follows structured Nritta (pure dance), Nritya (expressive), Natya (drama) elements; uses codified abhinaya (expression) — Angika (body), Vachika (speech), Aharya (costume), Sattvika (emotion). GLOBAL RECOGNITION: many classical dances are UNESCO ICH — Kutiyattam (2008), Ramlila, Chhau (2010). REGIONS → DANCES (match set): TAMIL NADU = Bharatanatyam; UP/RAJASTHAN/N. INDIA = Kathak; KERALA = Kathakali + Mohiniyattam; ANDHRA PRADESH = Kuchipudi; ODISHA = Odissi; MANIPUR = Manipuri; ASSAM = Sattriya; SERAIKELA/MAYURBHANJ/PURULIA (Jharkhand/Odisha/WB) = Chhau. Folk dances are separate + vast (Garba, Bhangra, Lavani, Bihu, Ghoomar, etc.). Very high-frequency SSC + Railway + State PSC topic. some sources also include Chhau making it 9.

cards.front:
BHARATANATYAM, the classical dance of Tamil Nadu, was originally known as:

(A) Kathak
(B) SADIR / DASI ATTAM
(C) Natyam
(D) Yakshagana
cards.back:
(B) SADIR / DASI ATTAM

Art, Culture & Heritage — BHARATANATYAM — the OLDEST of Indian classical dances (~2000 years old); originated in TEMPLES of Tamil Nadu. EARLIER NAMES: 'SADIR', 'Dasi Attam', 'Chinna Melam' — performed by DEVADASIS (temple dancers consecrated to deities). 1910s British colonial anti-nautch movement + Madras Presidency's 1947 Devadasi Abolition Act stigmatised + outlawed temple dancing. REVIVAL: Rukmini Devi Arundale (Theosophist + social reformer) + E. Krishna Iyer rescued the form, renamed it BHARATA NATYAM ('Bharat's dance' / combining BHA-va, RA-ga, TA-la). Rukmini founded KALAKSHETRA at Adyar (1936), where Bharatanatyam is rigorously taught to this day. ETYMOLOGY: (a) From Bharata Muni, author of Natya Shastra. (b) Folk etymology as above (bhava+raga+tala). TECHNIQUE: based on Natya Shastra + Abhinaya Darpana. Uses ARAMANDI (half-seated posture), MUDRAS (hand gestures — ~108 single-hand, 28 combined), aramandi, aduvus (basic movements), Nritta (pure)-Nritya (expressive)-Natya (dramatic). STANDARD REPERTOIRE (Margam, codified by the TANJORE QUARTET in 1800s): Alarippu → Jatiswaram → Shabdam → Varnam → Padam/Javali → Tillana. COSTUME: silk saree pleated + stitched; elaborate temple jewellery. MUSIC: Carnatic. LEADING EXPONENTS: Rukmini Devi, Balasaraswati, Yamini Krishnamurthy, Padma Subrahmanyam, Sonal Mansingh, Alarmel Valli, Malavika Sarukkai. practised by DEVADASIS in Tamil temples; renamed Bharatanatyam in the 1930s by RUKMINI DEVI ARUNDALE.

cards.front:
KATHAK, the classical dance of North India, has three major GHARANAS (schools). Which of these is NOT a Kathak gharana?

(A) Lucknow gharana
(B) Jaipur gharana
(C) Banaras gharana
(D) MAIHAR gharana
cards.back:
(D) MAIHAR gharana

Art, Culture & Heritage — KATHAK — classical dance of North India (UP, Rajasthan, MP, Delhi). NAME: from Sanskrit 'katha' = story, and 'kathakars' = storytellers. EVOLVED from temple recitation (of Ramayana/Mahabharata) to Mughal courts (secularised + Persian-influenced). THREE MAJOR GHARANAS of KATHAK: (1) LUCKNOW gharana — emphasis on GRACE + ABHINAYA (expression); evolved in court of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah (himself a great patron); exponents = Bindadin Maharaj, Achhan Maharaj, Shambhu Maharaj, BIRJU MAHARAJ (1938-2022; most celebrated modern Kathak dancer, Padma Vibhushan 1986). (2) JAIPUR gharana — emphasis on TECHNICAL footwork (tatkaar), speed, mathematical precision; Rajput warrior origin — exponents Jai Lal, Kundan Lal, Rajendra Gangani. (3) BANARAS gharana — founded by Janaki Prasad; distinctive body movements, less Persian influence, own tatkaar style. Also: Raigarh (smaller). MAIHAR GHARANA is a HINDUSTANI MUSIC gharana (sitar + sarod), founded by BABA ALLAUDDIN KHAN (1862-1972), guru of Ravi Shankar + Ali Akbar Khan — NOT Kathak. TECHNIQUE: chakkars (spins), tatkaar (footwork with ghungroos/ankle-bells), bols (rhythmic syllables), tihais, padhant, abhinaya. COSTUME: Lucknow = Angarkha + churidar/pyjama for men, anarkali/lehenga for women; Jaipur = lehenga-choli-odhani. MUSIC: Hindustani (tabla, sarangi, harmonium). EXPONENTS: Birju Maharaj, Sitara Devi (Padma Shri 1975), Kumudini Lakhia, Roshan Kumari, Shovana Narayan, Aditi Mangaldas. Maihar is a Hindustani MUSIC gharana of Baba Allauddin Khan, NOT of Kathak.

cards.front:
KATHAKALI, known for its elaborate MAKEUP + TOWERING HEADGEAR, is the classical dance-drama of:

(A) Andhra Pradesh
(B) KERALA
(C) Karnataka
(D) Tamil Nadu
cards.back:
(B) KERALA

Art, Culture & Heritage — KATHAKALI (literally 'story-play') — CLASSICAL DANCE-DRAMA of KERALA, ~17th c. origin; developed by Raja of Kottarakkara (Ramanattam) + Raja of Kottayam (Kottayam Tampuran, author of Nalacharitam + other attakathas). HALLMARKS: (1) ELABORATE MAKEUP + COSTUME — one of the most visually striking dance forms in the world. (2) Traditionally ALL-MALE cast — performances lasted all night in temple courtyards. (3) Based on HINDU epics (Ramayana, Mahabharata) + Puranas. (4) MAKEUP (VESHAM) types colour-coded: (a) PACHA (green face) — noble heroes like Rama, Krishna, Arjuna, Bhima. (b) KATHI (knife) — anti-heroes like Ravana, Duryodhana (green+red). (c) THADI (beard) — Red Beard = villainous (Dushasana); White Beard = Hanuman; Black Beard = hunter/forest-dweller. (d) KARI (black) — demonesses. (e) MINUKKU (shining) — sages, women, Brahmins. (5) CHUTTI — white rice-paste 'beard' extending beyond the chin; (6) towering KIREETAM (headgear) symbolising status. TECHNIQUE: 9 RASAS (emotions), 24 MUDRAS (hand gestures, from Hastalakshana Deepika), elaborate eye exercises (students spend years training). MUSIC: Sopanam (Kerala). Instruments: chenda, maddalam, cymbals. LANGUAGE: Manipravalam (Sanskrit-Malayalam hybrid). Ex: Kalamandalam Gopi, Rama Gopalan, Guru Kunchu Kurup. KERALA KALAMANDALAM — premier institution (founded by Vallathol Narayana Menon, 1930). traditionally performed by male dancers, based on Hindu epics; makeup is colour-coded to character types.

cards.front:
MOHINIYATTAM, the 'dance of the enchantress', comes from which state?

(A) Tamil Nadu
(B) KERALA
(C) Karnataka
(D) Andhra Pradesh
cards.back:
(B) KERALA

Art, Culture & Heritage — MOHINIYATTAM ('Mohini' + 'attam' = dance of the enchantress / bewitching woman) — classical dance of KERALA, distinct from Kerala's more dramatic Kathakali. NAME ORIGIN: MOHINI is a female avatar of VISHNU (Churning of the Ocean of Milk — distributed amrita only to devas; Bhasmasura episode — tricked the asura into burning himself). STYLE: CLASSIFIED as LASYA (graceful, feminine) — opposite of Kathakali's TANDAVA (vigorous, masculine). SOLO FEMALE form. COSTUME: distinctive white-cream saree with a GOLDEN BORDER (kasavu saree — Kerala's traditional textile); minimal jewellery; jasmine flowers in hair. MAKEUP: subtle. MUSIC: CARNATIC + Kerala-specific SOPANAM; lyrics in MANIPRAVALAM (Sanskrit-Malayalam hybrid) + Malayalam. DISTINCTIVE FEATURES: SWAYING movements (like the swaying of coconut palms + Kerala's backwaters — oft-cited visual metaphor), circular movements, emphasis on GRACE over ATHLETICS. HISTORY: references in temple records from 16th c.; patronised by KING SWATI THIRUNAL (19th c. Travancore); revived in 20th century by KAVALAM NARAYANA PANICKER + exponent KALAMANDALAM KALYANIKUTTY AMMA ('mother of Mohiniyattam' — revived it from near-extinction after colonial anti-nautch). EXPONENTS: Sunanda Nair, Bharati Shivaji, Kalamandalam Leelamma, Pallavi Krishnan, Smitha Rajan. REPERTOIRE: Cholkettu, Jatiswaram, Varnam, Padam, Tillana (borrowed structure from Bharatanatyam). a LASYA (graceful) classical dance, solo female form, based on the Mohini avatar of Vishnu.

cards.front:
SATTRIYA, added to the list of Classical Dances of India in 2000, originated in:

(A) Manipur
(B) ASSAM
(C) Tripura
(D) West Bengal
cards.back:
(B) ASSAM

Art, Culture & Heritage — SATTRIYA — the classical dance of ASSAM; NEWEST recognised (added by Sangeet Natak Akademi as the 8th classical form in the year 2000). ORIGIN: introduced in the late 15th century by MAHAPURUSHA SRIMANTA SANKARDEVA (1449-1568), the great Vaishnavite saint-reformer of Assam, founder of EKASARANA DHARMA (single-refuge devotion to Vishnu/Krishna). DEVELOPED as a medium of BHAKTI + storytelling in SATRAS (Vaishnava monasteries of Majuli + Barpeta). NAME: from SATRA (monastery). LONG the domain of MONK-DANCERS (Bhakats) — only taken to the public stage in the 20th century, brought out of the satras in the 1950s. TECHNIQUE: combines pure dance (Nritta) + expressive (Nritya); tandava + lasya balance. Hastas + mudras + bhangas as per Natya Shastra + Sankardeva's Hastamuktavali. THEMES: tales of Krishna from Ankiya Naat (plays written by Sankardeva + Madhavadeva). MUSIC: Borgeet (devotional songs composed by Sankardeva + Madhavadeva); instruments = KHOL (drum — signature instrument of Assamese Vaishnavism), CYMBALS (manjira, taal), FLUTE. COSTUME: traditional Assamese silk (muga, pat); paat chador; mekhela sador for women. TYPES: Apsara Nritya, Gopi Nritya, Jhumura, Nadu Bhangi, Bhortal nritya, ankiya naat. EXPONENTS: Jatin Goswami, Ghanakanta Bora, Indira P.P. Bora, Anwesa Mahanta. MAJULI, Assam — the world's largest inhabited river island + centre of Sattras. introduced in the 15th c. by Vaishnavite saint SRIMANTA SANKARDEVA in Satras (monasteries); recognised as 8th classical form by SNA in 2000.

cards.front:
KUCHIPUDI takes its name from:

(A) A king named Kuchipudi
(B) The VILLAGE of KUCHIPUDI (KUCHELAPURAM) in Krishna district, ANDHRA PRADESH, where it was developed by Siddhendra Yogi in the 17th century
(C) A Sanskrit shloka
(D) The word for 'dance' in Telugu
cards.back:
(B) The VILLAGE of KUCHIPUDI (KUCHELAPURAM) in Krishna district, ANDHRA PRADESH, where it was developed by Siddhendra Yogi in the 17th century

Art, Culture & Heritage — KUCHIPUDI — classical dance of ANDHRA PRADESH, named after the VILLAGE Kuchipudi (originally KUCHELAPURAM) in Krishna district, AP. FOUNDER: SIDDHENDRA YOGI — 17th century Vaishnavite saint-poet, who composed the KUCHIPUDI dance-drama BHAMAKALAPAM (on Satyabhama's jealousy of Rukmini). ORIGINALLY a MALE-only dance-drama tradition (Bhagavatars) performed in temple courtyards. Post-independence, women too learned Kuchipudi + solo formats developed (pioneered by LAKSHMINARAYAN SHASTRI + VEMPATI CHINNA SATYAM — the latter considered the modern father of solo Kuchipudi). UNIQUE FEATURES: (1) TARANGAM — the dancer performs on the RIM of a brass plate with water-pot balanced on the head! (signature item; requires extraordinary skill). (2) JATHISWARAM + shabdam + kalapam. (3) blend of NRITTA + natya, with VACHIKA (speech) playing a role — dancers traditionally spoke dialogues. (4) QUICK-FOOTWORK, sharp BRILLIANT movements, balance. REPERTOIRE: yakshaganams, Krishnaleelas, Bhama Kalapam, Gollakalapam. COSTUME: Silk saree 'typical' south-Indian with fan pleats. MUSIC: Carnatic; instruments = mridangam, flute, violin, tambura. LYRICS: Telugu + Sanskrit. EXPONENTS: Vempati Chinna Satyam, Raja + Radha Reddy, Yamini Krishnamurthy (also Bharatanatyam), Shobha Naidu, Swapna Sundari, Sobha Naidu. DIFF FROM BHARATANATYAM: more ROUNDED + curvilinear; uses more DRAMA; Tarangam unique.

cards.front:
ODISSI, the classical dance of ODISHA, centres around the TRIBHANGA posture. Tribhanga means:

(A) Three steps
(B) THREE BENDS of the body
(C) A circular motion
(D) A kind of hand gesture
cards.back:
(B) THREE BENDS of the body

Art, Culture & Heritage — ODISSI — classical dance of ODISHA, one of the OLDEST classical forms (references + temple sculptures date back to ~2nd c. BCE Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela). TEMPLE-BASED ORIGIN: MAHARIS (temple dancers of the Jagannath Temple at Puri) + later GOTIPUAS (boys dressed as girls, after the Mahari tradition was suppressed). DISTINCTIVE POSTURES: (1) TRIBHANGA — three body bends at NECK-TORSO-KNEE creating an S-shape; (2) CHAUKA — square stance, broad + grounded, associated with Jagannath; (3) ABHANGA — single bend. These are codified in NATYA SHASTRA + ABHINAYA CHANDRIKA. REPERTOIRE: Mangalacharan → Batu (Sthayee) → Pallavi → Tharijham → Abhinaya (Oriya songs of poet Jayadeva's GITA GOVINDA — Ashtapadi) → Moksha. LITERATURE: GITA GOVINDA (12th c. poet JAYADEVA, describes Krishna-Radha love) is central to Odissi abhinaya. MUSIC: Odissi music (distinct from Carnatic + Hindustani); instruments = Pakhawaj/mardala, flute, sitar, violin, manjira. COSTUME: silk saree in traditional patta draping + silver jewellery (tahia = flower crown). REVIVAL: Odissi nearly died out during British era; revived by Kavichandra Kalicharan Pattnaik + Guru DEBA PRASAD DAS + Guru PANKAJ CHARAN DAS + Guru KELUCHARAN MOHAPATRA (greatest modern Odissi guru, Padma Vibhushan 2000; his choreography = Gurukul style). Other exponents: Sanjukta Panigrahi, Sonal Mansingh, Madhavi Mudgal, Aruna Mohanty, Sujata Mohapatra. creating an S-shape characteristic of sculptures in Konark + Bhubaneswar temples; at neck, torso, and knee.

cards.front:
MANIPURI dance is characterised by its GENTLE, FLOWING movements + a distinctive wide-base costume called:

(A) Ghoomar skirt
(B) KUMIL / POTLOI
(C) Lehenga
(D) Sari
cards.back:
(B) KUMIL / POTLOI

Art, Culture & Heritage — MANIPURI (JAGOI) — classical dance of MANIPUR, distinctively LYRICAL + GENTLE, with no percussive movements. ORIGIN: ancient tribal dance of the Meitei people; transformed into a devotional form by KING BHAGYACHANDRA (18th c.) after he received a VISION OF KRISHNA + choreographed the RAAS LEELA. THEMES: primarily KRISHNA-RADHA love (Raas Leela — Krishna dances with 16,108 gopis in Vrindavan; Maha Raas, Vasant Raas, Kunj Raas, Nitya Raas are variants). COSTUME: FEMALE dancer wears the iconic POTLOI / KUMIL — a BARREL-shaped stiff skirt reaching the ankles, embellished with mirror work + embroidery; sheer veil over the face. RADHA dances in white veil; KRISHNA in peacock crown, yellow dhoti (male dancer). TECHNIQUE: TANDAVA (masculine) + LASYA (feminine), wafting movements, soft + understated abhinaya (NO exaggerated facial expressions — unlike Kathakali); emphasis on devotion + grace. MUSIC: manipuri ragas; instruments PUNG (drum worn around neck, signature of Manipuri), flute, cymbals, kartal. VAISHNAVISM in Manipur since King Pamheiba's time (~1700s). POLITICAL: Raas Leela performed at the ISKCON world headquarters + across Vaishnava communities globally. RABINDRANATH TAGORE championed Manipuri after seeing it in Sylhet; brought it to Santiniketan (1919). EXPONENTS: Jhaveri Sisters (Ranjana, Nayana, Suverna, Darshana), Guru Bipin Singh + his wife Kalavati Devi, Charu Sija Mathur. SANKIRTANA of Manipur = UNESCO ICH (2013). a barrel-shaped embellished skirt worn by female dancers, depicting Radha + the Gopis in Krishna-bhakti Raaslila.

Match the FOLK DANCE with its STATE: (1) GHOOMAR; (2) LAVANI; (3) BIHU; (4) CHHAU.

(A) Punjab; Kerala; Goa; Sikkim
(B) RAJASTHAN; MAHARASHTRA; ASSAM; Jharkhand/Odisha/West Bengal (Purulia)
(C) Rajasthan; Tamil Nadu; Manipur; Odisha only
(D) Haryana; Maharashtra; Bengal; Bihar
cards.back:
(B) RAJASTHAN; MAHARASHTRA; ASSAM; Jharkhand/Odisha/West Bengal (Purulia)

Art, Culture & Heritage — INDIAN FOLK DANCES by STATE (high-yield topic): (1) GHOOMAR — RAJASTHAN; traditionally performed by Rajput women in long ghaghras, pirouetting (ghoom = spin). Rajwada Bhagoria + royal Rajput weddings. Famously highlighted in the 2018 film 'Padmaavat'. (2) LAVANI — MAHARASHTRA; performed to dholki beats; known for powerful rhythm, erotic sringar, women dancers in nauvari saree; popularised in Marathi folk theatre (Tamasha). (3) BIHU — ASSAM; performed during the 3 BIHU FESTIVALS (Rongali / Bohag in April = Assamese New Year, Kongali / Kati in Oct, Bhogali / Magh in Jan). Young men + women in traditional gamosa-mekhela. (4) CHHAU — MASKED MARTIAL DANCE of three states (each with own style): SERAIKELA Chhau (Jharkhand), MAYURBHANJ Chhau (Odisha — no mask), PURULIA Chhau (West Bengal). UNESCO ICH 2010. Uses Ramayana/Mahabharata themes + martial movements. Other famous FOLK DANCES: (5) BHANGRA + GIDDHA (PUNJAB — harvest, Baisakhi); (6) GARBA + DANDIYA RAAS (GUJARAT — Navratri, devotional to Durga); (7) YAKSHAGANA (KARNATAKA — traditional theatre); (8) KALBELIA (RAJASTHAN — snake-charmer tribe, UNESCO ICH 2010); (9) KOLI + LEZIM + TAMASHA (MAHARASHTRA); (10) NATI (HP); (11) JHUMAR (Jharkhand/Haryana); (12) PADAYANI (Kerala); (13) ROUF (Kashmir); (14) CHERAW (bamboo dance — MIZORAM); (15) HOJAGIRI (Tripura); (16) THANG-TA + KHAMBA THOIBI (Manipur); (17) SINGHI CHHAM (Sikkim); (18) LAMBADI (Telangana).

cards.back:

cards.back:

Iqbal later wrote 'Tarana-e-Milli' supporting the idea of Pakistan. Tagore wrote Jana Gana Mana (1911) and Amar Sonar Bangla (1905, Bangladesh anthem). Bankim wrote Vande Mataram (1875).

The Garos' corresponding major festival is WANGALA ('100 Drums Festival') in November, post-harvest. Apatani: Dree festival.

Theyyam, a ritualistic dance where the performer embodies a deity, is performed in which state?

(A) Karnataka
(B) Kerala
(C) Tamil Nadu
(D) Andhra Pradesh
cards.back:
(B) Kerala

Art, Culture & Heritage — Theyyam (also Kaliyattam, Tira) is a sacred ritual dance-drama of North Malabar (Kannur, Kasaragod districts) of Kerala. Over 400 distinct Theyyam forms exist; the performer, after elaborate makeup and costume (often spanning 8-10 hours to don), is believed to become the deity itself — devotees seek blessings directly from 'the god'. Associated with Kaavu (sacred groves) and the Dravidian pre-Hindu pantheon. Other Kerala dances: Kathakali (classical), Mohiniyattam (classical), Padayani, Koodiyattam (UNESCO 2001), Ottamthullal.

India is a signatory to TRIPS (1995) which mandates GI protection. A GI is granted for goods (including agricultural, natural, manufactured) tied to a specific geographical origin and possessing qualities/reputation due to that origin.

Indian classical music has two main systems — Hindustani of the north and:

A composition is a 'bandish' or 'bhajan'.

Art, Culture & Heritage — Tansen — one of the 'nine jewels' (Navaratnas) of Akbar's court, patronised by Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior and then Akbar. Amir Khusrau (c. 1253-1325) is credited with origins of qawwali and the khayal form, and the invention of the sitar and tabla (by tradition); he lived long before Akbar.

(A) Swaras
(B) Shrutis
(C) Talas
(D) Alaaps
cards.back:
(A) Swaras

Art, Culture & Heritage — Swara — a musical note. The seven basic swaras are Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni (short for shadja, rishabha, gandhara, madhyama, panchama, dhaivata, nishada). Shrutis are the 22 microtonal intervals from which swaras are derived. Tala is the rhythm cycle. Alaap is the slow, improvised opening of a performance that unfolds the raga.

cards.front:
The Kumbh Mela rotates between four cities. Which of the following is NOT a Kumbh Mela site?

(A) Prayagraj (Allahabad)
(B) Mathura
(C) Haridwar
(D) Ujjain
cards.back:
(B) Mathura

Art, Culture & Heritage — Four Kumbh sites — Prayagraj (Triveni Sangam, U.P.), Haridwar (Ganga, Uttarakhand), Ujjain (Shipra, M.P.), Nashik (Godavari, Maharashtra). Mathura is NOT a Kumbh site. UNESCO inscribed Kumbh Mela on Intangible Cultural Heritage list (2017). Kumbh occurs at each site every 12 years; an 'Ardha (half) Kumbh' falls in between at Prayagraj and Haridwar (~6-year gap). Maha Kumbh 2025 at Prayagraj — one of the largest gatherings of humans ever (estimated >40 crore visitors over 45 days).

cards.front:
'Bidriware' — ornamental metal ware with silver inlay on a blackened zinc-copper alloy base — originates from:

(A) Bidar, Karnataka
(B) Moradabad, UP
(C) Tanjavur, Tamil Nadu
(D) Surat, Gujarat
cards.back:
(A) Bidar, Karnataka

Art, Culture & Heritage — Bidri — named after Bidar town (Karnataka, formerly part of Hyderabad State). 14th-century Bahmani Sultanate origin. Process: (1) cast a zinc-copper alloy (95:5) base; (2) engrave the design; (3) inlay pure silver wire / sheet; (4) treat with paste of soil (special Bidar soil + ammonium chloride) → permanent matte black background highlighting the silver. GI tag 2006. Moradabad — brassware. Tanjavur — Tanjore paintings + plates. Surat — zari embroidery.

cards.front:
'Dhokra' — non-ferrous metal casting using the lost-wax technique with tribal aesthetics — is most famously practiced in:

(A) Punjab
(B) Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha (tribal belt)
(C) Kerala
(D) Sikkim
cards.back:
(B) Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha (tribal belt)

Art, Culture & Heritage — Dhokra (also Dokra) — 4,000-year-old lost-wax bronze casting tradition. The famous 'Dancing Girl' of Mohenjodaro (~2500 BCE) was made by this technique. Process: clay core → wax model → covered in clay mold → fire melts wax out (lost wax) → molten bronze poured in → break mold to retrieve casting. Rural artisan communities — Ojha (Chhattisgarh), Sithulias (WB) — preserve the craft. GI tags: Dokra (Chhattisgarh), Bankura Dokra (WB).

'Kovalam' is to brass-engraved art-pieces as 'Aranmula' is to:

cards.back:

cards.front:
India's first newspaper, 'The Bengal Gazette' (or 'Hicky's Gazette'), was started in 1780 by:

(A) Robert Knight
(B) James Augustus Hicky in Calcutta
(C) Lord Hastings
(D) William Carey
cards.back:
(B) James Augustus Hicky in Calcutta

Art, Culture & Heritage — Hicky's Bengal Gazette — first issue 29 January 1780 in Calcutta. Weekly, English. Critical of Warren Hastings (Governor-General) — Hicky was prosecuted, jailed, and the paper shut down 1782. India's first English-language newspaper, first newspaper of the subcontinent. Other early titles — India Gazette (1781, less critical, government-friendly), Calcutta Gazette (1784, official). Indian-language press began later — Samachar Darpan (Bengali, 1818, by Carey at Serampore Mission Press).

cards.front:
Bal Gangadhar Tilak's two famous newspapers were:

(A) The Hindu and The Mahratta
(B) Kesari (Marathi) and The Mahratta (English)
(C) Young India and Navjivan
(D) Bombay Chronicle and Tribune
cards.back:
(B) Kesari (Marathi) and The Mahratta (English)

Art, Culture & Heritage — Tilak co-founded Kesari (Marathi, 1881) and Mahratta (English, 1881) with Gopal Ganesh Agarkar. Used these to attack British rule and rally Indian nationalism. Famously prosecuted twice for sedition — 1897, 1908 (sentenced to 6 years rigorous imprisonment, served in Mandalay, Burma). Published from Pune. Mahatma Gandhi later founded Young India (English, 1919) and Navjivan (Gujarati). Other notable papers: The Hindu (1878, founded by G. Subramania Iyer), Statesman, Pioneer, Bombay Chronicle.

cards.front:
The Vernacular Press Act, 1878 — which restricted Indian-language newspapers — was enacted by:

(A) Lord Curzon
(B) Lord Lytton
(C) Lord Ripon
(D) Warren Hastings
cards.back:
(B) Lord Lytton

Art, Culture & Heritage — Vernacular Press Act 1878 — passed by Viceroy Lord Lytton in response to vernacular criticism of British policies during the 1876-78 Bengal famine. Hindustan and other Indian-language papers were the target — English papers were exempted (clearly discriminatory; called 'gagging act'). Lord Ripon (Lytton's successor) repealed it in 1882. Other repressive press acts — Indian Press Act 1910 (Minto-Morley reforms era; deposit requirement), Indian Press Emergency Act 1931 (against Civil Disobedience Movement).

The 'Press Council of India' (PCI) is a statutory body established under:

(A) Constitution of India
(B) Press Council Act, 1978
(C) Indian Press Act, 1910
(D) Information & Broadcasting Code
cards.back:
(B) Press Council Act, 1978

Art, Culture & Heritage — PCI — established under Press Council Act 1978 (replacing earlier 1965 Act, which lapsed during Emergency). Self-regulatory body for the print media. 28 members + Chairman (a retired Supreme Court judge). Issues media norms, hears complaints. Not for electronic / digital media (those covered separately by IT Rules 2021, broadcasting code). Sevanti Ninan, Markandey Katju were past chairpersons. Headquartered in New Delhi.

cards.front:
The Tabla is classified under which category of Indian musical instruments?

(A) Tata Vadya (string)
(B) Sushir Vadya (wind)
(C) Avanaddha Vadya (percussion/membrane)
(D) Ghana Vadya (solid/self-sounding)
cards.back:
(C) Avanaddha Vadya (percussion/membrane)

Art, Culture & Heritage — Indian instruments are classified into 4 categories (Natya Shastra by Bharat Muni): (1) TATA VADYA = string (Sitar, Sarod, Veena, Sarangi, Santoor); (2) SUSHIR VADYA = wind (Bansuri, Shehnai, Nadaswaram, Shankh); (3) AVANADDHA VADYA = percussion with stretched membrane (Tabla, Mridangam, Dholak, Pakhawaj); (4) GHANA VADYA = solid/self-sounding, no strings or membrane (Manjira, Ghatam, Kartal, Jaltarang). Tabla was developed in the 18th c., reportedly by Amir Khusrau's disciple — hence it's relatively recent compared to Pakhawaj.

cards.back:

Art, Culture & Heritage — The Shehnai is a SUSHIR (wind/reed) instrument — a double-reed oboe-family instrument made of wood with a metal flared bell. Traditionally played at weddings, temples, and on auspicious occasions in North India; considered a symbol of auspiciousness ('mangal vadya'). The legendary Ustad BISMILLAH KHAN (1916-2006) — Bharat Ratna 2001 — was the Shehnai's greatest modern exponent; he played at Red Fort on 15 August 1947. South Indian counterpart: NADASWARAM (longer, louder, always played outdoors).

The Mridangam's Carnatic equivalents: Ghatam (clay pot), Kanjira (tambourine), Morsing (jaw harp). Palghat Mani Iyer, TK Murthy, Umayalpuram Sivaraman are legendary exponents.

The Trinity of Carnatic Music refers to which three 18th-century composers?

Art, Culture & Heritage — The PENA (also called Bana or Tingtelia) is a traditional single-stringed bowed chordophone of Manipur, made of a coconut-shell resonator covered with dry leather and a bamboo neck. Central to the Meitei people's cultural repertoire — especially accompanying the narration of the Khamba-Thoibi legend. Pena artists are called 'Pena Asheiba'. Other state-specific folk instruments worth knowing: PEPA (buffalo-horn flute — Assam's Bihu), GOGONA (reed-jaw harp — Assam), DHOL (Assam, Punjab etc.), BIHU DHOL, SUMUI (Manipur flute), DIMSA & RABAB (tribal).

cards.back:

cards.front:
Which Hindustani gharana is the OLDEST traditional gharana of classical vocal music?

(A) Kirana Gharana
(B) Gwalior Gharana
(C) Patiala Gharana
(D) Agra Gharana
cards.back:
(B) Gwalior Gharana

Art, Culture & Heritage — The GWALIOR gharana is the oldest school of Hindustani khayal singing, traced to Natthan Pir Baksh (late 18th c.) and the Haddu-Hassu brothers. Known for pure raga-based khayal, clear enunciation. Other major gharanas: AGRA (Ustad Faiyaz Khan — blend of khayal with dhrupad), JAIPUR-ATRAULI (Alladiya Khan — rare ragas, complex tans), KIRANA (Abdul Karim Khan, Bhimsen Joshi, Gangubai Hangal — emphasis on swara and mood), PATIALA (Bade Ghulam Ali Khan — thumri + khayal), RAMPUR-SAHASWAN (Mushtaq Husain Khan), BHENDIBAZAAR (Mumbai — influenced by Agra). Tabla has its own gharanas: Delhi, Lucknow, Ajrada, Farrukhabad, Benaras, Punjab.

Sarod is an adaptation of which Central Asian instrument, brought to India and evolved?

(A) Tanbur
(B) Rabab
(C) Setar
(D) Ney
cards.back:
(B) Rabab

Art, Culture & Heritage — The Sarod is a modified descendant of the Afghan RABAB, brought by Afghan warriors and refined in Gwalior during the 19th c. Unlike the wooden-fretted sitar, the Sarod has a fretless fingerboard covered with a steel plate and uses a coconut-shell resonator — giving it a deep, meditative tone. The GHULAM ALI KHAN / ALI AKBAR KHAN / AMJAD ALI KHAN lineage and the MAIHAR gharana (Ustad Allauddin Khan) are principal exponents. The original Afghan Rabab is also played in Kashmiri music; Sitar evolved from Persian Tanbur/Setar.

(C) Ghungroo

cards.back:
(D) Sarangi

Art, Culture & Heritage — GHANA VADYA = self-sounding (idiophones): MANJIRA (small cymbals), GHATAM (clay pot, Carnatic), GHUNGROO (ankle bells), KHARTAL (wooden clappers), CHIMTA (metal tongs), JALTARANG (tuned bowls of water). SARANGI is a TATA VADYA (bowed string) — played with a bow; main accompaniment for Hindustani vocal music and Kathak. Its smaller bamboo cousin, the DILRUBA & ESRAJ, are also strings. Students often confuse Sarangi with Sarod (plucked) and the wind instruments — these are distinct classifications.

Art, Culture & Heritage — Madhubani (also called Mithila) painting originates from the Mithila region of Bihar (and parts of Nepal's Janakpur). cards.back:

cards.front:
Which is the oldest martial art in the world, originating in Kerala?

(A) Silambam
(B) Kalaripayattu
(C) Gatka
(D) Mardani Khel
cards.back:
(B) Kalaripayattu

Art, Culture & Heritage — Kalaripayattu, from Kerala (dating to ~3rd c. BCE per legend; codified documentation from 13th c. CE), is widely acknowledged as one of the world's oldest surviving martial arts. 'Kalari' = training arena; 'Payattu' = fight/exercise. Four stages: Meithari (body), Kolthari (wooden weapons), Ankathari (metal weapons), Verumkai (empty hand). Three regional styles: Northern (Vadakkan), Southern (Thekkan), and Central (Madhya) — differ in stance, footwork, philosophy. Sage Parashurama is considered the mythical originator. Silambam (TN, bamboo staff), Gatka (Punjab, Sikh warrior art), Mardani Khel (Maharashtra, Maratha art) are younger.

cards.front:
Thang-Ta and Huyen Langlon are martial art traditions of which Indian state?

(A) Nagaland
(B) Manipur
(C) Mizoram
(D) Assam
cards.back:
(B) Manipur

Art, Culture & Heritage — Thang-Ta ('Thang' = sword, 'Ta' = spear) and its broader philosophical framework Huyen Langlon ('method of safeguarding life') are the traditional martial arts of the Meitei people of Manipur. Practised for centuries as both warfare and ritual; revived as cultural heritage after a British ban in 1891 post the Anglo-Manipur war. Includes sword, spear, unarmed combat (Sarit Sarak), and spiritual practices. Recognised by SANG (sports body). Manipur also has Mukna (indigenous wrestling).

(B) Sikh warriors of Punjab

cards.back:

Art, Culture & Heritage — Gatka is the traditional weapon-based martial art of the Sikhs of Punjab, codified under Guru Hargobind (6th Sikh Guru, 17th c.) and refined by Guru Gobind Singh (10th Guru). It uses the 'gatka' (wooden stick simulating sword), shield, and the Khanda. Practised prominently during Hola Mohalla at Anandpur Sahib every Holi. It is both a spiritual discipline and combat system — the Nihang warrior order keeps the tradition alive. Mardani Khel is the Maratha equivalent; Chavittu Kali is another Kerala martial dance distinct from Kalaripayattu.

cards.back:

Art, Culture & Heritage — Silambam originates in Tamil Nadu; 'silambu' refers to the sound of the bamboo staff. Today it is a recognised tournament sport under the Silambam Asia Federation. Not to be confused with Kalaripayattu (Kerala), though both are Dravidian systems.

Raja Ravi Varma (1848-1906), one of India's most famous modern painters, is especially known for:

(A) Cubist abstract art
(B) Oil paintings of Hindu mythological scenes
(C) Madhubani folk art
(D) Chinese ink landscapes
cards.back:
(B) Oil paintings of Hindu mythological scenes

Art, Culture & Heritage — Ravi Varma was a pioneer of Western-style oil painting in India and became famous for his dramatic canvases of Hindu mythological scenes — 'Shakuntala', 'Damayanti and the Swan', 'Ravana abducting Sita'. He opened a lithographic press near Mumbai so that inexpensive prints of his paintings could reach ordinary homes, shaping popular iconography of Hindu gods.

cards.front:
The Kailash Temple (Cave 16) at Ellora, the world's largest monolithic rock-cut structure, was commissioned by which king?

(A) Pulakeshin II of Chalukya
(B) Krishna I of Rashtrakuta
(C) Rajendra Chola I of Chola
(D) Dhruva of Rashtrakuta
cards.back:
(B) Krishna I of Rashtrakuta

Art, Culture & Heritage — The Kailash Temple (Cave 16, Ellora, Maharashtra) is a monolith carved top-down from a single basalt rock by the Rashtrakuta king KRISHNA I (r. 756-774 CE). Dedicated to Shiva, modelled after Mount Kailash. Covers 2x the area of the Parthenon in Athens and is 1.5x its height. An estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock were removed. One of the greatest engineering and artistic achievements in human history. Ellora overall has 34 caves: 12 Buddhist (600-700 CE, south), 17 Hindu (600-900 CE, middle), 5 Jain (800-1000 CE, north) — a unique coexistence.

(B) Raja Raja Chola I
(C) Kulothunga Chola I
(D) Vijayalaya Chola
cards.back:
(B) Raja Raja Chola I

Art, Culture & Heritage — The Brihadeshwara (Peruvudaiyar, RajaRajeshwaram) Temple at Thanjavur (Tamil Nadu) was built by RAJA RAJA CHOLA I between 1003-1010 CE. It is one of the 'Great Living Chola Temples' (UNESCO WHS 1987, extended 2004). Features: the main vimana (tower) is ~216 ft high, one of the tallest of any Indian temple; crowned by a 80-tonne single-stone kalash on top; the massive Nandi bull statue at the entrance weighs 20 tonnes. Other Living Chola Temples: Gangaikondacholapuram (Rajendra I, 1035 CE), Airavatesvara at Darasuram (Rajaraja II, 12th c.).

(B) Narasimhadeva I of Eastern Ganga
(C) Anantavarman Chodaganga
(D) Pratap Rudra Dev of Gajapati
cards.back:
(B) Narasimhadeva I of Eastern Ganga

Art, Culture & Heritage — The Sun Temple at Konark (Odisha) was built by King NARASIMHADEVA I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty around 1250 CE — to commemorate his military victory over Muslim invaders. Designed in the form of a gigantic CHARIOT with 12 pairs of intricately carved wheels (representing 12 months/zodiac signs) and 7 running horses (representing days of the week or the Sun god's chariot). UNESCO WHS 1984. The main shikhara collapsed long ago; only the jagmohan (audience hall) and the dance hall remain. Called the 'Black Pagoda' by European sailors (as a navigation landmark).

The Khajuraho Group of Monuments, famous for their erotic sculptures and Nagara-style temples, were built by which dynasty?

(A) Pratihara
(B) Chandela
(C) Paramara
(D) Rashtrakuta
cards.back:
(B) Chandela

Art, Culture & Heritage — The Khajuraho temples (MP) were built by the Chandela Rajputs between 950-1050 CE — originally 85 temples; only 25 survive today (20 Hindu + 5 Jain). Most famous: Kandariya Mahadev (tallest, 31m, dedicated to Shiva), Lakshmana, Vishwanath, Devi Jagadambi, Chitragupta. UNESCO WHS 1986. The erotic sculptures (only ~10% of total sculptures) represent the temple's tantric associations, or celebrate life / Kama (one of the 4 purusharthas). The temples were 'rediscovered' by British officer T.S. Burt in 1838 after being hidden by jungle for centuries. Classical example of Nagara architecture.

cards.front:
Hampi, a UNESCO WHS, was the capital of which medieval empire?

(A) Bahmani Sultanate
(B) Vijayanagara Empire
(C) Hoysala Empire
(D) Western Chalukya Empire
cards.back:
(B) Vijayanagara Empire

Art, Culture & Heritage — Hampi (Karnataka, on the Tungabhadra river) was the capital of the VIJAYANAGARA Empire (1336-1565/1646 CE). Founded by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty in 1336 under sage Vidyaranya's blessing. At its peak under Krishnadevaraya (1509-29), Hampi was one of the world's largest cities (500,000 people). Destroyed after the Battle of Talikota (1565) when the Deccan Sultanates combined to rout the Vijayanagara army. Key monuments: Virupaksha Temple (active since 7th c.), Vittala Temple (musical stone pillars, stone chariot), Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables, Hazara Rama Temple. UNESCO WHS 1986.

Which is the ONLY mixed (natural + cultural) UNESCO World Heritage Site in India?

(A) Sundarbans National Park
(B) Khangchendzonga National Park, Sikkim
(C) Western Ghats
(D) Nanda Devi & Valley of Flowers
cards.back:
(B) Khangchendzonga National Park, Sikkim

Art, Culture & Heritage — Khangchendzonga National Park (Sikkim) — inscribed in 2016 — is India's ONLY MIXED UNESCO WHS (both natural AND cultural criteria). Natural: includes Mt Khangchendzonga (8,586m — world's 3rd-highest peak, and sacred to Sikkimese Buddhists), glaciers, lakes, diverse flora/fauna. Cultural: sacred landscapes of the indigenous Lepcha people and Sikkimese Buddhists — Khangchendzonga is revered as 'Mount Kinchinjonga' by locals and worshipped. Globally, only ~40 mixed WHS exist. Sundarbans, Western Ghats, Nanda Devi & VoF are all pure-natural.

cards.back:
(B) Vishnu

Art, Culture & Heritage — The Jagannath Temple at Puri (Odisha) is dedicated to Lord Jagannath ('Lord of the Universe' — a form of Vishnu/Krishna), along with his elder brother BALABHADRA and sister SUBHADRA. Built in the 12th c. by Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. One of the CHAR DHAM of Hinduism (Puri + Rameswaram + Dwarka + Badrinath). The RATH YATRA (annual chariot festival, June-July) is world-famous — three huge wooden chariots (Nandighosha, Taladhwaja, Darpadalana) pull the deities the 3 km journey to Gundicha Temple and back. The English word 'juggernaut' derives from Jagannath. NOT a UNESCO WHS yet but on tentative list. Krishna as Jagannath, with Balabhadra and Subhadra.

cards.front:
Dholavira, one of the five largest Harappan sites and a 2021 UNESCO WHS, is located in which state?

(A) Haryana
(B) Gujarat
(C) Rajasthan
(D) Punjab
cards.back:
(B) Gujarat

Art, Culture & Heritage — Dholavira is located on Khadir Bet island in the Great Rann of Kutch, Gujarat. Discovered 1968, excavated 1989-2005 by RS Bisht (ASI). Features: a tripartite layout (Citadel, Middle Town, Lower Town), an ingenious water harvesting system with 16 reservoirs, and a famous 10-character 'Dholavira Signboard' — possibly the oldest signboard in the world. Inscribed as India's 40th UNESCO WHS on 27 July 2021. OTHER KEY HARAPPAN SITES: Mohenjo-daro (now Pakistan), Harappa (Pakistan), Lothal (Gujarat — world's earliest dockyard), Rakhigarhi (Haryana — largest), Kalibangan (Rajasthan — ploughed field, fire altars), Banawali (Haryana), Surkotada (Gujarat — horse remains). Kutch region.
cards.storedExplanation: Dholavira is located on Khadir Bet island in the Great Rann of Kutch, Gujarat. Discovered 1968, excavated 1989-2005 by RS Bisht (ASI). Features: a tripartite layout (Citadel, Middle Town, Lower Town), an ingenious water harvesting system with 16 reservoirs, and a famous 10-character 'Dholavira Signboard' — possibly the oldest signboard in the world. Inscribed as India's 40th UNESCO WHS on 27 July 2021. cards.front:
The TAJ MAHAL, UNESCO-listed in 1983, was built by:

(A) Akbar
(B) SHAH JAHAN (1632-1653)
(C) Jahangir
(D) Aurangzeb
cards.back:
(B) SHAH JAHAN (1632-1653)

Art, Culture & Heritage — TAJ MAHAL — 'Crown of Palaces' — most iconic monument of India. LOCATION: AGRA, Uttar Pradesh, on south bank of Yamuna River. BUILT by SHAH JAHAN (Mughal Emperor 1628-58) as MAUSOLEUM for his beloved WIFE MUMTAZ MAHAL (Arjumand Banu Begum, died 17 June 1631 giving birth to 14th child GAUHARA Begum at Burhanpur). CONSTRUCTION: started 1632 (foundations + main mausoleum 1632-1643); whole complex completed ~1653 (21 YEARS). COST ~₹32 million then (~₹70 BILLION today). WORKFORCE: 20,000 labourers + craftsmen from India, Persia, Ottoman empire. MAIN ARCHITECT: USTAD AHMAD LAHAURI (from Lahore); with assistants from Persia + Turkey. MATERIALS: (a) WHITE MAKRANA MARBLE from Rajasthan (main); (b) RED SANDSTONE for adjacent buildings; (c) 28 TYPES of SEMI-PRECIOUS + PRECIOUS STONES — LAPIS LAZULI (Afghanistan), JADE (China), TURQUOISE (Tibet), SAPPHIRE (Sri Lanka), crystal (China), malachite, onyx, carnelian, amethyst, etc. INLAY technique = 'PIETRA DURA' (parchin kari). STRUCTURE: (1) GATEWAY (Darwaza-i-rauza) — red sandstone, massive. (2) CHAR BAGH (garden) — Persian 4-part quartered garden; reflecting pool with Taj mirrored; cypress trees (death) + fruit trees (life). (3) MAIN MAUSOLEUM on plinth — 4-sided symmetric; CENTRAL DOME (ONION-shaped, double-shelled, 35m high); 4 MINARETS (40m each, tilted slightly outwards so they fall away if earthquake hits). (4) Inside: cenotaphs of Mumtaz (centre) + Shah Jahan (off-centre, added later by Aurangzeb) under the dome; ACTUAL GRAVES in crypt below (closed to public). Walls inlaid with CALLIGRAPHY from Quran (by Abd al-Haqq Amanat Khan Shirazi). (5) MOSQUE (west) + GUEST HOUSE / Mehman Khana (east, symmetric counterpart). LEGENDS: (1) Black Taj myth — Shah Jahan planned a mirror-image in BLACK marble across river, never built (no historical evidence — likely romantic myth). (2) Architects' hands amputated — false myth. THREATS: (a) YELLOWING / pollution (SPM from Mathura refinery + Agra cottage industries; SC intervention — Taj Trapezium Zone Pollution case 1996); (b) wood foundation concerns; (c) tourist footfall wear (now regulated — entry capped 40,000/day with timed slots since 2018). RESTORATION ongoing — MUD PACK TREATMENT to clean marble; ASI + MOEF oversight. UNESCO WHS 1983; 'NEW 7 Wonders of the World' poll 2007 ranked it. 'A TEARDROP ON THE CHEEK OF TIME' — Rabindranath Tagore. 'THE PALACE OF LOVE' — romantic canon. mausoleum for wife MUMTAZ MAHAL; main architect USTAD AHMAD LAHAURI; 20,000 workers; one of 7 Wonders of World (2007).

cards.front:
The WESTERN GHATS, added to UNESCO list in 2012, is a NATURAL heritage site stretching through:

(A) Himachal to Bihar
(B) 6 states
(C) Sikkim only
(D) Entire east coast of India
cards.back:
(B) 6 states

Art, Culture & Heritage — WESTERN GHATS (SAHYADRI) — UNESCO NATURAL WORLD HERITAGE SITE inscribed 2012 — world's 8th biodiversity hotspot + one of the most biodiverse mountain ranges in the world. DIMENSIONS: ~1600 km long, parallel to west coast of India from Tapti River (Gujarat-Maharashtra border) to Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu). WIDTH 30-50 km; AVG ELEVATION 900-1500m; highest peak = ANAMUDI (Kerala) 2,695m. PASSES through 6 INDIAN STATES: (1) MAHARASHTRA — Bhimashankar, Mahabaleshwar, Western Ghats-Maharashtra. (2) GOA — Bhagwan Mahavir NP, Mhadei. (3) KARNATAKA — Agumbe (Cherrapunji of South), Kudremukh NP, Someshwara, Dandeli-Anshi (Kali Tiger Reserve), Mookambika WLS. (4) KERALA — Silent Valley NP, Anamudi, Eravikulam NP, Periyar NP (+ Tiger Reserve), Parambikulam TR. (5) TAMIL NADU — Nilgiris BR, Kalakkad-Mundanthurai TR, Indira Gandhi WLS, Mukurthi NP, Mundanthurai. (6) TINY in GUJARAT (north tip). UNESCO listed 39 COMPONENT PROPERTIES (7 sub-clusters). FEATURES: (a) 5,000+ FLOWERING plant species (35% ENDEMIC — found ONLY here); 100+ endemic species of orchids. (b) Home to NILGIRI TAHR (TN, Kerala — endemic), LION-TAILED MACAQUE (Kerala, Karnataka — endangered), NILGIRI LANGUR, MALABAR CIVET, PURPLE FROG (endemic, 'Mahony's frog'), KING COBRA, MALABAR PIED HORNBILL. (c) 508 bird species, 180 amphibians, 225 reptiles (60% endemic reptiles, 78% endemic amphibians). (d) Origin of peninsular rivers — GODAVARI, KRISHNA, KAVERI, TUNGABHADRA, PERIYAR, PAMBA, BHARATAPUZHA. (e) Dominant vegetation: tropical evergreen forests (SOUTH — Kerala, TN), semi-evergreen, tropical moist + dry deciduous, montane shola-grassland (unique stunted forests in valleys + grassland on hilltops). CHERRAPUNJI-equivalent wetness: AGUMBE Karnataka ~7500mm; MAHABALESHWAR Maharashtra ~6000mm. PROTECTED AREAS within: 20 NATIONAL PARKS, 68 WLS, several TIGER RESERVES (Periyar, Parambikulam, Kalakkad, Sathyamangalam, Bhadra, Bandipur, Dandeli-Anshi, Mudumalai, Wayanad). THREATS: deforestation, mining, hydropower projects, tourism, plantations, invasive species (Lantana, Eupatorium, Acacia). CONSERVATION: NIYAMGIRI case (2013, rejected mining), Madhav Gadgil Committee 2011 + KASTURIRANGAN Committee 2013 (recommended Ecologically Sensitive Area designation for 37% of Western Ghats — politically contested by states). 2021 Kerala + Karnataka floods blamed partly on deforestation + quarrying. Western Ghats = 'WATER TOWER of PENINSULAR INDIA'. Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu (+ tiny Gujarat); 39 component properties listed by UNESCO.

cards.front:
The KHAJURAHO GROUP OF MONUMENTS, UNESCO-listed in 1986, is famous for:

(A) Medieval rose windows
(B) NAGARA-style HINDU + JAIN TEMPLES (10th-11th c.) with INTRICATE SCULPTURES including tantric + erotic motifs; built by CHANDELA dynasty
(C) Buddhist caves
(D) Mughal architecture
cards.back:
(B) NAGARA-style HINDU + JAIN TEMPLES (10th-11th c.) with INTRICATE SCULPTURES including tantric + erotic motifs; built by CHANDELA dynasty

Art, Culture & Heritage — KHAJURAHO GROUP OF MONUMENTS — UNESCO WHS 1986; complex of medieval Hindu + Jain TEMPLES at KHAJURAHO village, Chhatarpur district, MADHYA PRADESH. Built 950-1050 CE by CHANDELA dynasty rulers (esp. YASHOVARMAN + DHANGADEVA + VIDYADHARA). ORIGINALLY 85 temples built; 25 survive today. STYLE: NAGARA (North Indian) — characterised by shikhara (tower) rising to a single point; curvilinear outline; square sanctum; 5 sub-elements (mandovara, shikhara, garbhagriha, antarala, mandapa). Temples grouped: (1) WESTERN GROUP (largest + most famous) — 14 temples; includes KANDARIYA MAHADEVA (tallest, 31m, ~870 sculptures), LAXMANA, VISHVANATHA, CHITRAGUPTA. (2) EASTERN GROUP (Jain) — PARSHVANATHA, ADINATHA, GHANTAI. (3) SOUTHERN GROUP (smaller) — Duladeo, Chaturbhuj. FAMOUS SCULPTURES (5% of total is erotic): renowned for 'MITHUNA' (amorous couples) + tantric iconography — rightly framed in context of EPIC-MAHAKAVYA tradition, Kamasutra-era social philosophy + goddess-tantrism. Most sculptures show DAILY LIFE, gods, celestial beings, guardians, yogis, secular subjects; erotic only on OUTER walls of specific temples. ICONOGRAPHY also celebrates FEMININE DIVINITY + PROLIFIC life + worldly concerns leading up to moksha — conceptual framework of Kama, Artha, Dharma, Moksha of Hindu life-purposes. HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE: (1) Peak of NAGARA architecture before Islamic invasions (Ghurid, Ghaznavid, Delhi Sultanate from ~1200 onwards). (2) Chandelas were major N Indian power — competed with Cholas + Palas + Rashtrakutas. FORGOTTEN for 500 years under jungle; REDISCOVERED BY CAPTAIN T.S. BURT (British army) in 1838. Alexander Cunningham mapped in 1852. ASI conservation since 1920s. KHAJURAHO DANCE FESTIVAL — annual week-long classical dance festival (since 1975), held in Feb-Mar outdoors against temple backdrop; features Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Odissi, Kuchipudi, Manipuri, Kathakali. Major cultural event; organized by MP Kala Parishad. RELATED Nagara-style heritage sites: KONARK SUN TEMPLE (Odisha 1984), SUN TEMPLE MODHERA (Gujarat, not WHS yet), LINGARAJA + Jagannath Puri (Odisha), Osian (Rajasthan), Bhubaneshwar Kalinga group, Kashi Vishwanath (rebuilt). DRAVIDA (South) style sites: Brihadeshvara, Mahabalipuram, Hampi, Pattadakal. VESARA (hybrid, Deccan) — Hoysala temples 2023 WHS.

RELATED Nagara-style heritage sites: KONARK SUN TEMPLE (Odisha 1984), SUN TEMPLE MODHERA (Gujarat, not WHS yet), LINGARAJA + Jagannath Puri (Odisha), Osian (Rajasthan), Bhubaneshwar Kalinga group, Kashi Vishwanath (rebuilt). DRAVIDA (South) style sites: Brihadeshvara, Mahabalipuram, Hampi, Pattadakal. VESARA (hybrid, Deccan) — Hoysala temples 2023 WHS.

cards.front:
The RANI-KI-VAV (Queen's Stepwell), UNESCO-listed in 2014 and FEATURED on the ₹100 currency note, is located at:

(A) Hyderabad
(B) PATAN, Gujarat
(C) Ajmer
(D) Jaipur
cards.back:
(B) PATAN, Gujarat

Art, Culture & Heritage — RANI-KI-VAV (Queen's Stepwell) — at PATAN, Gujarat (formerly Anahilavada, medieval capital of Chalukyas/Solankis of Gujarat). BUILT ~1063 CE by QUEEN UDAYAMATI (widow of King BHIMDEV I of Chaulukya dynasty, ruled 1022-64) as MEMORIAL to her husband. STEPWELL (BAOLI / BAORI / VAV) = multi-level well structure with steps descending to water table, for water storage, community gathering, pilgrimage. Rani-ki-Vav is the GRANDEST stepwell in India. STRUCTURE: (1) 7 LEVELS of steps descending to well; (2) 64m long × 20m wide × 28m DEEP; (3) oriented EAST-WEST; (4) 500+ SCULPTURES + 1000+ smaller motifs; (5) themes from HINDU MYTHOLOGY — DASHAVATARA of Vishnu (10 incarnations — Matsya, Kurma, Varaha, Narasimha, Vamana, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha, Kalki), plus scenes from Ramayana + Mahabharata; (6) APSARAS (celestial nymphs), yoginis, Brahmanic + tantric figures; (7) Seshashayi Vishnu (reclining Vishnu) at bottom. FATE: flooded + silted by SARASWATI river changes; rediscovered + excavated by ASI (1940s-1980s). Restored extensively. INSCRIBED on UNESCO World Heritage in 2014. Featured on INDIA's ₹100 CURRENCY NOTE (introduced in new Mahatma Gandhi series 2018). SIGNIFICANCE: (1) unique MARU-GURJARA / SOLANKI architectural style; (2) INVERTED TEMPLE form — unique in world architecture; (3) cultural + engineering achievement. OTHER FAMOUS STEPWELLS in INDIA: (1) CHAND BAORI (Abhaneri, Rajasthan) — ~800-900 CE, 3500 narrow steps, 13 storeys, 100ft deep — deepest stepwell. (2) AGRASEN KI BAOLI (Delhi, 14th c.) — 60m × 15m, atmospheric. (3) DADA HARIR STEPWELL (Ahmedabad, 1499, Queen Harir). (4) ADALAJ STEPWELL (Gujarat, 1499, Rudabai) — 5 storeys, Islamic + Hindu motifs. (5) RAJON KI BAOLI (Delhi, Lodi-era, 16th c.). (6) ROYAL STEPWELL (Dholavira IVC). (7) Raniji ki Baori + 100+ baoris in Bundi, Rajasthan. TRADITIONAL PURPOSE: (a) water for drinking + bathing + rituals; (b) cool sanctuary in hot summer; (c) gathering place for women (who fetched water); (d) TEMPLE SHRINE at water's edge (Vav = 'stepwell' OR 'wading place' OR 'well of wisdom'); (e) fort / caravanserai on trade routes. DECLINED with modern piped water + pumps; 1000s of stepwells abandoned → filled with debris. REVIVAL movements trying to restore them. built 1063 CE by Queen UDAYAMATI as memorial to Chalukya king BHIMDEV I; 7 levels of intricate sculptures + 500+ motifs.

cards.front:
SANTINIKETAN, inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2023, is associated with:

(A) Rudyard Kipling
(B) RABINDRANATH TAGORE
(C) Swami Vivekananda
(D) Sri Aurobindo
cards.back:
(B) RABINDRANATH TAGORE

Art, Culture & Heritage — SANTINIKETAN ('Abode of Peace') — UNESCO WHS 2023; the place immortalised by RABINDRANATH TAGORE (1861-1941) — poet, playwright, novelist, painter, composer, educator, Nobel Laureate. LOCATION: Birbhum district, West Bengal (~160 km from Kolkata). HISTORY: (1) 1862 — Tagore's father DEBENDRANATH TAGORE established 'Santiniketan Ashram' as meditation retreat on 20 acres donated by Raipur zamindars. (2) 1901 — Tagore (age 40) established experimental school 'Patha Bhavana' with 5 students (including his son Rathindranath) — open-air, nature-based education; students sat UNDER TREES. (3) 1913 — Tagore awarded NOBEL PRIZE in LITERATURE for GITANJALI ('Song Offerings', trans by Tagore + W.B. Yeats); FIRST ASIAN NOBEL LAUREATE in any field; only INDIAN Nobel in Lit until now. (4) 1921 — founded VISVA-BHARATI UNIVERSITY ('world university'); motto 'YATRA VISHVAM BHAVATYEKA NIDAM' ('where the world makes a home in a single nest'). (5) 1951 — declared CENTRAL UNIVERSITY by Indian Parliament; PM = Visitor, Prez = Visitor. TAGORE's VISION: (a) BREAK walls between disciplines — arts + music + literature + science + agriculture + rural reconstruction; (b) BENGALI + Indian cultural resurgence; (c) UNIVERSAL humanism; (d) INDO-foreign dialogue — foreign scholars invited (Leonard Elmhirst, Arthur Geddes, Christopher Isherwood, Aldous Huxley, Yukteswar Giri, Einstein's interactions). ICONIC STRUCTURES + FACULTIES: (a) KALA BHAVANA (Institute of Fine Arts) — nurtured NANDALAL BOSE, BINODE BIHARI MUKHERJEE, RAMKINKAR BAIJ (sculptor of 'Santhal Family' + 'Mill Call'), Satyajit Ray, K.G. Subramanyan. (b) SANGIT BHAVANA (music) — home of RABINDRA SANGEET. (c) PATHA BHAVANA (open-air school); (d) UTTARAYANA (Tagore's residence complex: Udayana, Shyamali, Punascha, Udichi, Konark houses; museum); (e) CHHATIMTALA (meditation tree grove). (f) VISHWA-BHARATI Library. TAGORE AUTHORED national anthems of INDIA ('JANA GANA MANA', first sung 1911 at Cong Calcutta session, adopted 1950) + BANGLADESH ('Amar Sonar Bangla', 1971) + strongly influenced Sri Lanka's anthem ('Sri Lanka Matha', by his student Ananda Samarakoon, 1940). RENOUNCED KNIGHTHOOD (1919 after Jallianwala Bagh). Called 'GURUDEV' by Gandhi, 'Bishwokobi' (World Poet). His paintings developed after age 65. FESTIVALS at Santiniketan: POUSH MELA (Dec, 3 days), BASANTA UTSAV (Holi), VARSHAMANGAL (monsoon). STUDENTS: Indira Gandhi, Amartya Sen, Satyajit Ray (trained in Kala Bhavana), Ritwik Ghatak, Suchitra Mitra. SANTINIKETAN was a STRONG CONTENDER for WHS list since 2010; finally inscribed at Riyadh (Saudi Arabia) WHC meeting, 17 Sep 2023.

cards.front:
HAMPI (UNESCO 1986), a UNESCO World Heritage site with spectacular ruins, was the capital of which empire?

(A) Maratha
(B) VIJAYANAGAR EMPIRE (1336-1646)
(C) Chola
(D) Chalukya
cards.back:
(B) VIJAYANAGAR EMPIRE (1336-1646)

Art, Culture & Heritage — HAMPI — UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986; initially 'endangered' list, removed 2006 after improvement). Ruins of the VIJAYANAGAR EMPIRE's capital (1336-1565), on south bank of Tungabhadra River, Ballari district, Karnataka. Area: 41.5 sq km; ~1,600 monuments. HISTORY: (1) 1336 — founded by HARIHARA + BUKKA brothers with blessing of sage Vidyaranya on ruins of earlier Anegondi settlement. (2) Peak 1500s under KRISHNADEVARAYA (1509-29) — Portuguese traveller DOMINGO PAES (1520) called it 'as large as Rome + much more beautiful to the sight'. (3) DESTROYED by combined armies of 4 DECCAN SULTANATES (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) at BATTLE OF TALIKOTA (23 Jan 1565); last ruler RAMA RAYA killed; city razed over 6 months. Never recovered. KEY MONUMENTS: (1) VIRUPAKSHA TEMPLE — ONLY temple still in active worship (pre-dates Vijayanagar, 7th c. Pallava origin; expanded by Vijayanagar); 50m main gopura. (2) VITTALA TEMPLE complex — 16th c., famous STONE CHARIOT (facing it) + MUSICAL PILLARS (musical sounds when tapped; 'saptaswara' pillars). Iconic image. (3) LOTUS MAHAL (royal pavilion, Indo-Islamic fusion). (4) ELEPHANT STABLES (11 domed chambers). (5) HAZARA RAMA TEMPLE (private chapel of royal family, 1000s of Rama reliefs). (6) KRISHNA TEMPLE complex. (7) QUEEN's BATH. (8) ACHYUTARAYA Temple. (9) NARASIMHA monolith (6.7m). (10) BADAVI LINGA. (11) Royal Enclosure + Mahanavami Dibba platform. (12) Talarigatta Gateway. (13) SASIVEKALU + KADALEKALU GANESHA monoliths. (14) Tungabhadra bridge ruins. BAZAARS: Virupaksha Bazaar (to main temple), Sule Bazaar, Krishna Bazaar — each once bustling with international traders (Portuguese, Arab, Persian, Chinese). LIVING HERITAGE at Hampi — PUSHPA RATHAYATRA festival continues; small village ANEGUNDI across river preserves traditions. LANDSCAPE: huge BOULDER-STREWN terrain — distinctive; dry arid Deccan with Tungabhadra providing water. ASI + Karnataka govt + UNESCO support conservation. TOURISM hit by 2019 Tungabhadra flooding; infrastructure expanding. Nearby sites: (1) HOSPETE town; (2) TUNGABHADRA DAM (1953); (3) ANEGUNDI. Hampi is one of India's most PHOTOGENIC sites — ruins against orange-red boulders + green paddy + blue river. Bollywood + international filming (PS-1, Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam, Guru). razed after BATTLE OF TALIKOTA 1565 by combined Deccan Sultanates.

cards.front:
AJANTA CAVES (UNESCO 1983), famous for Buddhist rock-cut paintings + sculptures, are in:

(A) Madhya Pradesh
(B) MAHARASHTRA
(C) Karnataka
(D) Odisha
cards.back:
(B) MAHARASHTRA

Art, Culture & Heritage — AJANTA CAVES — 30 BUDDHIST rock-cut cave temples + monasteries carved into a horseshoe-shaped cliff along the WAGHORA river valley, at AJANTA village, Aurangabad district, MAHARASHTRA. DATED: two phases — (1) 2nd c. BCE to 1st c. CE (Hinayana phase, caves 9, 10, 12, 13, 15A). (2) 5th c.-6th c. CE (Mahayana phase, most others — Gupta era; Vakataka patronage). ABANDONED + forgotten by 7th c.; lost to jungle. REDISCOVERED 28 April 1819 by a British Army officer CAPTAIN JOHN SMITH of the 28th Cavalry while hunting TIGER; carved his name + date in Cave 10 (graffiti still visible!). Subsequently surveyed by James Fergusson, Major Gill, Robert Gill (who documented 30 caves for 27 years, most lost in 1866 fire), John Griffiths (1872 onwards — copies again lost in 1885 fire at Imperial Institute London). Most of original copies now at Victoria + Albert Museum London. UNESCO WHS 1983. SIGNIFICANCE: (1) BEST-preserved examples of ANCIENT INDIAN PAINTING + SCULPTURE in the world. (2) Masterpieces of Buddhist religious art. KEY CAVES: (1) CAVE 1 — Mahayana era (5th c.); 'PADMAPANI' (Bodhisattva with lotus) mural — most famous painting in India; exquisite facial expression, serene meditation, 'compassion personified'. Also 'VAJRAPANI' (Bodhisattva with thunderbolt). (2) CAVE 2 — Jataka scenes. (3) CAVE 10 — Hinayana chaitya (stupa hall); earliest paintings (2nd c. BCE-ish). (4) CAVE 16 — 'MAHAJANAKA JATAKA' (Prince abandoning worldly life). (5) CAVE 17 — 'VESSANTARA JATAKA' + 'SHIBI JATAKA' (compassionate king gives flesh to eagle). (6) CAVE 19 — chaitya with superb facade. (7) CAVE 26 — reclining Buddha + parinirvana scene. TECHNIQUE: frescoes (Tempera on lime-plaster + clay-hair mixture base); vegetable + mineral pigments (lapis lazuli, ochre). Colours preserved 1500+ years due to cave microclimate. THEMES: mostly JATAKA tales (previous lives of Buddha), life of Buddha, Buddhist deities, court life, everyday scenes, nature, animals, apsaras. STYLE: vibrant, tactile, emotive — 'the birth of Indian classical painting'; influenced entire East Asian Buddhist art (Dunhuang, Bamiyan, Afghanistan + Central Asia caves). RELATED: ELLORA CAVES (100 km away, UNESCO 1983) — 34 caves (Buddhist + Hindu + Jain, 6-10th c.) — even more varied. PITALKHORA + BHAJA + KARLE + KANHERI + NASIK — other Buddhist rock-cut sites in Maharashtra. INDIAN rock-cut tradition = world's finest; ~1,200 rock-cut caves in India. Aurangabad district; 30 caves; 2nd c. BCE-6th c. CE; Jataka-tale murals; rediscovered 1819 by British soldier John Smith.

cards.front:
The KONARK SUN TEMPLE (UNESCO 1984) is shaped like a giant CHARIOT of the Sun God, with:

(A) 6 wheels + 3 horses
(B) 24 CARVED WHEELS + 7 HORSES pulling the chariot
(C) 12 wheels + 4 horses
(D) No chariot symbolism
cards.back:
(B) 24 CARVED WHEELS + 7 HORSES pulling the chariot

Art, Culture & Heritage — KONARK SUN TEMPLE (Surya Devalaya) — one of India's greatest temples; UNESCO WHS 1984. LOCATION: Konark, Puri district, ODISHA, on the Bay of Bengal coast. BUILT: 1238-1264 CE by KING NARASIMHADEVA I (r. 1238-1264) of EASTERN GANGA dynasty — to COMMEMORATE his military victories. DESIGNED as colossal STONE CHARIOT of SURYA (Sun God): (a) 24 EXQUISITELY CARVED WHEELS (2 sets of 12 on each side) — symbolism debated: 24 hrs of day, 12 months × 2 (solstices), or 12 zodiac signs × 2 halves; wheels function as SUNDIALS too (shadow cast on spokes tells time). (b) 7 HORSES pulling the chariot — representing 7 days of the week + 7 colours of the rainbow + Sun's 7 rays. (c) Temple stands on raised platform. NAME 'KONARK' = 'KONA' (corner) + 'ARKA' (sun). Dedicated to Surya, whose chariot is pulled by 7 horses in Hindu mythology. STRUCTURE: (1) DEUL / SHIKHARA (main tower) — originally 70m tall; COLLAPSED (partially early 1600s, entirely by 1837); only dattoraam + anunated walls remain (still 30m). (2) JAGMOHAN (porch/mandapa) — INTACT 38m tall, pyramidal. (3) NATA MANDIR (dance hall) — ruins. (4) Bhoga Mandira (offering hall) — partial. MATERIAL: khondalite stone (ferruginous, weathered, red-brown). CARVINGS: outer walls carved with intricate sculptures — erotic motifs, dancers, musicians, daily life, aquatic scenes, animals, gods, celestial beings — rivalling Khajuraho. PROBLEMS: (1) PARTIAL collapse of main tower (possibly built on weak base; some say struck by lightning; some say Muslim invaders; some say sinking base; debated). (2) SEA encroachment (sand-filling of interior by 1903 British to arrest further collapse). (3) Today remains standing + major tourist draw. KONARK was called 'BLACK PAGODA' (kalakhet pagoda) by European sailors — darker than Puri's 'White Pagoda' (Jagannath temple). SURYA idol originally stood in sanctum — unclear fate (destroyed or moved; current statue in Delhi National Museum). KONARK DANCE FESTIVAL — annual 5-day classical dance festival (December) held in temple grounds — Odissi, Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Chhau, Manipuri. TAGORE wrote: 'Here the language of stone surpasses the language of man'. ODISHA'S 3-TEMPLE 'GOLDEN TRIANGLE': Konark + Puri Jagannath + Bhubaneswar (Lingaraja). cards.storedExplanation: KONARK SUN TEMPLE (Surya Devalaya) — one of India's greatest temples; UNESCO WHS 1984. LOCATION: Konark, Puri district, ODISHA, on the Bay of Bengal coast. BUILT: 1238-1264 CE by KING NARASIMHADEVA I (r. 1238-1264) of EASTERN GANGA dynasty — to COMMEMORATE his military victories. DESIGNED as colossal STONE CHARIOT of SURYA (Sun God): (a) 24 EXQUISITELY CARVED WHEELS (2 sets of 12 on each side) — symbolism debated: 24 hrs of day, 12 months × 2 (solstices), or 12 zodiac signs × 2 halves; wheels function as SUNDIALS too (shadow cast on spokes tells time). (b) 7 HORSES pulling the chariot — representing 7 days of the week + 7 colours of the rainbow + Sun's 7 rays. (c) Temple stands on raised platform. NAME 'KONARK' = 'KONA' (corner) + 'ARKA' (sun). Dedicated to Surya, whose chariot is pulled by 7 horses in Hindu mythology. STRUCTURE: (1) DEUL / SHIKHARA (main tower) — originally 70m tall; COLLAPSED (partially early 1600s, entirely by 1837); only dattoraam + anunated walls remain (still 30m). (2) JAGMOHAN (porch/mandapa) — INTACT 38m tall, pyramidal. (3) NATA MANDIR (dance hall) — ruins. (4) Bhoga Mandira (offering hall) — partial. MATERIAL: khondalite stone (ferruginous, weathered, red-brown). CARVINGS: outer walls carved with intricate sculptures — erotic motifs, dancers, musicians, daily life, aquatic scenes, animals, gods, celestial beings — rivalling Khajuraho. PROBLEMS: (1) PARTIAL collapse of main tower (possibly built on weak base; some say struck by lightning; some say Muslim invaders; some say sinking base; debated). (2) SEA encroachment (sand-filling of interior by 1903 British to arrest further collapse). (3) Today remains standing + major tourist draw. KONARK was called 'BLACK PAGODA' (kalakhet pagoda) by European sailors — darker than Puri's 'White Pagoda' (Jagannath temple). SURYA idol originally stood in sanctum — unclear fate (destroyed or moved; current statue in Delhi National Museum). cards.front:
DHOLAVIRA, UNESCO-inscribed in 2021, is a major archaeological site of the:

(A) Mauryan era
(B) INDUS VALLEY / HARAPPAN CIVILISATION
(C) Gupta empire
(D) Vijayanagar
cards.back:
(B) INDUS VALLEY / HARAPPAN CIVILISATION

Art, Culture & Heritage — DHOLAVIRA — UNESCO WHS 2021 (added in Fuzhou, China online session). INDUS VALLEY CIVILISATION (IVC / Harappan) site on KHADIR BET island in the RANN OF KUTCH, Gujarat. 4th or 5th LARGEST IVC site (after Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Rakhigarhi + possibly Ganeriwala). DATED: ~3000-1500 BCE; 7 cultural stages identified. DISCOVERED 1967-68 by J.P. JOSHI of ASI. Fully excavated 1989 onwards by R.S. BISHT (ASI Director of Excavations). SIGNIFICANCE: (1) UNIQUE urban planning — 3 divisions (Citadel + Middle town + Lower town); (2) SOPHISTICATED WATER MANAGEMENT — 16 HUGE reservoirs (largest 73m × 29m × 10m deep!) capturing monsoon run-off + spring + groundwater; DAM, storm-water drains, check dams; RAINWATER HARVESTING on heroic scale (critical in arid zone receiving only 300mm rain). Largest reservoir system in IVC. (3) MAJOR SIGNBOARD — 10-character Indus script sign (each ~37 cm tall!) — world's earliest SIGNBOARD of its size; hung like a modern signboard, believed to be above gateway; letters carved on wooden boards inlaid with gypsum. INDUS SCRIPT remains undeciphered. (4) Extensive TRADE — seals, beads (agate, carnelian), copper objects — linked to Mesopotamia, Elam, Magan (Oman). (5) DEFENSIVE WALLS of massive stones (up to 18m thick at base); not seen at most other IVC sites. (6) ADVANCED 'STADIUM' or ceremonial ground (283m × 47m) — may have been ritual space. MATERIALS: built of CUT + DRESSED STONES (unusual — most IVC sites use mud-brick), plaster, some baked brick. OTHER MAJOR HARAPPAN SITES in India: (1) LOTHAL (Gujarat — first tidal DOCKYARD, Maritime Museum coming up, UNESCO tentative list); (2) RAKHIGARHI (Haryana — likely LARGEST IVC site, 550 hectares; 2019 DNA study on skeletons); (3) KALIBANGAN (Rajasthan — world's earliest ploughed field, fire altars); (4) BANAWALI (Haryana); (5) SURKOTADA (Gujarat — earliest evidence of horse?); (6) ROPAR (Punjab); (7) ALAMGIRPUR (UP — eastern-most); (8) MEHRGARH (Balochistan, Pakistan — precursor, 7000 BCE). FAMOUS FOREIGN SITES: MOHENJO-DARO + HARAPPA (both in Pakistan), GANWERIWALA (Pakistan). Total ~2000 IVC SITES identified; most in India post-partition. IVC covered ~1.5 million sq km — larger than contemporary Mesopotamia + Egypt COMBINED. Characteristics: planned cities, script, grid roads, drainage, standardised weights + measures, fire altars, no temples/palaces identified, terracotta figurines (Mother Goddess, Pashupati seal, Dancing Girl bronze, bearded priest-king steatite), bath complex at Mohenjo-daro, granaries. Khadir Bet, Gujarat; sophisticated water management + urban planning; 2600-1900 BCE.

cards.front:
Humayun's Tomb in Delhi — a UNESCO WHS — is architecturally significant because it:

(A) Is the oldest mosque in India
(B) Was the prototype inspiration for the Taj Mahal
(C) Features Dravidian gopuram style

cards.back:

Art, Culture & Heritage — Built 1569-70 by Humayun's widow Bega Begum, architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas (Persian). First garden-tomb on the subcontinent; charbagh layout; central double dome. Directly influenced the Taj Mahal (1653). Inscribed 1993.

cards.front:
The Battle of Plassey (1757) was a victory of the English East India Company over the Nawab of Bengal. Who led the English forces?

(A) Warren Hastings
(B) Robert Clive
(C) Hector Munro
(D) Lord Cornwallis
cards.back:
(B) Robert Clive

India — States & Symbols — Plassey, 23 June 1757 — Robert Clive with ~3,000 troops defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah's ~50,000 after the secret defection of Mir Jafar, Siraj's own commander. Mir Jafar was installed as a puppet Nawab. Hector Munro led the British at Buxar (1764); Warren Hastings was later Governor-General (1772-85); Cornwallis came in 1786.

The Battle of Wandiwash (1760) effectively ended the colonial ambitions in India of which European power?

(A) Dutch
(B) French
(C) Portuguese
(D) Danish
cards.back:
(B) French

India — States & Symbols — Wandiwash, 22 January 1760, during the Third Carnatic War — Sir Eyre Coote (English EIC) decisively defeated Comte de Lally (French). cards.back:
