cards.front:
HAL TEJAS, India's indigenously-developed LIGHT COMBAT AIRCRAFT, is manufactured by:

(A) ISRO
(B) HINDUSTAN AERONAUTICS LIMITED (HAL), Bengaluru
(C) DRDO
(D) BEL
cards.back:
(B) HINDUSTAN AERONAUTICS LIMITED (HAL), Bengaluru

Science, Tech & Defence — TEJAS — HAL LIGHT COMBAT AIRCRAFT (LCA); India's indigenously-developed 4.5-generation single-engine multirole fighter. DESIGNER: AERONAUTICAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCY (ADA, Bengaluru — under DRDO). MANUFACTURER: HINDUSTAN AERONAUTICS LIMITED (HAL) — PSU; India's premier aerospace company, HQ Bengaluru. PROGRAMME HISTORY: sanctioned 1983 (to replace ageing MiG-21); first flight Jan 2001; IOC (Initial Operational Clearance) 2011; FOC (Final Operational Clearance) 2019; series production began. VARIANTS: (1) Tejas Mk-1 — initial variant; 40 ordered (2005, 2010); currently in IAF service with 45 Sqn 'Flying Daggers' (Sulur TN) + 18 Sqn. (2) Tejas Mk-1A — upgraded; AESA radar (Uttam indigenous), SPJ (self-protection jammer), mid-air refueling probe, advanced weaponry (Astra, BrahMos-NG, BVRAAM); 83 ordered 2021 (Rs. 48,000 cr deal) + 97 more cleared 2023 — total 180 Mk-1A by 2028. (3) Tejas Mk-2 / MWF (Medium Weight Fighter) — bigger + more capable (17.5 tonnes MTOW, vs Mk-1's 13.5); Higher-thrust GE F414 engine; avionics + payload upgrade; first flight 2025-26; will replace MiG-29, Mirage 2000, Jaguar. 108 planned. (4) Tejas Navy — carrier variant for INS Vikrant (tested but pivoted to MiG-29K + future TEDBF — Twin Engine Deck-Based Fighter). ENGINE: currently GE F404-IN20; Mk-2 uses GE F414; 'KAVERI' engine (indigenous) still not fighter-grade ready after 40+ years. EXPORT: offered to MALAYSIA, ARGENTINA, EGYPT, PHILIPPINES, USA (test-bed), Indonesia. First export contract expected 2025-26. HAL OTHER PRODUCTS: (1) HAL DHRUV (advanced light helicopter, ~390 delivered); (2) HAL Rudra (Dhruv-WSI, attack variant); (3) HAL LCH Prachand (Light Combat Helicopter, FOC 2022); (4) HAL Chetak + Cheetah (licensed Aérospatiale); (5) HAL HTT-40 (basic trainer); (6) HAL IJT (intermediate jet trainer, troubled); (7) HAL Sukhoi Su-30MKI (licensed assembly, 272 in IAF); (8) HAL Hawk (licensed BAE AJT trainer); (9) HAL Dornier 228 (licensed utility). DEFENCE PSUs: (1) HAL — aero. (2) BEL (Bharat Electronics Ltd, Bengaluru) — electronics, radars. (3) BEML (Bharat Earth Movers, Bengaluru) — tanks, mining. (4) BDL (Bharat Dynamics, Hyderabad) — missiles. (5) MIDHANI (Mishra Dhatu Nigam, Hyderabad) — alloys. (6) GRSE (Garden Reach Shipbuilders, Kolkata). (7) MDL (Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Mumbai). (8) GSL (Goa Shipyard). (9) CSL (Cochin Shipyard). (10) HSL (Hindustan Shipyard, Vizag). OFB (Ordnance Factory Board) split into 7 DPSUs in 2021. PSU under MoD; HAL is also India's primary helicopter + aero-engine manufacturer.

PROGRAMME HISTORY: sanctioned 1983 (to replace ageing MiG-21); first flight Jan 2001; IOC (Initial Operational Clearance) 2011; FOC (Final Operational Clearance) 2019; series production began. VARIANTS: (1) Tejas Mk-1 — initial variant; 40 ordered (2005, 2010); currently in IAF service with 45 Sqn 'Flying Daggers' (Sulur TN) + 18 Sqn. (2) Tejas Mk-1A — upgraded; AESA radar (Uttam indigenous), SPJ (self-protection jammer), mid-air refueling probe, advanced weaponry (Astra, BrahMos-NG, BVRAAM); 83 ordered 2021 (Rs. 48,000 cr deal) + 97 more cleared 2023 — total 180 Mk-1A by 2028. (3) Tejas Mk-2 / MWF (Medium Weight Fighter) — bigger + more capable (17.5 tonnes MTOW, vs Mk-1's 13.5); Higher-thrust GE F414 engine; avionics + payload upgrade; first flight 2025-26; will replace MiG-29, Mirage 2000, Jaguar. 108 planned. (4) Tejas Navy — carrier variant for INS Vikrant (tested but pivoted to MiG-29K + future TEDBF — Twin Engine Deck-Based Fighter). ENGINE: currently GE F404-IN20; Mk-2 uses GE F414; 'KAVERI' engine (indigenous) still not fighter-grade ready after 40+ years. EXPORT: offered to MALAYSIA, ARGENTINA, EGYPT, PHILIPPINES, USA (test-bed), Indonesia. First export contract expected 2025-26. HAL OTHER PRODUCTS: (1) HAL DHRUV (advanced light helicopter, ~390 delivered); (2) HAL Rudra (Dhruv-WSI, attack variant); (3) HAL LCH Prachand (Light Combat Helicopter, FOC 2022); (4) HAL Chetak + Cheetah (licensed Aérospatiale); (5) HAL HTT-40 (basic trainer); (6) HAL IJT (intermediate jet trainer, troubled); (7) HAL Sukhoi Su-30MKI (licensed assembly, 272 in IAF); (8) HAL Hawk (licensed BAE AJT trainer); (9) HAL Dornier 228 (licensed utility). DEFENCE PSUs: (1) HAL — aero. (2) BEL (Bharat Electronics Ltd, Bengaluru) — electronics, radars. (3) BEML (Bharat Earth Movers, Bengaluru) — tanks, mining. (4) BDL (Bharat Dynamics, Hyderabad) — missiles. (5) MIDHANI (Mishra Dhatu Nigam, Hyderabad) — alloys. (6) GRSE (Garden Reach Shipbuilders, Kolkata). (7) MDL (Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Mumbai). (8) GSL (Goa Shipyard). (9) CSL (Cochin Shipyard). (10) HSL (Hindustan Shipyard, Vizag). OFB (Ordnance Factory Board) split into 7 DPSUs in 2021. PSU under MoD; HAL is also India's primary helicopter + aero-engine manufacturer.

cards.front:
India became the 4TH COUNTRY to successfully demonstrate ANTI-SATELLITE (ASAT) capability with Mission Shakti on:

(A) 15 February 2019
(B) 27 MARCH 2019
(C) 11 May 2018
(D) 26 January 2020
cards.back:
(B) 27 MARCH 2019

Science, Tech & Defence — MISSION SHAKTI — India's ANTI-SATELLITE (ASAT) weapon test. CONDUCTED 27 MARCH 2019 by DRDO from Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam Island (Wheeler Island), Odisha. TARGET: Microsat-R (DRDO-launched in Jan 2019) — a 740 kg satellite in LOW EARTH ORBIT at 283 KM altitude. INTERCEPTOR: PDV (Prithvi Defence Vehicle) Mk-II — a kinetic kill vehicle based on Prithvi + Ashwin missile tech, part of India's BMD (Ballistic Missile Defence) programme. Hit target in ~3 MINUTES after launch in 'direct ascent' kinetic kill. OUTCOME: INDIA became 4th country (after USA 1959+2008, Russia/USSR 1968+2021, China 2007) to demonstrate ASAT. MOTIVATION: deter adversary's space assets (primarily China's; China's 2007 ASAT test shook India's strategic calculus). SPACE DEBRIS CONCERN: unlike China's 2007 test (at 865 km, created 3000+ long-lasting debris pieces), Mission Shakti chose LOW altitude (283 km) — most debris burned up in atmosphere within weeks to months; ISS + other high-orbit satellites unaffected. India announced test in advance to US Space Command. ~400 trackable debris pieces created, 24 crossing ISS altitude (fell within days). BY 2023, virtually all Mission Shakti debris decayed. POLITICAL: PM Modi announced the test to the nation via TV address 30 min after strike. Timing (just before 2019 general elections) was criticised by opposition as electioneering. Election Commission probe found no MCC violation. STRATEGIC: India established DEFENCE SPACE AGENCY (DSA, 2019) + DEFENCE SPACE RESEARCH ORGANISATION (DSRO) to build dedicated space assets for military. Joining a newer push by major space powers: (a) USA Space Force (2019, 6th military branch); (b) China PLA Strategic Support Force (2015, upgraded Aerospace Force 2024); (c) France Space Command (2019); (d) Russia Space Forces (2015). INDIA's NEXT: (a) MICROSAT-R-class ASATs; (b) Space-Situational Awareness (SSA) — Bengaluru centre + radars; (c) EMISAT, CartoSat-3, RISAT-2B — military ELINT/ SAR. SPACE DEFENCE TREATY: INDIA is party to OUTER SPACE TREATY 1967 (no WMDs in space); not to specific ASAT ban; global norms still being debated (UN COPUOS, Artemis Accords 2020 signed by India in 2023). DRDO destroyed a target satellite in LEO (283 km) using indigenous ballistic missile; after USA, Russia, China.

cards.front:
The RAFALE multirole fighter jets inducted by IAF (36 aircraft) are manufactured by:

(A) Lockheed Martin (USA)
(B) DASSAULT AVIATION (France) — ordered 2016 at €7.87 billion; all 36 delivered by Dec 2022; Ambala + Hasimara bases
(C) Sukhoi (Russia)
(D) Boeing (USA)
cards.back:
(B) DASSAULT AVIATION (France) — ordered 2016 at €7.87 billion; all 36 delivered by Dec 2022; Ambala + Hasimara bases

Science, Tech & Defence — RAFALE — 4.5-generation TWIN-ENGINE multirole omnirole fighter made by DASSAULT AVIATION, France. INDIA's INDUCTION: 36 RAFALE purchased via GOVERNMENT-TO-GOVERNMENT deal signed 23 September 2016 by Indian PM Modi + French President François Hollande at Paris. COST: €7.87 BILLION (~₹59,000 crore). Originally India's MMRCA tender (2007-2015) chose Rafale in 2012 for 126 fighters but deal collapsed over pricing + local manufacture (Transfer of Technology terms with HAL). Modi govt replaced with smaller 36-jet 'off-the-shelf' outright purchase. DELIVERY: all 36 delivered between July 2020 + Dec 2022. BASED at: 17 Squadron 'Golden Arrows' — Ambala (Haryana), 101 Squadron 'Falcons of Chamb + Akhnoor' — Hasimara (West Bengal, near Chinese border). SPECIFICATIONS: (1) Engines — 2× Snecma M88-4E (75 kN each afterburning). (2) Max speed Mach 1.8 (2,222 km/h). (3) Range: 3,700 km ferry. (4) Combat radius: 1,850 km with 3 drop tanks. (5) 14 weapon hardpoints. (6) AESA radar — Thales RBE2-AA. WEAPONS: Meteor BVRAAM (150+ km, beyond any Chinese/Pakistani BVRAAM), MICA IR + EM, SCALP-EG cruise missile (560 km), AM39 Exocet anti-ship, HAMMER PGM. Nuclear-capable. INDIA-specific modifications ('Rafale-DH' = with helmet-mounted sight, Israeli jammers, etc.). CONTROVERSY: 'RAFALE DEAL' became major political issue 2018-19; Congress accused price inflation + HAL being dropped as offset partner (Anil Ambani's Reliance Defence chosen). SC dismissed PIL in Dec 2018. CAG report (Feb 2019) found Modi-era deal 2.86% CHEAPER than UPA-era terms. NAVAL RAFALE ORDER: 26 Rafale-M (Marine) signed 28 April 2024 — for INS Vikrant, replacing MiG-29K; ₹63,887 crore. IAF FIGHTER INVENTORY (2025): Su-30MKI (272), Rafale (36, +plus naval), Mirage 2000 (45, upgrade by Thales), Jaguar (117, upgrade), MiG-29 (66), MiG-21 Bison (being retired), Tejas Mk-1/1A (40+180=220 total planned), Tejas Mk-2 future. FIFTH-GENERATION: AMCA (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft) — 5.5-gen stealth under development, first flight 2028-29, induction 2035+. S-400 TRIUMF air defence system: Russian, 5 squadrons ordered 2018 for $5.4 billion; 3 delivered by 2024, remaining 2 delayed by Ukraine war. Most potent long-range SAM in Indian arsenal.

cards.front:
The PARAM VIR CHAKRA (PVC), India's highest WARTIME gallantry award, was first awarded (posthumously) for the:

(A) 1971 Bangladesh War
(B) 1947-48 J&K War
(C) Kargil War 1999
(D) 1962 Sino-Indian War
cards.back:
(B) 1947-48 J&K War

Science, Tech & Defence — PARAM VIR CHAKRA (PVC) — India's HIGHEST wartime military GALLANTRY AWARD. Instituted 26 January 1950; RETROSPECTIVE to 15 Aug 1947. DESIGNED BY Savitribai Khanolkar, an Indian-born Swiss woman. MEDAL: bronze, 3.5 cm diameter, with Ashok Chakra + 4 crossed swords in middle. INSCRIBED 'PARAM VIR CHAKRA' in Hindi + English. WORN on chest. RESERVED for 'MOST CONSPICUOUS ACT of BRAVERY or SELF-SACRIFICE' in presence of the enemy. FIRST RECIPIENT: MAJOR SOMNATH SHARMA, 4 Kumaon Regiment — KIA at BADGAM (near Srinagar Airport) on 3 NOVEMBER 1947 defending Srinagar airfield against Pakistani raiders during 1947-48 JK War. His last message: 'Enemy only 50 yards away. Heavily outnumbered. Devastating fire. WILL NOT WITHDRAW an inch BUT WILL FIGHT TO OUR LAST MAN + last ROUND'. His COURAGEOUS stand + that of his company delayed the raiders + saved Srinagar — without which J&K's fate could have been very different. His sister-in-law Savitribai Khanolkar designed the PVC medal; IRONIC that it was first awarded posthumously to her brother-in-law. GAZETTE: notified 21 June 1950. TOTAL AWARDED: 21 so far (since 1947). 14 POSTHUMOUS + 7 LIVING. RECIPIENTS (select): (1) Maj. Somnath Sharma (1947 JK). (2) Lance Naik Karam Singh (1947 JK). (3) Second Lt. Rama Raghoba Rane (1947 JK). (4) Havildar Major Piru Singh (1947 JK). (5) Naik Jadunath Singh (1947 JK). (6) Captain Gurbachan Singh Salaria (1961 Katanga UN Congo). (7) Major Dhan Singh Thapa (1962 Sino-Indian). (8) Subedar Joginder Singh (1962). (9) Major Shaitan Singh (1962). (10) Company Quartermaster Havildar Abdul Hamid (1965). (11) Lt. Col. Ardeshir Tarapore (1965). (12) Lance Naik Albert Ekka (1971). (13) Major Hoshiar Singh (1971). (14) Second Lt. Arun Khetarpal (1971 — AGE 21, posthumous). (15) Flying Officer Nirmaljit Singh Sekhon (1971 — ONLY IAF PVC). (16) Naib Subedar Bana Singh (1987 Siachen). (17) Major Ramaswamy Parameswaran (1987 Sri Lanka IPKF). (18) Captain Vikram Batra (1999 Kargil). (19) Captain Manoj Kumar Pandey (1999 Kargil). (20) Grenadier Yogendra Singh Yadav (1999 Kargil, LIVING). (21) Rifleman Sanjay Kumar (1999 Kargil, LIVING). KARGIL WAR (1999): 4 PVC awarded — largest cluster post-1971.

cards.front:
The KYOTO PROTOCOL (1997) was the FIRST international treaty to set BINDING emission reduction targets. It was SUCCEEDED by:

(A) Montreal Protocol
(B) PARIS AGREEMENT
(C) Copenhagen Accord
(D) Rio Declaration
cards.back:
(B) PARIS AGREEMENT

Science, Tech & Defence — UNFCCC (UN Framework Convention on Climate Change) — adopted 9 May 1992 at RIO EARTH SUMMIT (UNCED); entered force 21 Mar 1994. 197 parties. Annual Conference of Parties (COP) meetings. KEY MILESTONES: (1) 1997 — KYOTO PROTOCOL (COP-3, Kyoto, Japan) — first binding commitments. ONLY on 'Annex-I' countries (developed); commitment period 2008-2012 (~5% reduction below 1990 levels). Mechanisms: CDM (Clean Development Mechanism), JI (Joint Implementation), Emissions Trading. USA signed but didn't ratify; China + India exempted (emerging economies). 2nd commitment period 2013-20 (Doha Amendment) ratified late (2020) — ineffective. (2) 2009 — COPENHAGEN ACCORD (COP-15) — non-binding; 2°C target introduced; $100 billion/yr Green Climate Fund by 2020. (3) 2015 — PARIS AGREEMENT (COP-21 Paris, 12 Dec 2015, entered force 4 Nov 2016) — LANDMARK. All parties, bottom-up 'Nationally Determined Contributions' (NDCs). Target: limit temp rise to WELL BELOW 2°C above pre-industrial levels + pursuing efforts to limit 1.5°C. 5-year ratchet mechanism — NDCs reviewed + strengthened every 5 yrs. Global stocktake every 5 yrs starting 2023. India's NDC (updated 2022): (a) Reduce EMISSIONS INTENSITY of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030; (b) 50% cumulative electric power installed capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030; (c) Net Zero by 2070 (announced by PM Modi at COP-26 Glasgow 2021 as 'PANCHAMRIT' 5-point pledge); (d) Additional 2.5-3 GtCO2 carbon sink through tree cover. (4) 2018 — Katowice rulebook (COP-24). (5) 2021 — Glasgow Climate Pact (COP-26) — India's 'Phase DOWN' (not phase out) of coal; USA + EU committed to tripling renewables. (6) 2022 — Sharm el-Sheikh (COP-27, Egypt) — 'LOSS + DAMAGE' fund approved (historic — developed pay for climate damages in developing). (7) 2023 — Dubai (COP-28, UAE) — Global Stocktake 1; 'transitioning away from fossil fuels'; triple renewables + double efficiency by 2030. Ambition gap persists; current policies lead to ~2.7°C warming. (8) 2024 — Baku (COP-29, Azerbaijan) — 'Finance COP'; agreed NCQG (New Collective Quantified Goal) of $300 B/yr by 2035 for developing nations (criticised as inadequate; G77+China demanded $1.3T). limits global warming to WELL BELOW 2°C + pursuing 1.5°C; universal participation; 196 parties; Dec 2015, COP-21.

USA signed but didn't ratify; China + India exempted (emerging economies). 2nd commitment period 2013-20 (Doha Amendment) ratified late (2020) — ineffective. (2) 2009 — COPENHAGEN ACCORD (COP-15) — non-binding; 2°C target introduced; $100 billion/yr Green Climate Fund by 2020. (3) 2015 — PARIS AGREEMENT (COP-21 Paris, 12 Dec 2015, entered force 4 Nov 2016) — LANDMARK. All parties, bottom-up 'Nationally Determined Contributions' (NDCs). Target: limit temp rise to WELL BELOW 2°C above pre-industrial levels + pursuing efforts to limit 1.5°C. 5-year ratchet mechanism — NDCs reviewed + strengthened every 5 yrs. Global stocktake every 5 yrs starting 2023. India's NDC (updated 2022): (a) Reduce EMISSIONS INTENSITY of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030; (b) 50% cumulative electric power installed capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030; (c) Net Zero by 2070 (announced by PM Modi at COP-26 Glasgow 2021 as 'PANCHAMRIT' 5-point pledge); (d) Additional 2.5-3 GtCO2 carbon sink through tree cover. (4) 2018 — Katowice rulebook (COP-24). (5) 2021 — Glasgow Climate Pact (COP-26) — India's 'Phase DOWN' (not phase out) of coal; USA + EU committed to tripling renewables. (6) 2022 — Sharm el-Sheikh (COP-27, Egypt) — 'LOSS + DAMAGE' fund approved (historic — developed pay for climate damages in developing). (7) 2023 — Dubai (COP-28, UAE) — Global Stocktake 1; 'transitioning away from fossil fuels'; triple renewables + double efficiency by 2030. Ambition gap persists; current policies lead to ~2.7°C warming. (8) 2024 — Baku (COP-29, Azerbaijan) — 'Finance COP'; agreed NCQG (New Collective Quantified Goal) of $300 B/yr by 2035 for developing nations (criticised as inadequate; G77+China demanded $1.3T). limits global warming to WELL BELOW 2°C + pursuing 1.5°C; universal participation; 196 parties; Dec 2015, COP-21.

cards.front:
The GREENHOUSE GAS with the HIGHEST contribution to global warming (by volume + impact) is:

(A) Ozone
(B) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂)
(C) Water vapor
(D) Argon
cards.back:
(B) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂)

Science, Tech & Defence — GREENHOUSE GASES (GHGs) — trap HEAT in the atmosphere by absorbing infrared radiation (re-emitted from Earth's warm surface). Natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth at habitable 15°C (without it, would be -18°C); human emissions have ENHANCED it. KEY GHGs: (1) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂) — ~76% of human GHG emissions (CO2-eq); Global Warming Potential (GWP) = 1 (reference). Long-lived (centuries-millennia residence). Sources: fossil fuel combustion (coal, oil, gas), deforestation, cement making, land-use change. Concentration: 280 ppm pre-industrial → 420+ ppm (April 2025, NOAA Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii) → HIGHEST in 3-4 million years. Accelerating: +2-3 ppm/yr currently. (2) METHANE (CH₄) — ~16%; GWP 28-34 (100-yr) or 80+ (20-yr). Shorter-lived (~12 years). Sources: cattle (enteric fermentation), paddy fields, landfills, fossil fuel extraction (fracking, coal mines), wetlands. Rising rapidly 2020s. (3) NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O) — ~6%; GWP 265-298. Sources: fertilisers (Haber-Bosch N), biomass burning, industrial processes. (4) F-GASES (HFCs, PFCs, SF6, NF3) — ~2%; very HIGH GWP (1,000-25,000+); synthetic; used in refrigeration, electronics. Covered by Kigali Amendment 2016 to Montreal Protocol (HFCs to be phased down; India ratified Aug 2021). (5) WATER VAPOR — actually the most abundant greenhouse gas + accounts for ~50% of natural greenhouse effect, but NOT directly emitted by humans — a FEEDBACK (warming → more evaporation → more water vapor → more warming). (6) OZONE (O₃) — ground-level ozone is GHG + pollutant; stratospheric is protective. SOURCES of GLOBAL EMISSIONS (sector-wise, ~54 Gt CO2-eq/yr): energy 73% (electricity + heat 30%, transport 16%, manufacturing 12%, buildings 6%, fugitive 5%, other 10%), agri + forestry + land-use 18%, industrial processes (cement, chemicals) 5%, waste 3%. TOP EMITTERS (cumulative historical 1850-2021): USA 25%, EU 18%, China 14%, Russia 7%, Japan 4%, India 3%. TOP ANNUAL (2022): China 30%, USA 13%, EU 8%, India 7%, Russia 4%. INDIA's PER-CAPITA: ~2 tonnes CO2 (vs USA 15, China 8, world avg 4.7). IPCC AR6 (2021-23): 1.5°C warming likely reached by 2030s; limits to avoid 'catastrophic' tipping points; need 45% global emission cut by 2030. ~76% of anthropogenic GHG emissions (CO2-eq); atmospheric CO₂ 420+ ppm (April 2025) vs 280 ppm pre-industrial.

cards.front:
India has FOUR BIODIVERSITY HOTSPOTS (of the world's 36). Which of these is NOT one?

(A) Western Ghats + Sri Lanka
(B) Indo-Burma Region
(C) Himalaya
(D) THAR DESERT
cards.back:
(D) THAR DESERT

Science, Tech & Defence — BIODIVERSITY HOTSPOTS — term coined by Norman Myers (1988); regions with EXCEPTIONAL endemic species (≥1,500 endemic vascular plants) + LOST 70%+ of original habitat. 36 global hotspots identified by Conservation International. INDIA has 4 hotspots (FULLY or PARTIALLY): (1) HIMALAYA — entire Indian Himalayan range; covers W Himalaya (HP, UK, J&K) + E Himalaya (Sikkim, Arunachal, parts of NE); species: snow leopard, red panda, blue poppy, Himalayan monal (national bird of Uttarakhand), musk deer, takin (Arunachal state animal). (2) INDO-BURMA — includes NE India (except Assam Brahmaputra plain) extending into Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, S China; ~70% habitat loss; species: Hoolock gibbon (India's only ape), Brown hornbill, Swallowtail butterflies, ~1,300 bird species. (3) WESTERN GHATS + SRI LANKA — 'Sahyadri' range; 6 states (Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat tiny); UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012, 39 properties listed); ~6,000 flowering plants (35% endemic), Nilgiri tahr, Lion-tailed macaque (India's most endangered primate), Malabar civet, purple frog, Hampi, Agastyamalai, Silent Valley. (4) SUNDALAND — includes Nicobar Islands (India's piece) + entire Sumatra + Java + Borneo + Malay Peninsula; Nicobar macaque, Nicobar megapode, Nicobar scrubfowl; orangutans (just outside India). NOT in this list: Thar Desert (arid; low endemism; not a hotspot). 36 GLOBAL HOTSPOTS include Mediterranean Basin, California Floristic Province, Mesoamerica, Atlantic Forest (Brazil), Cape Floristic (South Africa), Madagascar, Caucasus, New Zealand. INDIA's BIODIVERSITY stats: (1) 8% of world's recorded species on 2.4% of land. (2) ~47,000 plant + ~89,000 animal species described; est total 1 lakh + 2 lakh. (3) 18 BIOSPHERE RESERVES (12 on UNESCO MAB list: Nilgiri 1986 first, Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar, Sundarban, Manas, Nokrek, Pachmarhi, Similipal, Achanakmar-Amarkantak, Great Nicobar, Agasthyamalai, Kanchenjunga, Khangchendzonga later additions, Cold Desert, Panna, Dehang-Debang). (4) 106 National Parks + 573 Wildlife Sanctuaries (as of 2024). (5) 54 TIGER RESERVES (largest tiger range in world; India has ~75% of world's wild tigers — 3,682 in 2022 census, up from 1,411 in 2006). (6) 33 ELEPHANT RESERVES. (7) 85 RAMSAR SITES (wetlands of international importance — India 2nd largest tally in Asia after China; Sundarbans, Chilika, Loktak, Wular, Harike, Keoladeo, etc.). PROJECT TIGER (1973), PROJECT ELEPHANT (1992), PROJECT CHEETAH (2022 — reintroduction from Namibia + South Africa into Kuno NP, MP), GREAT INDIAN BUSTARD (critically endangered, Rajasthan). is NOT a biodiversity hotspot (fourth is SUNDALAND-NICOBAR islands).

cards.front:
OZONE LAYER depletion was caused primarily by:

(A) Methane emissions
(B) CFCs (ChloroFluoroCarbons) — synthesized for refrigeration + aerosol propellants; banned by MONTREAL PROTOCOL (1987 — only universal-ratification environment treaty)
(C) Carbon monoxide
(D) Nitrogen compounds
cards.back:
(B) CFCs (ChloroFluoroCarbons) — synthesized for refrigeration + aerosol propellants; banned by MONTREAL PROTOCOL (1987 — only universal-ratification environment treaty)

Science, Tech & Defence — OZONE LAYER — the STRATOSPHERE (~15-35 km above Earth) has 90% of atmospheric ozone (O₃); protects Earth from UV-B + UV-C radiation (which causes skin cancer, cataracts, crop damage). DEPLETION DISCOVERED 1985 by Joe FARMAN + scientists of British Antarctic Survey — 'OZONE HOLE' over Antarctic (seasonal thinning in Sept-Oct each year); alarmed world. CAUSES: CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs, 'Freons') — synthetic stable gases used as: (a) refrigerants in fridges + ACs (DuPont's Freon-12 since 1928); (b) aerosol propellants in deodorants, paints, cosmetics; (c) solvents; (d) foam-blowing agents. At stratosphere, CFCs photolysed by UV → release CHLORINE atoms → catalyse destruction of OZONE (1 Cl atom destroys ~100,000 O3 molecules). Also HALONS, HCFCs, methyl bromide, carbon tetrachloride contributing. 1985 — PAUL CRUTZEN, MARIO MOLINA, F. SHERWOOD ROWLAND (Nobel Chemistry 1995) for identifying ozone depletion chemistry. MONTREAL PROTOCOL (16 Sept 1987) — international treaty to PHASE OUT Ozone Depleting Substances (ODS). Entered into force 1989; subsequent Amendments (London 1990, Copenhagen 1992, Montreal 1997, Beijing 1999) progressively tightened. ONLY UN TREATY ratified by EVERY UN MEMBER STATE (universal ratification). RESULT: (1) ODS production / consumption down 99% globally since 1990. (2) Ozone layer RECOVERING; expected full recovery by 2045 (Arctic) - 2066 (Antarctic). 'SUCCESS story' of international environmental action. KIGALI AMENDMENT to Montreal Protocol (2016) — added HFCs (HydroFluoroCarbons) — which had replaced CFCs but are potent GHGs (though don't deplete ozone). HFCs to be phased down by 80-85% by 2047. India signed 2021. 16 SEPTEMBER = INTERNATIONAL DAY for PRESERVATION OF OZONE LAYER. DIFFERENCE from CLIMATE CHANGE: Ozone depletion (UV) + climate change (IR) are DIFFERENT mechanisms but overlap (e.g., CFCs are also GHGs; recovering ozone affects circulation). Mario Molina said 'the ozone layer's recovery shows global environmental action is possible if science + politics align'. India played key role — CFC manufacturers (Navin Fluorine, SRF) had to retool. Post-2000, India banned CFC imports / production in stages; consumption 1 Jan 2010 fully phased out for major CFCs.

cards.front:
India's target for NON-FOSSIL FUEL installed electricity capacity by 2030 (per updated NDCs 2022) is:

(A) 100 GW
(B) 500 GW (total)
(C) 1000 GW
(D) 50 GW
cards.back:
(B) 500 GW (total)

Science, Tech & Defence — INDIA'S CLIMATE + RENEWABLE TARGETS (PANCHAMRIT — 'five nectars', pledged by PM Modi at COP-26 Glasgow, 1 Nov 2021): (1) Reach 500 GW of NON-FOSSIL ENERGY capacity by 2030. (2) 50% of electricity REQUIREMENTS from renewable energy by 2030. (3) Reduce total projected carbon emissions by 1 BILLION TONNES from now to 2030. (4) Reduce carbon intensity of economy by 45% (UP from earlier 33-35% target) below 2005 levels by 2030. (5) NET ZERO by 2070. INDIA'S CURRENT RENEWABLE STATUS (2024-25): (a) TOTAL installed capacity: ~452 GW (of which ~210 GW non-fossil, ~46% — on track for 50% by 2030). (b) SOLAR: ~93 GW (world's 4th largest; targeting 280+ GW by 2030); massive solar parks (Bhadla 2.25 GW Rajasthan world's largest, Pavagada 2 GW Karnataka, Kurnool 1 GW AP, Rewa 0.75 GW MP). Rooftop solar: 11 GW. Solar PM-KUSUM (agriculture pump solarisation), PM Surya Ghar (Feb 2024 launch — 1 crore rooftop solar for free 300-unit electricity). (c) WIND: ~47 GW (world's 4th largest; Tamil Nadu + Gujarat + Maharashtra dominate). (d) LARGE HYDRO: ~47 GW. (e) SMALL HYDRO: ~5 GW. (f) BIOMASS: ~11 GW. (g) NUCLEAR: ~7.5 GW (7.5% of non-fossil). (h) THERMAL (Coal + gas + oil): ~240 GW (~53%). INTERNATIONAL SOLAR ALLIANCE (ISA) — launched by India + France at COP-21 Paris 2015; HQ Gurugram, India (first global HQ of an intergovernmental body in India); 120+ member states; promotes solar in tropical countries between Tropic of Cancer + Capricorn. GREEN HYDROGEN MISSION (Jan 2023) — ₹19,744 cr National Mission; target 5 MMT green hydrogen production + 125 GW renewables by 2030. 'Green Hydrogen' via electrolysis of water using renewable electricity. MAJOR RE developers: Adani Green (world's largest RE portfolio coming up), Tata Power, Reliance, NTPC (now big RE player), ReNew Power, JSW Energy, Vedanta, Azure. India also has 8 GW of AGRI-VOLTAIC + FLOATING SOLAR potential. EV PUSH: FAME-II subsidy, PLI for batteries, NITI Aayog targets 30% EV penetration by 2030; CEEW estimates India will need 50+ GWh battery capacity by 2030. aim is 50% CUMULATIVE INSTALLED CAPACITY from non-fossil sources by 2030; part of 'PANCHAMRIT' Glasgow 2021 pledge.

cards.front:
The NATIONAL GREEN TRIBUNAL (NGT) is a SPECIALISED body for environmental protection, established under:

(A) Indian Forest Act 1927
(B) NGT Act 2010
(C) Environment Protection Act 1986
(D) Wildlife Protection Act 1972
cards.back:
(B) NGT Act 2010

Science, Tech & Defence — NATIONAL GREEN TRIBUNAL (NGT) — specialised statutory tribunal for environmental disputes. ESTABLISHED under NATIONAL GREEN TRIBUNAL ACT, 2010 (effective 18 Oct 2010). HEADQUARTERS: New Delhi (Principal Bench). 5 BENCHES: Delhi (Principal), Bhopal (Central Zone), Pune (Western), Kolkata (Eastern), Chennai (Southern). FIRST CHAIRMAN: Justice Lokeshwar Singh Panta (2011-12); then Justice Swatanter Kumar, etc. STRUCTURE: (1) Chairperson (retired SC judge or senior HC CJ); (2) Judicial Members (HC judges); (3) Expert Members (qualified in environment + science + engineering); (4) Total ~20 members. JURISDICTION: (1) CIVIL cases involving substantial environmental issue + 7 specified laws: Water (Prevention + Control of Pollution) Act 1974, Water (Cess) Act 1977, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Air (Prevention + Control of Pollution) Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, Biological Diversity Act 2002. (2) Appeals from Pollution Control Board / Forest Dept decisions. (3) Compensation + restoration. TIME-BOUND: NGT must dispose cases in 6 months. APPEAL: to SUPREME COURT within 90 days. LANDMARK ORDERS: (1) 2014 — banned 15-year-old diesel + 10-year-old petrol vehicles in NCR Delhi. (2) 2015-17 — odd-even scheme enforcement, ban on private vehicles on Yamuna floodplain. (3) 2017 — Art of Living Festival damages ₹5 crore for Yamuna floodplain damage. (4) BAN on sand mining Ganga basin. (5) Cleanup of Yamuna, Ganga. (6) 2016 — ₹100 crore penalty on Volkswagen for Dieselgate emissions cheating. (7) Pollution fine on industries (polluter pays principle). (8) Vizag gas leak (2020) compensation. POWERS (POLLUTER PAYS + PRECAUTIONARY + SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT principles enshrined): (a) order compensation/damages; (b) direct restoration of environment; (c) order closure of polluting unit; (d) suo-motu cognisance (added 2022 by SC in Municipal Corp of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha). COMPOSITION issues: NGT has faced VACANCIES + understaffing. Key ENV LEGISLATIONS in India: (1) ENVIRONMENT (Protection) ACT 1986 — umbrella law; post-Bhopal gas tragedy 1984. (2) WATER ACT 1974 — CPCB + SPCBs created. (3) AIR ACT 1981 — CPCB + SPCBs. (4) FOREST (Conservation) ACT 1980. (5) FOREST RIGHTS ACT 2006. (6) WILDLIFE (Protection) ACT 1972. (7) BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY ACT 2002 — NBA (National Biodiversity Authority, Chennai). (8) EIA NOTIFICATIONS (1994, 2006). (9) COMPENSATORY AFFORESTATION FUND ACT 2016 (CAMPA). 5 benches (Delhi principal + Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai); handles environmental + forest + biodiversity cases; orders time-bound.

(2) Appeals from Pollution Control Board / Forest Dept decisions. (3) Compensation + restoration. TIME-BOUND: NGT must dispose cases in 6 months. APPEAL: to SUPREME COURT within 90 days. LANDMARK ORDERS: (1) 2014 — banned 15-year-old diesel + 10-year-old petrol vehicles in NCR Delhi. (2) 2015-17 — odd-even scheme enforcement, ban on private vehicles on Yamuna floodplain. (3) 2017 — Art of Living Festival damages ₹5 crore for Yamuna floodplain damage. (4) BAN on sand mining Ganga basin. (5) Cleanup of Yamuna, Ganga. (6) 2016 — ₹100 crore penalty on Volkswagen for Dieselgate emissions cheating. (7) Pollution fine on industries (polluter pays principle). (8) Vizag gas leak (2020) compensation. POWERS (POLLUTER PAYS + PRECAUTIONARY + SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT principles enshrined): (a) order compensation/damages; (b) direct restoration of environment; (c) order closure of polluting unit; (d) suo-motu cognisance (added 2022 by SC in Municipal Corp of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha). COMPOSITION issues: NGT has faced VACANCIES + understaffing. Key ENV LEGISLATIONS in India: (1) ENVIRONMENT (Protection) ACT 1986 — umbrella law; post-Bhopal gas tragedy 1984. (2) WATER ACT 1974 — CPCB + SPCBs created. (3) AIR ACT 1981 — CPCB + SPCBs. (4) FOREST (Conservation) ACT 1980. (5) FOREST RIGHTS ACT 2006. (6) WILDLIFE (Protection) ACT 1972. (7) BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY ACT 2002 — NBA (National Biodiversity Authority, Chennai). (8) EIA NOTIFICATIONS (1994, 2006). (9) COMPENSATORY AFFORESTATION FUND ACT 2016 (CAMPA). 5 benches (Delhi principal + Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai); handles environmental + forest + biodiversity cases; orders time-bound.

cards.front:
PROJECT TIGER, India's flagship tiger conservation programme, was launched in:

(A) 1947
(B) 1 April 1973
(C) 1972 (WPA enactment)
(D) 1992
cards.back:
(B) 1 April 1973

Science, Tech & Defence — PROJECT TIGER — India's CONSERVATION FLAGSHIP; one of the world's most successful tiger conservation efforts. LAUNCHED 1 APRIL 1973 at Corbett NP by PM INDIRA GANDHI following alarming decline (1950s ~40,000 tigers → 1972 census ~1,827 tigers). BASED on KAILASH SANKHALA's work (first director). INITIAL 9 TIGER RESERVES: (1) JIM CORBETT (UP now UK); (2) RANTHAMBORE (Rajasthan); (3) SIMILIPAL (Odisha); (4) PALAMAU (Bihar now Jharkhand); (5) KANHA (MP); (6) SUNDARBANS (WB); (7) BANDIPUR (Karnataka); (8) MELGHAT (Maharashtra); (9) MANAS (Assam). TODAY: 54 TIGER RESERVES (as of 2024) across 18 states; ~75,000 sq km. NATIONAL TIGER CONSERVATION AUTHORITY (NTCA) — statutory body constituted 2005 under Wildlife Protection Act; chaired by Environment Minister. TIGER CENSUS (every 4 years, using camera traps + DNA + scat analysis): (a) 2006: 1,411 tigers (alarm — only 1,411 left; new methodology). (b) 2010: 1,706. (c) 2014: 2,226. (d) 2018: 2,967. (e) 2022 (released 9 April 2023, 50th anniversary of Project Tiger): 3,682 TIGERS. INDIA has ~75% of world's wild tigers (globally ~5,500). Key tiger reserves: BANDHAVGARH (MP, highest density), CORBETT (largest tiger population ~260), NAGARHOLE (Karnataka), PARAMBIKULAM (Kerala), TADOBA (Maharashtra), KAZIRANGA (Assam — tiger AND rhino), SARISKA (recovered from losing all tigers 2005; reintroduced 2008), PANNA (similarly recovered). 9th April = INTERNATIONAL TIGER DAY (WWF) — no wait, 29 JULY. FELINE SUBSPECIES: BENGAL tiger (Panthera tigris tigris) — India/Bangladesh/Nepal/Bhutan; 2nd largest tiger subspecies. WHITE TIGER — not a separate subspecies; colour mutation (leucism). SIBERIAN/AMUR TIGER — Russia/China; largest. South China, Sumatran, Indo-Chinese, Malayan are other extant subspecies; Bali, Javan, Caspian tigers EXTINCT. Other INDIAN Projects: (1) PROJECT ELEPHANT (1992) — 33 Elephant Reserves; ~30,000 Asian elephants in India (60% of global population). (2) PROJECT SNOW LEOPARD (2009) — 12 Himalayan states/UTs. (3) PROJECT RHINO (1987) — Assam, WB; Greater one-horned rhino (Indian Rhino) — 3,700+ (world's 80%). (4) PROJECT CHEETAH (2022, 17 Sep) — cheetah reintroduction to Kuno NP, MP; 20 cheetahs from Namibia + SAfrica; many cubs; adult deaths + heat issues; ongoing — India's first reintroduction of an extinct (since 1952) species. (5) PROJECT DOLPHIN (2020) — Gangetic River Dolphin (national aquatic animal since 2010). by Indira Gandhi; initial 9 reserves incl. JIM CORBETT, Ranthambore, Kanha, Sundarbans; now 54 tiger reserves.

cards.front:
The IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change), which produces ASSESSMENT REPORTS on climate change, was established by:

(A) G20
(B) UNEP + WMO (World Meteorological Organization) in 1988
(C) US Congress
(D) Greenpeace
cards.back:
(B) UNEP + WMO (World Meteorological Organization) in 1988

Science, Tech & Defence — IPCC (INTERGOVERNMENTAL PANEL ON CLIMATE CHANGE) — UN body assessing scientific basis of climate change. ESTABLISHED 1988 jointly by UNEP (UN Environment Programme) + WMO (World Meteorological Organization). HQ: Geneva, Switzerland. MEMBERSHIP: 195 member states. SCIENTIFIC WORK: Does NOT do original research; ASSESSES + SYNTHESISES peer-reviewed scientific literature + prepares reports. ASSESSMENT REPORTS (AR): every 5-7 years; written by hundreds of volunteer scientists; approved line-by-line by government representatives in plenary. AR1 (1990), AR2 (1995), AR3 (2001), AR4 (2007 — 'Unequivocal warming' declared; shared NOBEL PEACE PRIZE with AL GORE 'An Inconvenient Truth'), AR5 (2013-14), AR6 (2021-23 — 3 Working Group reports + Synthesis Report + 3 Special Reports). AR6 KEY FINDINGS: (1) HUMAN INFLUENCE unequivocally causing warming. (2) Temperature rise ~1.1°C since 1850-1900; likely 1.5°C by early 2030s. (3) LIMITING warming to 1.5°C requires 45% GLOBAL emission CUT by 2030 + NET ZERO by ~2050. (4) Many tipping points (WAIS + GrIS collapse, Amazon dieback, AMOC slowdown, permafrost methane) may be crossed. (5) ADAPTATION has limits. SPECIAL REPORTS: (a) SR15 (2018) — 1.5°C special report; galvanised pre-Paris ambition. (b) SRCCL (2019) — Climate Change + Land. (c) SROCC (2019) — Ocean + Cryosphere. WORKING GROUPS: WG-I (Physical Science Basis), WG-II (Impacts, Adaptation, Vulnerability), WG-III (Mitigation). CURRENT CHAIR: Jim SKEA (UK, elected July 2023; replaced India's Hoesung Lee 2015-23 — South Korean). HOESUNG LEE was 1st Asian Chair. NOTABLE INDIAN climate scientists: (1) RAJENDRA PACHAURI — IPCC Chair 2002-2015; resigned amid controversy; led TERI. (2) Jayanth Pasricha. (3) Dinesh K. Paul. OTHER KEY CLIMATE INSTITUTIONS: (1) UNFCCC Secretariat (Bonn). (2) World Bank + IMF's increasing climate focus. (3) G20 under Indian Presidency 2023 — strong climate dialogue. (4) COP (Conference of Parties) to UNFCCC — COP-29 Baku 2024. INDIA's CLIMATE INSTITUTIONS: (1) Ministry of Environment, Forest + Climate Change (MoEFCC). (2) Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB). (3) IMD (India Meteorological Department). (4) Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM, Pune). (5) National Institute of Oceanography. (6) Forest Survey of India. (7) State Action Plans on Climate Change (SAPCC). (8) National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008) with 8 missions: Solar, Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge. 'science agency' of UN climate action; Nobel Peace Prize 2007 (shared with Al Gore).

cards.front:
The RAMSAR CONVENTION, 1971, is an international treaty for the conservation of:

(A) Forests
(B) WETLANDS of international importance
(C) Deserts
(D) Grasslands
cards.back:
(B) WETLANDS of international importance

Science, Tech & Defence — RAMSAR CONVENTION on WETLANDS — intergovernmental treaty for 'the conservation + wise use of wetlands'. Signed on 2 February 1971 at RAMSAR, Iran (a city on Caspian Sea). Effective 1975. 170 parties + 2,500+ Ramsar Sites globally (~257 million hectares). INDIA became party 1982. WETLAND — area where water is the primary factor controlling environment + plant + animal life; includes lakes, rivers, marshes, swamps, mangroves, peatlands, ponds, coral reefs, estuaries, mudflats. INDIA's RAMSAR SITES: 85 (as of 2024, expanded rapidly — was 26 in 2018, pushed aggressively to 75 for 75th Independence anniversary 2022, now 85). 2nd LARGEST TALLY in ASIA after China; 3rd LARGEST in world after UK + Mexico. FAMOUS SITES: (1) CHILIKA LAKE, ODISHA — 1st Ramsar site designated 1981; India's largest brackish-water lagoon (~1100 sq km, varying); home to Irrawaddy dolphins + flamingos. (2) KEOLADEO GHANA / Bharatpur, RAJASTHAN (1981) — 29 sq km; migratory birds paradise (Siberian crane once, now gone); UNESCO WHS too (1985). (3) SAMBHAR LAKE (RAJ) — largest inland saltwater lake. (4) WULAR LAKE (J&K) — Himalaya's largest freshwater lake. (5) HARIKE WETLAND (Punjab) — largest wetland in North India; migratory birds. (6) LOKTAK LAKE (MANIPUR) — largest freshwater lake in NE; floating 'phumdis' (islands of vegetation); Sangai (brow-antlered deer, state animal of Manipur) habitat in Keibul Lamjao NP (world's only FLOATING national park). (7) KOLLERU LAKE (AP). (8) POINT CALIMERE (TN) — flamingos. (9) DEEPOR BEEL (Assam). (10) NALSAROVAR (Gujarat). (11) SUNDARBANS (WB) — mangrove UNESCO WHS + biosphere reserve; royal bengal tiger. (12) RENUKA (HP). (13) CHANDERTAL (HP). (14) HOKERA (J&K). (15) TSOMORIRI (Ladakh). (16) UPPER GANGA RIVER (UP). WORLD WETLANDS DAY — 2 FEBRUARY each year. UNIQUE INDIAN WETLAND FACTS: (1) CHILIKA is Asia's largest coastal lagoon + LARGEST wintering ground for migratory waterfowl in India. (2) KANJLI (Punjab) — 1st man-made Ramsar. (3) INDIA's 10 LARGEST Ramsar sites are >150 sq km each. WETLAND CONSERVATION programmes: National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA), Amrit Dharohar (2023 budget), Mishti mangrove scheme (2023). Threats: urbanisation (wetland loss 40% since 1970s), pollution, encroachment, invasive species (Eichhornia water hyacinth), drying + siltation, sand mining. signed at Ramsar, Iran; India has 85 Ramsar sites (2nd largest in Asia after China); covers lakes, marshes, estuaries.

cards.front:
The SWACHH BHARAT ABHIYAN (Clean India Mission), launched in 2014, aimed for:

(A) Air pollution reduction only
(B) UNIVERSAL SANITATION
(C) Rainwater harvesting
(D) Plastic ban
cards.back:
(B) UNIVERSAL SANITATION

Science, Tech & Defence — SWACHH BHARAT ABHIYAN (SBA) / SWACHH BHARAT MISSION (SBM) — India's largest-ever SANITATION drive. LAUNCHED 2 OCT 2014 (Gandhi Jayanti) by PM NARENDRA MODI at Rajghat, Delhi. Mission symbol: GANDHI's SPECTACLES. FOUNDING GOAL: 'Open Defecation Free (ODF) INDIA by 2 October 2019' — 150th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi. TWO COMPONENTS: (1) SBM (Grameen) — rural, implemented by Ministry of Drinking Water + Sanitation (now Jal Shakti). (2) SBM (Urban) — urban, implemented by Ministry of Housing + Urban Affairs. KEY TARGETS + ACHIEVEMENTS (Phase-I 2014-19): (1) 11+ CRORE household TOILETS built (rural + urban). (2) Rural household sanitation coverage rose from ~39% (2014) to 100% (officially 2 Oct 2019; self-declaration). (3) Over 6 lakh villages declared ODF. (4) 4,300+ cities declared ODF. (5) Solid waste management: door-to-door collection, segregation at source, waste processing; ~66% urban waste processed (up from 18%). FUNDING: Centre-state 60:40 (rural), 75:25 (Northeast + Himalayan). Total spend ~₹1.35 lakh crore. PHASE II (2020-2025 / 2025-26 extension): (a) 'ODF-PLUS' — beyond toilet construction to include SLWM (solid + liquid waste management), greywater treatment, faecal sludge management. Target: ODF-Plus for all villages by 2025. (b) 100% door-to-door waste segregation in urban areas. (c) Dump-site remediation. (d) PLASTIC WASTE management (single-use plastics banned July 2022). SUB-SCHEMES: Nirmal Bharat, GOBAR-Dhan (biogas), Individual Household Latrines (IHHL), Community/Public Toilets, Swachhata App, Swachh Sarvekshan (annual urban cleanliness survey — Indore has TOPPED the rankings 6 times consecutively). ACHIEVEMENTS notable: (1) India reduced reported open defecation from ~564 million people (2014) to ~12 million (2022 estimates — partial; real figure disputed, WHO/UNICEF JMP says varies). (2) 8.5+ lakh community + public toilets in urban areas. (3) 'Aspirational Districts' + state rankings drive performance. CRITIQUES: (a) quality of toilets variable; many not used (habit, water availability); (b) ODF-status contested by independent studies (SQUAT, RICE); (c) sanitation worker safety — manual scavenging persists (banned since 1993, 2013 law); (d) behaviour change (Swachh Bharat IEC) incomplete. Related: NAMAMI GANGE (Ganga cleaning 2014), JAL JEEVAN MISSION (piped water in every rural household 2019; 75%+ coverage as of 2024). ending open defecation + building toilets; target India OPEN-DEFECATION FREE by 2 Oct 2019 (150th birth anniv of Gandhi).

cards.front:
India's first CENSUS was conducted in:

(A) 1872
(B) 1881 (under Lord Ripon)
(C) 1951
(D) 1911
cards.back:
(A) 1872

Science, Tech & Defence — First NON-SYNCHRONOUS census: 1872 (Viceroy Mayo). First SYNCHRONOUS (regular, decennial): 1881 (Lord Ripon). Conducted every 10 years; the 2021 Census was postponed due to covid and is still pending (as of 2026). Registrar General conducts it. under Lord Mayo.

cards.front:
The Union BUDGET presentation schedule was CHANGED to 1st February from 2017 onwards by:

(A) Manmohan Singh as FM
(B) Arun Jaitley as FM
(C) P. Chidambaram as FM

cards.front:
The TELEPHONE was patented in 1876 by:

(A) Thomas Edison
(B) ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL
(C) Guglielmo Marconi
(D) Nikola Tesla
cards.back:
(B) ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL

Science, Tech & Defence — TELEPHONE — electrical device to transmit voice over distance. ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL (1847-1922) — Scottish-born, emigrated to Canada + then USA; deep interest in phonetics + speech (his mother + wife were deaf; elocution was family profession). US PATENT #174,465 granted on 7 MARCH 1876 — just hours before rival inventor ELISHA GRAY's similar patent. FIRST successful call on 10 March 1876 — Bell to his assistant: 'MR. WATSON, COME HERE — I WANT TO SEE YOU' (he spilled acid on himself). Controversial due to possible conflict with Gray's work + with earlier inventor ANTONIO MEUCCI (Italian immigrant who filed 'caveat' in 1871, could not afford to renew). US Congress in 2002 resolved that Meucci was the rightful inventor of the telephone. Bell also inventor of: (a) GRAPHOPHONE (phonograph improvement, with Chichester Bell + Charles Tainter, 1886); (b) photophone (1880, voice on light beam — precursor to fiber optics); (c) METAL DETECTOR (1881, trying to find assassin's bullet in President Garfield — Garfield's deathbed). Founded BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY (1877, → AT&T). AT&T Bell Labs was USA's greatest industrial R&D lab (transistor 1947, UNIX 1969, C language 1972, solar cell 1954, laser). OTHER KEY INVENTORS (communication): (1) SAMUEL MORSE + Alfred Vail — telegraph (1838) + Morse code. (2) GUGLIELMO MARCONI — radio transmission (1895, Nobel 1909); India connection: first trans-oceanic wireless 1901. (3) J.C. BOSE (Indian) — microwaves, wireless demonstrations 1895 London (before Marconi's patent); millimetre-wave detectors; often underappreciated. (4) PHILO FARNSWORTH — TV (1927). (5) VINTON CERF + BOB KAHN — TCP/IP (1973). (6) TIM BERNERS-LEE — WORLD WIDE WEB at CERN (1989, first page 1991). Scottish-born American, patent granted 7 March 1876; his first words 'Mr Watson, come here...'.

cards.front:
Who invented the STEAM ENGINE that powered the Industrial Revolution?

(A) Benjamin Franklin
(B) JAMES WATT
(C) Thomas Edison
(D) Michael Faraday
cards.back:
(B) JAMES WATT

Science, Tech & Defence — STEAM ENGINE — key driver of the Industrial Revolution (~1760-1840). EVOLUTION: (1) 1698 — THOMAS SAVERY patented crude 'Miner's Friend' steam pump. (2) 1712 — THOMAS NEWCOMEN (+ John Calley) built the first practical atmospheric steam engine for pumping water out of mines; very inefficient (fuel-hungry). (3) 1765-1776 — JAMES WATT (1736-1819, Scottish engineer of Glasgow + Birmingham) revolutionised it with: (a) SEPARATE CONDENSER (1765 eureka moment on Glasgow Green — kept cylinder always hot, condenser always cool → 4× fuel efficiency; patent 1769); (b) DOUBLE-ACTING ENGINE (steam on both sides of piston, 1782); (c) SUN-AND-PLANET GEARING (1781) — converted linear piston motion to ROTARY; (d) PARALLEL MOTION + centrifugal governor (speed control). Partnered with MATTHEW BOULTON in Birmingham (Boulton & Watt) from 1775 — built hundreds of engines, dominated UK market. (4) RICHARD TREVITHICK (1804) — high-pressure steam engine; first steam locomotive. (5) GEORGE STEPHENSON (1814) + son Robert — practical locomotive ('Rocket', 1829) + opened Stockport-Darlington Railway (1825) + Liverpool-Manchester Railway (1830). Unit of POWER = WATT — named after him at British Assoc meeting 1882; 1 HP ≈ 746 W. WATT's inventions ENABLED: textile factories (mechanical spinning/weaving), steam locomotives, steamships, mass manufacturing → INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION → Britain's 19th-c. dominance; urbanisation; globalisation of trade. WATT'S BIRTHDAY January 19 — celebrated as EUREKA DAY by engineers. Scottish engineer; massively improved efficiency with separate condenser (patent 1769); unit WATT named after him.

cards.front:
PENICILLIN, the first effective antibiotic, was discovered by:

(A) Louis Pasteur
(B) ALEXANDER FLEMING
(C) Robert Koch
(D) Edward Jenner
cards.back:
(B) ALEXANDER FLEMING

Science, Tech & Defence — PENICILLIN — the first true antibiotic; revolutionary anti-bacterial drug. DISCOVERY: SIR ALEXANDER FLEMING (1881-1955), Scottish bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital, London. On 3 SEPTEMBER 1928, Fleming returned from a holiday to find a STAPHYLOCOCCUS culture plate left on his bench had been contaminated by a GREENISH MOULD (later identified as PENICILLIUM NOTATUM); bacteria around the mould had been killed. Fleming wrote: 'When I saw those bacteria fading, I suppose that was the most famous thing in medicine I'd ever done'. Initially called 'mould juice', renamed PENICILLIN. Published 1929 but attracted little attention. Fleming couldn't stabilise or purify it. DEVELOPMENT: HOWARD FLOREY + ERNST CHAIN (at Oxford, 1940-41) + NORMAN HEATLEY purified + mass-produced penicillin in time for WORLD WAR II — saved MILLIONS of Allied soldiers from wound infections + STDs. NOBEL PRIZE in Medicine 1945 shared by FLEMING + FLOREY + CHAIN. MOULD WAS: Penicillium notatum (later replaced in industrial production by Penicillium chrysogenum — higher-yield strain found on a rotting cantaloupe in Peoria, Illinois, 1943). MECHANISM: β-lactam antibiotic — binds to + inactivates bacterial transpeptidases, preventing peptidoglycan cross-linking in cell walls → bacterial lysis. EFFECTIVE against Gram-POSITIVE bacteria (Strep, Staph, pneumococci, syphilis treponema). OTHER KEY ANTIBIOTIC discoveries: (1) Streptomycin (Selman Waksman, 1943 — TB treatment, Nobel 1952). (2) Tetracycline (1945). (3) Erythromycin (1952). (4) Vancomycin (1956). Modern CRISIS: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE (MRSA, XDR-TB, CRE) — UN declares AMR (Antimicrobial Resistance) a global health emergency. INDIA = 'SUPERBUG HOTSPOT' due to OTC antibiotic misuse. Fleming famously warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture about misuse-driven resistance — predicted the problem decades early. 1928 at St Mary's Hospital London; observed a mould killing bacteria on a plate left unwashed while on vacation.

cards.front:
The WORLD WIDE WEB (the Internet's hypertext system) was invented by:

(A) Bill Gates
(B) TIM BERNERS-LEE
(C) Mark Zuckerberg
(D) Vint Cerf
cards.back:
(B) TIM BERNERS-LEE

Science, Tech & Defence — WORLD WIDE WEB (WWW) — hypertext-based global information system. INVENTOR: SIR TIM BERNERS-LEE (b.1955), British computer scientist. AT CERN (Geneva, Switzerland) in 1989 he proposed 'INFORMATION MANAGEMENT: A PROPOSAL' describing a global hypertext system. 6 AUGUST 1991 — FIRST-EVER WEB PAGE published on 'info.cern.ch' (still accessible at web.archive.org). INVENTED: (1) HTML (HyperText Markup Language); (2) HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol); (3) URL (Uniform Resource Locator); (4) first web BROWSER ('WorldWideWeb' later renamed Nexus); (5) first web SERVER (on NeXT computer). GAVE AWAY royalty-free in 1993 — a decision credited with the Web's explosive growth. Founded W3C (World Wide Web Consortium, 1994, at MIT). Knighted 2004; Turing Award 2016; OBE. FUNDAMENTAL DIFFERENCE: INTERNET ≠ WEB — Internet is the network infrastructure (TCP/IP, 1970s, ARPANET); WEB is one of many services running on the Internet. INTERNET BUILT by: (1) VINT CERF + BOB KAHN — TCP/IP protocol (1973); (2) J.C.R. LICKLIDER, LEONARD KLEINROCK — ARPANET (1969, first message 'LO' sent 29 Oct 1969 from UCLA to SRI Stanford; 'LOGIN' crashed after 2 letters); (3) PAUL BARAN — packet-switching theory; (4) RAY TOMLINSON — e-mail + @ (1971). INDIAN NAME: SABEER BHATIA co-founded HOTMAIL (1996), sold to Microsoft 1997 for ~$400M. OTHER WEB milestones: (1) MOSAIC browser (1993, Marc Andreessen, NCSA) — first popular graphical browser → Netscape. (2) GOOGLE (1998, Larry Page + Sergey Brin). (3) Wikipedia (2001, Jimmy Wales). (4) Facebook (2004, Zuckerberg). (5) YouTube (2005). (6) iPhone (2007). (7) ChatGPT (2022). TIM BERNERS-LEE critical of modern web: concerns over centralisation, privacy; founded Inrupt + SOLID project (decentralised personal data). British scientist at CERN, Switzerland (1989-91); invented HTML, HTTP, URL.

cards.front:
DYNAMITE was invented in 1867 by the Swedish chemist:

(A) Marie Curie
(B) ALFRED NOBEL
(C) Henry Bessemer
(D) Svante Arrhenius
cards.back:
(B) ALFRED NOBEL

Science, Tech & Defence — DYNAMITE — inventor: ALFRED BERNHARD NOBEL (1833-1896), Swedish chemist, engineer + industrialist. PATENTED 1867. BACKGROUND: Nobel's family manufactured NITROGLYCERIN — a liquid explosive (invented 1846 by Italian Ascanio Sobrero) that was powerful but dangerously unstable; small shock could detonate it → frequent lethal accidents, including one that killed Alfred's younger brother EMIL NOBEL + 4 others at the Heleneborg factory (1864). DYNAMITE was Nobel's breakthrough — MIXING nitroglycerin with KIESELGUHR (diatomaceous earth) to absorb it + stabilise → safe to handle + transport. Later improved with GELIGNITE (1875, nitroglycerin + nitrocellulose) + BALLISTITE (1887, smokeless powder). COMMERCIAL SUCCESS: dynamite transformed MINING, QUARRYING, TUNNELING (e.g., Transcontinental Railroad, St Gotthard Tunnel), DAM construction, SUBWAY tunnelling. Became very wealthy — patented 350 inventions, owned 90+ factories in 20 countries. IRONY / NOBEL PRIZE: in 1888 a French newspaper mistakenly published Nobel's obituary (when his brother Ludvig died) titled 'Le marchand de la mort est mort' ('The merchant of death is dead') — lamenting he had 'become rich by finding ways to kill more people faster than ever before'. Deeply affected. In his FINAL WILL (signed 27 Nov 1895, Paris Swedish-Norwegian Club, 1 year before death), Nobel left 94% of his fortune (~SEK 31 million, ~$250M in today's money) to establish FIVE NOBEL PRIZES — PHYSICS, CHEMISTRY, PHYSIOLOGY OR MEDICINE, LITERATURE + PEACE (the Peace Prize awarded in Oslo, others in Stockholm — honouring his Norwegian connection). First awarded 10 Dec 1901 (anniversary of Nobel's death). ECONOMICS Prize added 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank — officially 'Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences'. INDIAN NOBEL laureates: Tagore (Lit 1913), C.V. Raman (Phy 1930), Har Gobind Khorana (Med 1968, Indian-American), Mother Teresa (Peace 1979), S. Chandrasekhar (Phy 1983, Indian-American), Amartya Sen (Eco 1998), V.S. Naipaul (Lit 2001, Trinidadian-Indian), V. Ramakrishnan (Chem 2009, US-Indian), Kailash Satyarthi (Peace 2014), Abhijit Banerjee (Eco 2019). whose industrial fortune funded the NOBEL PRIZES (established in his will, first awarded 1901).

cards.front:
The AEROPLANE (powered, manned heavier-than-air flight) was INVENTED in 1903 by:

(A) Charles Lindbergh
(B) WRIGHT BROTHERS
(C) Count von Zeppelin
(D) Santos-Dumont
cards.back:
(B) WRIGHT BROTHERS

Science, Tech & Defence — AEROPLANE — powered, heavier-than-air, controllable flight. INVENTORS: WILBUR WRIGHT (1867-1912) + ORVILLE WRIGHT (1871-1948) — American bicycle mechanics from Dayton, Ohio. FIRST SUCCESSFUL FLIGHT: 17 DECEMBER 1903 at KILL DEVIL HILLS, near KITTY HAWK, NORTH CAROLINA. FLYER I flown by ORVILLE — 12 SECONDS, 36 metres (120 ft), 6.8 mph. Three more flights same day; longest = 260 m by Wilbur. First flight to fulfill all criteria: heavier-than-air + powered + sustained + controlled + with a pilot. ONLY 5 witnesses at the flight. INNOVATIONS: (a) Wing WARPING (later AILERONS) for lateral/roll control; (b) 3-axis control system (pitch, yaw, roll); (c) propeller theory treating propeller as rotating wing; (d) lightweight 12 HP gasoline engine (custom-built by mechanic Charlie Taylor). FIRST PATENTED 1906 as 'Flying-Machine'. PIONEERS + CONTEMPORARIES: (a) OTTO LILIENTHAL (Germany, 1891-96) — glider flights; death in glider crash 1896 directly inspired Wrights. (b) SIR GEORGE CAYLEY (1799-1853) — 'father of aerodynamics'; built first unmanned glider 1853. (c) ALBERTO SANTOS-DUMONT (Brazilian) — 14-bis flight Oct 1906 Paris; Brazil claims first 'public' flight. (d) HENRI FARMAN, Glenn Curtiss — early aviators. MILESTONES: 1909 — LOUIS BLÉRIOT crossed English Channel (36 min). 1914 — first AIRLINE (Tampa-St Petersburg, St Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line). 1919 — Alcock + Brown first non-stop transatlantic (Newfoundland-Ireland). 1927 — CHARLES LINDBERGH's solo NY-Paris (33.5 h, 'Spirit of St Louis'). 1947 — CHUCK YEAGER breaks sound barrier (Bell X-1, Mach 1.06). INDIA: J.R.D. TATA (first Indian pilot, 1929 licence); TATA AIRLINES 1932 (Karachi-Ahmedabad-Bombay), became AIR INDIA 1946. Indian Air Force (1932 as Royal Indian Air Force). Wilbur + Orville Wright, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina on 17 December 1903 with the Flyer I (12-second, 36-metre flight).

(c) ALBERTO SANTOS-DUMONT (Brazilian) — 14-bis flight Oct 1906 Paris; Brazil claims first 'public' flight. (d) HENRI FARMAN, Glenn Curtiss — early aviators. MILESTONES: 1909 — LOUIS BLÉRIOT crossed English Channel (36 min). 1914 — first AIRLINE (Tampa-St Petersburg, St Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line). 1919 — Alcock + Brown first non-stop transatlantic (Newfoundland-Ireland). 1927 — CHARLES LINDBERGH's solo NY-Paris (33.5 h, 'Spirit of St Louis'). 1947 — CHUCK YEAGER breaks sound barrier (Bell X-1, Mach 1.06). INDIA: J.R.D. TATA (first Indian pilot, 1929 licence); TATA AIRLINES 1932 (Karachi-Ahmedabad-Bombay), became AIR INDIA 1946. Indian Air Force (1932 as Royal Indian Air Force). Wilbur + Orville Wright, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina on 17 December 1903 with the Flyer I (12-second, 36-metre flight).

cards.front:
The ELECTRIC LIGHT BULB is most famously associated with:

(A) Alessandro Volta
(B) THOMAS ALVA EDISON
(C) James Clerk Maxwell
(D) Michael Faraday
cards.back:
(B) THOMAS ALVA EDISON

Science, Tech & Defence — ELECTRIC LIGHT BULB — incandescent lamp. THOMAS ALVA EDISON (1847-1931, American inventor, 'Wizard of Menlo Park') is most famously credited, but the story is more nuanced: (1) Many precursors 1800-1870s — Humphry Davy (carbon-arc 1800), Warren de la Rue (1820), Heinrich Göbel (1854 carbonised bamboo), Moses Farmer (1859), Alexander Lodygin (1872-74 Russia — patent), Henry Woodward (1874 Canadian, sold patent to Edison). (2) SIR JOSEPH WILSON SWAN (1828-1914, English physicist/chemist) — developed + DEMONSTRATED an incandescent lamp on 18 Dec 1878 in Newcastle; patent 1880 (UK). (3) EDISON — after methodical testing of 1,600+ filament materials, patented on 27 JANUARY 1880 (US) a practical carbon-filament (carbonised bamboo) incandescent lamp, lasting ~1200 hours. Established Edison Electric Light Co. + Edison Illuminating Co. (1882 Pearl Street station, Manhattan — world's first commercial power plant, DC current). (4) SETTLED: SWAN + EDISON MERGED — formed EDISWAN Electric Co. (1883, UK). (5) Later: TUNGSTEN filament (William Coolidge, 1906 — longer-lasting, still used). EDISON'S OTHER INVENTIONS: phonograph (1877), motion picture camera (Kinetograph 1891), alkaline battery, carbon-button microphone, stock ticker, kinetoscope + >1000 patents. Held rivalry with NIKOLA TESLA + GEORGE WESTINGHOUSE over DC vs AC power ('War of Currents'); AC won (better long-distance transmission). TYPES OF LIGHT: (1) INCANDESCENT (resistive heating of filament — being phased out for energy efficiency); (2) FLUORESCENT tube (1938, Peter Cooper Hewitt → GE commercialised); (3) CFL (compact fluorescent, 1980s); (4) LED (light-emitting diode; Nick Holonyak Jr 1962 visible red; Shuji Nakamura 1993 BLUE LED → enabled white LEDs; Nobel Phy 2014 to Akasaki, Amano, Nakamura). LEDs now dominate — 80%+ market share by 2024; most energy-efficient light source; key to India's UJALA scheme (2015) + LED revolution. patented 1879 practical incandescent lamp; but JOSEPH SWAN in England had demonstrated similar lamp in 1878.

cards.front:
The POLIO VACCINE (inactivated) was developed in 1952 by:

(A) Edward Jenner
(B) JONAS SALK
(C) Louis Pasteur
(D) Albert Sabin
cards.back:
(B) JONAS SALK

Science, Tech & Defence — POLIO VACCINE: (1) JONAS SALK (1914-1995) — IPV (Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine) — injectable. Developed at University of Pittsburgh 1952; field trials 1954 (largest clinical trial ever — 1.8 million 'polio pioneers'); licensed 12 April 1955 (anniversary of Franklin Roosevelt's death; FDR had polio). Famously said 'could you patent the sun?' when asked about patenting it — CHOSE NOT TO PATENT, ensuring wide access. Made possible by HeLa cells (from Henrietta Lacks). (2) ALBERT SABIN (1906-1993) — OPV (Oral Polio Vaccine) — live attenuated, drops; licensed 1962. Easier to administer en masse + induces intestinal immunity; became WHO-preferred. Revert rate very low but non-zero (Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus, VDPV). FATHER: FRANKLIN ROOSEVELT paralysed by polio in 1921 aged 39 — founded MARCH OF DIMES to fund research (named after Roosevelt's dime coin). POLIO IN INDIA: (1) 1994 — launched PULSE POLIO IMMUNISATION programme (mass OPV drives); 150 million kids under 5 immunised on National Immunisation Days. Ambassadors incl. AMITABH BACHCHAN. (2) LAST WILD CASE in India: Rukhsar Khatun (Howrah, WB), 13 Jan 2011, aged 2. (3) 27 MARCH 2014 — WHO declared INDIA + SE Asia Region POLIO-FREE — a massive public health victory given India's population + density. GLOBAL POLIO ERADICATION: WPV1 endemic only in PAKISTAN + AFGHANISTAN (as of 2024-25); WPV2 eradicated 2015, WPV3 eradicated 2019. GLOBAL ERADICATION would be 2nd disease after SMALLPOX (WHO 1980, certified) + first viral eradication in 21st c. OTHER MAJOR vaccine pioneers: (a) EDWARD JENNER — smallpox (1796, cowpox); (b) LOUIS PASTEUR — rabies (1885), anthrax; (c) CAMILLE GUÉRIN + ALBERT CALMETTE — BCG (TB, 1921); (d) Maurice Hilleman — 40+ vaccines incl MMR; (e) KATALIN KARIKÓ + DREW WEISSMAN — mRNA vaccines (COVID-19, Nobel 2023). India: BHARAT BIOTECH Covaxin; SERUM INSTITUTE Covishield (world's largest vaccine maker). American medical researcher at University of Pittsburgh; licensed 1955; refused to patent ('Could you patent the sun?').

cards.front:
The INDIAN scientist who invented the ZERO as a numerical symbol + articulated decimal place-value is BY TRADITION:

(A) Aryabhata (5th c. CE)
(B) Brahmagupta (7th c.) — formalised rules of arithmetic using 0, but not inventor
(C) Bhaskara
(D) Sulba Sutras authors
cards.back:
(A) Aryabhata (5th c. CE)

Science, Tech & Defence — ZERO — India's great gift to mathematics. EVOLUTION: (1) EARLIER number-less placeholder — Mesopotamians (Babylonians, ~300 BCE) used a blank/punctuation as placeholder in sexagesimal (base-60) — not a number. (2) Mayans independently used a shell-symbol for zero (~4th c. CE) — but confined to calendars. (3) In INDIA, the concept of ZERO as a NUMBER + placeholder in DECIMAL place-value system was fully developed: (a) PINGALA (~3rd-2nd c. BCE, Chhandasutra) — used a symbol for the void in his binary classification of poetic metres. (b) ARYABHATA (476-550 CE, Kusumapura/Patna) — used a place-value decimal system in his ARYABHATIYA (499 CE); computed π ≈ 3.1416; defined sine function; helio-centric hints; approximate diameter of Earth. Used 'kha' for space (Zero's seed). (c) BRAHMAGUPTA (598-668, BrahmaSphutaSiddhanta 628 CE) — FIRST TO FORMALLY DEFINE rules of arithmetic with zero: 0+a=a, 0×a=0; also negative numbers — 'debts' vs 'fortunes'; but his division-by-zero rule a/0 = undefined was unclear. (d) BHASKARA II (1114-1185, Lilavati + Siddhanta Shiromani) — refined zero; stated a/0 = infinity (some say incorrectly but thought-provoking). (e) MAHAVIRA (9th c.) Jain mathematician; MADHAVA of SANGAMAGRAMA (14th c. KERALA SCHOOL, precursor of calculus). WRITTEN 0 SYMBOL (a small dot, later the circle) found in BAKHSHALI MANUSCRIPT (3rd-4th c. CE, Peshawar; carbon-dated 2017 Oxford), GWALIOR INSCRIPTION 876 CE (Chaturbhuja Temple — 270 malaa carved with '0'). TRANSMISSION TO THE WEST via ARABS (9th c. — 'Al-Kitab al-hind' = 'Indian Book'; mathematician Al-Khwarizmi, from whose name we get 'algorithm') → Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (1202) popularised 'Arabic numerals' (more accurately Hindu-Arabic numerals) in Europe. KERALA SCHOOL of Mathematics (14th-16th c. — Madhava, Neelakantha) developed infinite series (for π, sin, cos) centuries before Newton + Leibniz. NOT YET PROVEN whether transmitted to Europe via Portuguese Jesuits. place-value system + concept of zero as placeholder.

cards.front:
Match the Indian scientist with their contribution: (1) C.V. RAMAN; (2) J.C. BOSE; (3) S. CHANDRASEKHAR; (4) S.N. BOSE.

(A) Supernovae; black holes; solar; light
(B) RAMAN EFFECT (inelastic light scattering, Nobel 1930); MICROWAVE / PLANT RESPONSE pioneer; BLACK HOLES / CHANDRASEKHAR LIMIT (Nobel 1983); BOSE-EINSTEIN statistics
(C) Atom; genes; stars only; oxygen
(D) Botany; engineering; rocketry; computer science
cards.back:
(B) RAMAN EFFECT (inelastic light scattering, Nobel 1930); MICROWAVE / PLANT RESPONSE pioneer; BLACK HOLES / CHANDRASEKHAR LIMIT (Nobel 1983); BOSE-EINSTEIN statistics

Science, Tech & Defence — FOUR LEGENDARY INDIAN SCIENTISTS: (1) SIR C.V. RAMAN (Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman, 1888-1970) — discovered the RAMAN EFFECT (28 Feb 1928) = INELASTIC scattering of light by molecules; change in wavelength reveals molecular vibrations → basis of RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY (for chemistry + materials). NOBEL PRIZE in Physics 1930 — FIRST Asian to win Nobel in Physics / any science. 28 FEBRUARY celebrated as NATIONAL SCIENCE DAY in India. Founded RAMAN RESEARCH INSTITUTE (Bangalore, 1948) + Indian Academy of Sciences. (2) JAGADISH CHANDRA BOSE (1858-1937) — Physicist + botanist; pioneered wireless microwave (mm-wave) research at 60 GHz (1895 Calcutta; demonstrated in London 1897 — BEFORE Marconi's famous trans-Atlantic transmission using longer waves); invented crescograph to measure plant growth; demonstrated plants have 'feelings', electrical signalling. Founded BOSE INSTITUTE, Calcutta (1917). Got a U.S. patent 1904 on semiconductor detector (crystal radio precursor). Under-recognised — Nobel Committee overlooked him. (3) SUBRAHMANYAN CHANDRASEKHAR (1910-1995, Indian-American, nephew of CV Raman) — worked at University of Chicago. Derived CHANDRASEKHAR LIMIT (1930, age 19, on sea voyage from India to Cambridge!): white dwarf stars cannot exceed ~1.44 solar masses; above it, star collapses to neutron star or BLACK HOLE. NOBEL PHYSICS 1983 (50+ years after his original work). Also NASA's CHANDRA X-ray Observatory (1999) named after him. Elected Royal Society 1944. (4) SATYENDRA NATH BOSE (1894-1974) — Bengali physicist. In 1924 sent a paper to EINSTEIN describing statistics of INDISTINGUISHABLE BOSONS (photons). Einstein extended to matter → BOSE-EINSTEIN STATISTICS + BOSE-EINSTEIN CONDENSATE (5th state of matter; experimentally created 1995 by Cornell + Wieman + Ketterle, Nobel 2001). 'BOSON' fundamental particles (photon, gluon, Higgs) named after him — 'Higgs Boson' (LHC 2012). Bose himself NEVER got Nobel (Nobel rules don't retroactively include developers of foundational statistics); some say biggest snub in Nobel history. OTHER giants: RAMANUJAN (math), MEGHNAD SAHA (astrophysics, Saha ionisation equation), HOMI BHABHA (atomic energy), VIKRAM SARABHAI (space), HAR GOBIND KHORANA (genetic code, Nobel Med 1968), VENKATRAMAN RAMAKRISHNAN (ribosome, Nobel Chem 2009), M.S. SWAMINATHAN (green revolution), CNR RAO (chemistry, Bharat Ratna 2014). with Einstein.

cards.front:
Penicillin — the first widely used antibiotic — was discovered by:

(A) Alexander Fleming
(B) Louis Pasteur
(C) Robert Koch
(D) Jonas Salk
cards.back:
(A) Alexander Fleming

Science, Tech & Defence — Alexander Fleming, 1928, at St Mary's Hospital London — noticed mould (Penicillium notatum) inhibited bacterial growth. Shared 1945 Nobel with Florey and Chain, who turned it into a usable drug. Pasteur pioneered germ theory and vaccines; Koch identified tuberculosis and anthrax bacilli; Salk developed polio vaccine.

cards.front:
The INDIAN SPACE RESEARCH ORGANISATION (ISRO) was established on:

(A) 15 August 1947
(B) 15 AUGUST 1969
(C) 26 January 1975
(D) 1 April 1975
cards.back:
(B) 15 AUGUST 1969

Science, Tech & Defence — ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation) — India's national space agency. ESTABLISHED: 15 AUGUST 1969 (Independence Day). REPLACED earlier INCOSPAR (Indian National Committee for Space Research, est. 1962 under Atomic Energy Commission). FOUNDER + FIRST CHAIRMAN: DR. VIKRAM SARABHAI ('Father of Indian Space Programme'); HOMI BHABHA key early backer. HQ: BENGALURU (known as 'Space City'). Governs under DEPARTMENT OF SPACE (DoS), which reports DIRECTLY to the PRIME MINISTER (no separate minister). FIRST ROCKET LAUNCH: Nike-Apache sounding rocket launched 21 NOVEMBER 1963 from THUMBA EQUATORIAL ROCKET LAUNCHING STATION (TERLS), near Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala. PARTS TRANSPORTED on BICYCLE + BULLOCK CART — iconic images. EVOLUTION: (1) 1972 — Dept of Space created. (2) 1975 — ARYABHATA, India's first satellite (launched by USSR Soyuz from Kapustin Yar). cards.front:
India's first satellite, ARYABHATA, was launched in 1975 by:

(A) USA via NASA
(B) USSR (Soviet Union) from KAPUSTIN YAR cosmodrome on 19 April 1975; named after the 5th-century Indian mathematician-astronomer
(C) France
(D) India's own SLV-3
cards.back:
(B) USSR (Soviet Union) from KAPUSTIN YAR cosmodrome on 19 April 1975; named after the 5th-century Indian mathematician-astronomer

Science, Tech & Defence — ARYABHATA — INDIA's FIRST SATELLITE. LAUNCHED 19 APRIL 1975 from KAPUSTIN YAR cosmodrome (USSR, now Russia) aboard a COSMOS-3M rocket. Indo-Soviet space cooperation. Named after ARYABHATA, the 5th-century Indian mathematician-astronomer (authored Aryabhatiya 499 CE; place-value system). SPECIFICATIONS: ~360 kg; 26-faced polyhedron body; carried 3 experiments — X-ray astronomy, aeronomy (study of upper atmosphere), solar physics. Operated only 4 days before power failure (due to bit error + failure of internal electronics); re-entered atmosphere 11 Feb 1992 after 17 years in orbit. Still considered a major success as it established India's satellite-engineering capability. Design + development at SHAR (Sriharikota HIGH Altitude Range), Peenya, Bengaluru, Thiruvananthapuram. Image of Aryabhata was on INDIAN ₹2 NOTE during 1976-97. SUBSEQUENT EARLY ISRO MISSIONS: (1) 1979 — BHASKARA-I — Earth observation; (2) 1980 — ROHINI (RS-1) — FIRST satellite launched by INDIGENOUS Indian rocket (SLV-3, developed under Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam). India became 7th space-faring nation. (3) 1981 — BHASKARA-II. (4) 1981 — APPLE (Ariane Passenger Payload Experiment) — first 3-axis stabilised communication satellite; launched by ESA Ariane-1. (5) 1982 — INSAT-1A (first Insat). (6) 1983 — INSAT-1B (milestone — communication + weather). (7) 1988 — IRS-1A (Indian Remote Sensing). (8) 1992 — SROSS-C (student satellite). (9) 1993 — PSLV-D1 (failed); 1994 — PSLV-D2 successful. (10) 1999 — GSLV-D1 launched. MILESTONES via PSLV — 58+ LAUNCHES as of 2024 with 95%+ success rate; earned INDIA the 'WORKHORSE LAUNCHER' reputation. PSLV LAUNCHED SATELLITES for 30+ countries (commercial customers) via ANTRIX (ISRO commercial arm), later NSIL (2019). India's per-kg launch cost is AMONG THE LOWEST globally — ~$5000-6000/kg (vs $20000+ for US competitors pre-SpaceX).

cards.front:
CHANDRAYAAN-3, which made INDIA the FIRST COUNTRY to soft-land near the Moon's SOUTH POLE, touched down on:

(A) 15 August 2022
(B) 23 AUGUST 2023
(C) 14 July 2023
(D) 26 January 2024
cards.back:
(B) 23 AUGUST 2023

Science, Tech & Defence — CHANDRAYAAN-3 — India's THIRD lunar mission + FIRST successful soft-landing. LAUNCHED: 14 July 2023 on LVM3-M4 from Sriharikota. TOUCH-DOWN: 23 AUGUST 2023 at 6:04 PM IST (Local Indian time 18:04 Hours UTC+5:30). LANDING SITE: Statio Shiv Shakti (later officially named by PM Modi) near Manzinus C and Simpelius N craters, near the Moon's SOUTH POLE (69.37°S, 32.35°E). INDIA BECAME: (1) FOURTH country to soft-land on Moon (after USSR 1966 Luna 9, USA 1966 Surveyor 1, China 2013 Chang'e-3); (2) FIRST country ever to land near the LUNAR SOUTH POLE (Russia's Luna-25 crashed Aug 19, 2023 — failed; Chandrayaan-3 succeeded 4 days later). KEY COMPONENTS: (1) PROPULSION MODULE — orbits Moon; retained in orbit for year+ (SHAPE experiment on it studied Earth as 'habitable' exoplanet-analog). (2) VIKRAM LANDER (~1,752 kg) — named after Vikram Sarabhai; equipped with ChaSTE (thermal), ILSA (seismology), RAMBHA-LP (plasma), LRA (laser retroreflector). (3) PRAGYAN ROVER (~26 kg, 6-wheeled, solar-powered) — deployed from Vikram; traveled ~100m over 14 Earth days on lunar surface; 10-day operational life before lunar night shut it down. Confirmed sulfur, aluminum, calcium, iron, titanium, oxygen, chromium, manganese, silicon on lunar south polar region; temperature measurements by ChaSTE revealed subsurface temperature -10°C. MISSION COST: ₹615 CRORE (~$75 million) — compared with NASA Artemis $4.1 billion. LEADERSHIP: Chairman S. SOMANATH; Project Director P. VEERAMUTHUVEL; Mission Director M. SANKARAN. IMPACT: INDIA celebrated; PM Modi announced 23 Aug as 'NATIONAL SPACE DAY' annually. Worldwide tributes; elevated ISRO's stature. PREVIOUS ATTEMPTS: CHANDRAYAAN-1 (2008) — discovered water ice on Moon (Moon Impact Probe); ended Aug 2009 when communication lost. CHANDRAYAAN-2 (July 2019) — Vikram lander CRASHED (7 Sep 2019) 2km from target; Orbiter (still operational, providing data) was successful. CHANDRAYAAN-3 was REDESIGNED from Chandrayaan-2 lessons — no orbiter (used the CH-2 orbiter), stronger legs, more fuel, hazard detection, multiple backup sensors. FUTURE: CHANDRAYAAN-4 (2027?) — sample return mission; LUPEX (Lunar Polar Exploration) joint with JAXA (Japan). 6:04 PM IST; celebrated as NATIONAL SPACE DAY annually since 2023.

cards.front:
The MARS ORBITER MISSION (MANGALYAAN) was notable for:

(A) Being the most expensive space mission
(B) Making INDIA the FIRST ASIAN + FIRST COUNTRY EVER to reach Mars ORBIT on MAIDEN ATTEMPT; at under ₹450 cr, cheaper than Hollywood's 'Gravity' ($100M)
(C) Being the first mission to land on Mars
(D) Carrying astronauts to Mars
cards.back:
(B) Making INDIA the FIRST ASIAN + FIRST COUNTRY EVER to reach Mars ORBIT on MAIDEN ATTEMPT; at under ₹450 cr, cheaper than Hollywood's 'Gravity' ($100M)

Science, Tech & Defence — MARS ORBITER MISSION (MOM) / 'MANGALYAAN' — India's first interplanetary mission. LAUNCHED: 5 NOVEMBER 2013 from Sriharikota on PSLV-C25. ARRIVAL at MARS ORBIT: 24 SEPTEMBER 2014 (after 298-day cruise). KEY ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) INDIA = FIRST ASIAN COUNTRY to reach Mars orbit (Japan Nozomi 1998 + China Yinghuo-1 2011 failed). (2) ISRO = first space agency EVER to achieve Mars orbit on MAIDEN ATTEMPT (USA, Europe, USSR, Japan, China all failed on first attempts). (3) COST: ₹450 CRORE ($73 million) — LOWER COST than the Hollywood movie 'Gravity' ($100M, 2013) — famous cost-comparison point showing Indian frugal engineering. NASA's MAVEN mission to Mars in same window cost $671M. (4) Payloads (5 instruments, 15 kg total): (a) LAP (Lyman Alpha Photometer) — deuterium/hydrogen ratio; (b) MENCA (neutral composition analyzer); (c) Mars Colour Camera (MCC) — stunning Mars + phobos images; (d) TIS (Thermal Infrared Spectrometer); (e) MSM (Methane Sensor). DESIGN LIFE: 6 months; ACTUAL LIFE: 8+ YEARS (ran till 2 October 2022 when contact lost due to eclipse-induced battery drain). NOMINAL 6-month orbit of 366×80000 km. HIGHLIGHTS: (1) Captured iconic 'Full DISK of MARS' with clouds + Olympus Mons visible. (2) Mapped Mars surface; measured atmospheric dust, methane, escape rates. (3) Provided key data for next decade of Mars science. TEAM: Project Director — M. ANNADURAI; ISRO Chairman K. RADHAKRISHNAN. WOMEN SCIENTISTS at MOM: RITU KARIDHAL (Deputy Director Operations), NANDINI HARINATH (deputy operations), MINAL SAMPATH, Anuradha TK — popularised as 'Rocket Women of India'. MOM-2 / MANGALYAAN-2 — in planning for late 2020s; orbiter + possibly lander. NEXT INTERPLANETARY MISSIONS: (1) VENUS ORBITER Mission (Shukrayaan-1) — approved 2024, planned 2028 launch. (2) Space-based Gravitational Wave detector (LISA-India? / LIGO-India Hingoli operational 2030). (3) ADITYA-L1 (ALREADY at L1 Lagrange point since Jan 2024) — first Indian solar observatory. ISRO has 'DRE' culture (Do it Rightful + Efficient + economical) as its famous engineering ethos.
cards.option1: Being the most expensive space mission
cards.option2: Being the first mission to land on Mars

cards.front:
The GAGANYAAN mission, India's first HUMAN SPACEFLIGHT programme, aims to launch Indian astronauts (Vyomanauts) to:

(A) Moon
(B) LOW EARTH ORBIT (~400 km) for 3 days
(C) International Space Station
(D) Mars
cards.back:
(B) LOW EARTH ORBIT (~400 km) for 3 days

Science, Tech & Defence — GAGANYAAN ('Sky Vehicle') — India's first HUMAN SPACEFLIGHT PROGRAMME. Announced 2018 (PM Modi's 15 Aug Independence Day speech). OBJECTIVE: launch 3-member Indian crew to LOW EARTH ORBIT (400 km altitude) for 3 days; safe recovery in Arabian Sea. LAUNCH VEHICLE: LVM3 (previously GSLV Mk-III; HUMAN-RATED variant HLVM3). CREW SELECTION: 4 IAF pilots selected + announced 27 Feb 2024 by PM Modi at ISRO Trivandrum: (1) Group Captain Prashanth Balakrishnan Nair; (2) Group Captain Ajit Krishnan; (3) Group Captain Angad Pratap; (4) Wing Commander Shubhanshu Shukla. ALL 4 undergoing cosmonaut training in ROSCOSMOS (Russia) + in India at Astronaut Training Facility Bengaluru. ONE of them will likely become India's first crewed astronaut via an Indian rocket (RAKESH SHARMA 1984 went via Soviet Soyuz; Gaganyaan will use Indian vehicle). TIMELINE: (1) 21 Oct 2023 — TV-D1 (Test Vehicle Demonstration-1) pad abort test successful; tested Crew Escape System; CES propelled Crew Module from simulated rocket failure at Mach 1.2, 17 km, separated, splashdown in Bay of Bengal. (2) 2024 — G1 uncrewed mission (with humanoid robot VYOMMITRA onboard); delayed to late 2024 / 2025. (3) 2025-26 — G2 uncrewed; then H1 crewed. CURRENT TARGET: H1 crewed mission by 2025/2026. COSTS: ~₹9,000-10,000 CRORE. BUDGET: allocated ₹10,000 cr in 2018. KEY SYSTEMS: (1) CREW MODULE (CM) — re-entry capsule; life support for 3; ~5 tonnes. (2) SERVICE MODULE (SM). (3) CREW ESCAPE SYSTEM (CES) — rockets to pull capsule away from failing booster. (4) Environment Control + Life Support System (ECLSS). POST-Gaganyaan: (a) BHARATIYA ANTARIKSH STATION — India's proposed space station by 2035; first module 2028; (b) Chandrayaan-4 sample return mission (2027); (c) VYOMMITRA Humanoid robot in TV-D1/G1 tests. Gaganyaan will make India the FOURTH country with independent human spaceflight capability after USSR/Russia, USA, China. IAF's INSTITUTE OF AEROSPACE MEDICINE (IAM, Bengaluru) medical + psychological selection. VIKAS ENGINE (2-engine crew version), C-25 cryogenic upper stage, + indigenous pad abort motors developed. targeted 2025-26; uses LVM3; 4 astronauts selected in 2024 for training.
