cards.front:
ISRO's WORKHORSE launch vehicle for SMALL + MEDIUM satellites into POLAR ORBIT is:

(A) SLV-3
(B) PSLV
(C) ASLV
(D) LVM3
cards.back:
(B) PSLV

Science, Tech & Defence — PSLV (POLAR SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLE) — ISRO's most reliable + workhorse launcher. First launch 1993 (PSLV-D1 failed); first success PSLV-D2 in 1994. 50+ consecutive successful launches since then (as of 2025). STAGES: 4 stages alternating SOLID (PS1, PS3) + LIQUID (PS2, PS4). Payload: ~1,750 kg to SSO (Sun Synchronous Orbit ~620 km), ~1,425 kg to GTO. CONFIGURATIONS: PSLV-CA (Core Alone, no strap-ons), PSLV-DL (2 strap-ons), PSLV-QL (4), PSLV-XL (6) — most powerful. PSLV LAUNCHES: has orbited 400+ satellites from 30+ countries; many commercial launches through ANTRIX / NSIL. RECORD: (1) PSLV-C37 (15 Feb 2017) launched 104 SATELLITES in SINGLE mission — WORLD RECORD at the time (3 Indian satellites + 88 Planet Labs Flock-3p + 1 UAE + 5 Kazakhstan + 5 Switzerland + 1 Israel + 8 Spire Global + 1 UAE); India's primary payload was CARTOSAT-2 series. (2) 2023 — PSLV-C55 launched TeLEOS-2 + Lumelite-4 for Singapore. FAMOUS PSLV MISSIONS: (a) CHANDRAYAAN-1 (2008); (b) MARS ORBITER MISSION (2013); (c) ASTROSAT (2015, India's 1st astronomy satellite); (d) IRNSS / NavIC constellation (PSLV launched 7 IRNSS satellites 2013-16); (e) RISAT (radar imaging); (f) CARTOSAT series (remote sensing); (g) OCEANSAT. OTHER ISRO LAUNCHERS: (1) SLV-3 (1980) — India's 1st indigenous; 40 kg to LEO; 4 missions (2 success, 2 failure); Dr Kalam was project director. (2) ASLV (Augmented SLV, 1987-94) — improvement; 150 kg LEO; 4 missions, 2 success. (3) GSLV Mk-II (2014-present) — 2.5 ton to GTO; uses CRYOGENIC upper stage (CE-7.5, indigenous since 2014). Reliability mixed. (4) GSLV Mk-III / LVM3 (2014-) — HEAVY-LIFT; 4 ton to GTO, 8 ton to LEO; flies LVM3 = Launch Vehicle Mark 3 since 2022 renaming; cryogenic CE-20 upper stage; used for Chandrayaan-2, 3, OneWeb constellation launches (36 OneWeb satellites per launch). HUMAN-RATED for Gaganyaan. (5) SSLV (Small Satellite Launch Vehicle, 2022-) — new; 500 kg to 500 km LEO; designed for rapid commercial small-sat market (SmallSat demand). (6) RLV-TD (Reusable Launch Vehicle Tech Demonstrator) — test flights in 2016, 2023, 2024; technology for Indian reusable rocket. 4-stage rocket, 1994 onward; payload ~1,750 kg to 600 km SSO; holds 104-satellite single-launch record; Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle.

Payload: ~1,750 kg to SSO (Sun Synchronous Orbit ~620 km), ~1,425 kg to GTO. CONFIGURATIONS: PSLV-CA (Core Alone, no strap-ons), PSLV-DL (2 strap-ons), PSLV-QL (4), PSLV-XL (6) — most powerful. PSLV LAUNCHES: has orbited 400+ satellites from 30+ countries; many commercial launches through ANTRIX / NSIL. RECORD: (1) PSLV-C37 (15 Feb 2017) launched 104 SATELLITES in SINGLE mission — WORLD RECORD at the time (3 Indian satellites + 88 Planet Labs Flock-3p + 1 UAE + 5 Kazakhstan + 5 Switzerland + 1 Israel + 8 Spire Global + 1 UAE); India's primary payload was CARTOSAT-2 series. (2) 2023 — PSLV-C55 launched TeLEOS-2 + Lumelite-4 for Singapore. FAMOUS PSLV MISSIONS: (a) CHANDRAYAAN-1 (2008); (b) MARS ORBITER MISSION (2013); (c) ASTROSAT (2015, India's 1st astronomy satellite); (d) IRNSS / NavIC constellation (PSLV launched 7 IRNSS satellites 2013-16); (e) RISAT (radar imaging); (f) CARTOSAT series (remote sensing); (g) OCEANSAT. OTHER ISRO LAUNCHERS: (1) SLV-3 (1980) — India's 1st indigenous; 40 kg to LEO; 4 missions (2 success, 2 failure); Dr Kalam was project director. (2) ASLV (Augmented SLV, 1987-94) — improvement; 150 kg LEO; 4 missions, 2 success. (3) GSLV Mk-II (2014-present) — 2.5 ton to GTO; uses CRYOGENIC upper stage (CE-7.5, indigenous since 2014). Reliability mixed. (4) GSLV Mk-III / LVM3 (2014-) — HEAVY-LIFT; 4 ton to GTO, 8 ton to LEO; flies LVM3 = Launch Vehicle Mark 3 since 2022 renaming; cryogenic CE-20 upper stage; used for Chandrayaan-2, 3, OneWeb constellation launches (36 OneWeb satellites per launch). HUMAN-RATED for Gaganyaan. (5) SSLV (Small Satellite Launch Vehicle, 2022-) — new; 500 kg to 500 km LEO; designed for rapid commercial small-sat market (SmallSat demand). (6) RLV-TD (Reusable Launch Vehicle Tech Demonstrator) — test flights in 2016, 2023, 2024; technology for Indian reusable rocket. 4-stage rocket, 1994 onward; payload ~1,750 kg to 600 km SSO; holds 104-satellite single-launch record; Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle.

cards.front:
India's satellite NAVIGATION system (like GPS) is called:

(A) GAGAN
(B) NavIC
(C) IRNSS only
(D) Bhuvan
cards.back:
(B) NavIC

Science, Tech & Defence — NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) — India's regional satellite navigation system. ORIGINAL NAME: IRNSS (Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System). RENAMED NavIC by PM Modi in 2016 post first operational. COVERAGE: India + 1500 km beyond its borders. OWNER + OPERATOR: ISRO. CONSTELLATION: 7 SATELLITES — (1) 3 GEOSTATIONARY (GEO) — at longitudes 32.5°E, 83°E, 131.5°E; (2) 4 GEOSYNCHRONOUS (GSO) — at 55°E + 111.75°E (2 each); inclination 29°. 8TH satellite being built as backup. First satellite IRNSS-1A launched 1 JULY 2013; last of initial 7 IRNSS-1G on 28 APRIL 2016 (making NavIC OPERATIONAL). 7-of-9 launched; 1A failed (atomic clock stopped, replaced 2018 by 1I); 1H also failed in 2017 (heat shield stuck). SIGNALS: 2 FREQUENCY BANDS — L5 (1176.45 MHz) + S-band (2492.028 MHz). Better multi-path performance than single-frequency. 2 SERVICES: (1) SPS (Standard Positioning Service) — civilian, open; 5m accuracy over land. (2) RS (Restricted Service) — encrypted, military + strategic; few-cm accuracy. GLOBAL COMPETITORS: (1) GPS (USA, 24+3 satellites, global); (2) GLONASS (Russia, 24 operational, global); (3) GALILEO (EU, 30 sat, global); (4) BeiDou (China, 35+ sat, global); (5) QZSS (Japan, 4-7 sat, regional); (6) NavIC (India, 7 sat, regional). GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation) — SEPARATE system; India's SBAS (Satellite Based Augmentation System) — augments GPS signals with corrections for aviation + other precision uses. Launched 2015. USES of NavIC: (a) Terrestrial + marine navigation; (b) Disaster management; (c) Vehicle tracking + fleet management; (d) Mobile phone integration (Android phones with NavIC chips since 2018 — Xiaomi, RealMe); (e) Surveying + mapping; (f) Time synchronisation (telecom, banking); (g) Strategic + defence use. MANDATED for all vehicles (commercial) in India for tracking post-2020. POLICY: Govt mandated NavIC in all new smartphones by ~2023-24 for better indigenous adoption. Successor NVS-01 satellite launched 2023 with Rubidium atomic clocks (indigenous); replaces failed IRNSS-1A. 7 satellites covering India + 1500 km; official name IRNSS earlier; Navigation with Indian Constellation.

cards.front:
The ADITYA-L1 mission, India's FIRST SOLAR OBSERVATORY, is parked at:

(A) Low Earth Orbit
(B) LAGRANGE POINT L1
(C) The Moon
(D) Mars orbit
cards.back:
(B) LAGRANGE POINT L1

Science, Tech & Defence — ADITYA-L1 (Sanskrit 'Aditya' = Sun; L1 = Lagrange Point 1) — INDIA'S FIRST DEDICATED SOLAR MISSION. LAUNCHED 2 SEPTEMBER 2023 from Sriharikota on PSLV-C57. REACHED L1 Halo Orbit 6 JANUARY 2024. LAGRANGE POINT L1 — a point ~1.5 MILLION KM from Earth (about 1% of Earth-Sun distance) along the Earth-Sun line where the gravitational pull of Sun + Earth BALANCE with the centrifugal force on a third small body. 5 Lagrange points (L1-L5) exist for any 2-body system. L1 allows UNINTERRUPTED observation of SUN (no eclipse by Earth) + continuous solar wind monitoring BEFORE it reaches Earth — 1-hour early warning of solar storms (coronal mass ejections, CMEs). STATION-KEEPING: halo orbit around L1 (not fixed at L1 itself; L1 is unstable, needs periodic thruster firing). SCIENTIFIC INSTRUMENTS (7 payloads): (1) VELC (Visible Emission Line Coronagraph) — images corona, India-developed by IIA (Indian Institute of Astrophysics, Bengaluru). Key instrument. (2) SUIT (Solar UV Imaging Telescope). (3) SoLEXS (Soft X-ray Spectrometer). (4) HEL1OS (High Energy L1 Orbiting Spectrometer). (5) ASPEX (Aditya Solar wind Particle Experiment). (6) PAPA (Plasma Analyzer Package for Aditya). (7) MAG (MAGnetometer). OBJECTIVES: (a) Study of chromosphere + corona; (b) CME initiation + propagation; (c) solar wind origin + composition; (d) solar flares; (e) corona heating paradox (why corona at millions of Kelvin is hotter than surface at 5800 K?). DESIGN LIFE: 5+ years. OTHER L1 MISSIONS (world): (1) SOHO (Solar + Heliospheric Observatory, NASA-ESA 1995-; still operational); (2) DSCOVR (NASA 2015, Deep Space Climate Observatory — replaces Triana; at L1 monitoring Earth + space weather); (3) ACE (Advanced Composition Explorer, NASA 1997-). OTHER LAGRANGE POINT MISSIONS: JWST (NASA) at L2 (1.5 million km opposite direction). L4 + L5 host 'trojan' asteroids (Sun-Jupiter trojans). SIGNIFICANCE for INDIA: (a) FIRST solar mission; (b) demonstrates INTERPLANETARY capability (after MOM 2013); (c) joins elite 'L1 club' of space agencies; (d) crucial solar + space weather data for India + global science. CHAIRMAN when launched: S. SOMANATH. MISSION OPERATIONS Centre at ISTRAC Bengaluru. halo orbit; uninterrupted view of Sun; reached 6 Jan 2024; 1.5 million km from Earth towards Sun.

cards.front:
The RAKESH SHARMA became the FIRST Indian in space on:

(A) 3 April 1984 aboard Soyuz T-11 from Baikonur
(B) 15 August 1985 via NASA Space Shuttle
(C) 26 January 1988 aboard Mir
(D) 2008 aboard ISS
cards.back:
(A) 3 April 1984 aboard Soyuz T-11 from Baikonur

Science, Tech & Defence — RAKESH SHARMA (b. 13 Jan 1949, Patiala, Punjab) — FIRST INDIAN IN SPACE. IAF Squadron Leader (test pilot, ex-MiG-21). SELECTED 1982 from shortlist of IAF pilots under Indo-Soviet Intercosmos programme; trained at Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre, Star City (Moscow). MISSION: SOYUZ T-11 launched 3 APRIL 1984 from BAIKONUR COSMODROME (Kazakhstan, USSR); docked with SALYUT-7 SPACE STATION on 4 April. Spent 7 DAYS, 21 HOURS, 40 MINUTES in space; returned 11 April 1984 via Soyuz T-10. CREWMATES: Soviet cosmonauts Yuri Malyshev (Commander) + Gennady Strekalov. EXPERIMENTS: (1) Bio-medical experiments on YOGA in microgravity — Rakesh Sharma performed yoga to study muscle efficacy; confirmed yoga's utility. (2) Remote sensing of Indian Himalayan region (10 sites). (3) Metallurgical experiments on silicon + multi-layer melting. (4) Photography of sub-continent. FAMOUS MOMENT: On 5 April 1984, during in-flight conference with PM Indira Gandhi: 'Apki nazar se India kaisa dikhta hai?' ('How does India look from up there?'); Rakesh replied 'SAARE JAHAN SE ACHCHHA' (quote from Iqbal's 1904 patriotic song — 'Better than the entire world'). Iconic line resonates to this day. HONOURS: HERO OF SOVIET UNION (Russia's highest military honor — 1984); ASHOK CHAKRA (India's highest peacetime military award). INDIA became 14TH country to put a person in space (USSR, USA, Czechoslovakia, Poland, E. Germany, Bulgaria, Hungary, Vietnam, Cuba, Mongolia, Romania, France, Germany-W had gone before; India was 14th via Intercosmos). POST-FLIGHT: continued as IAF test pilot; retired 2001; now settled in Tamil Nadu. KALPANA CHAWLA (Haryana-born, naturalised American) went on NASA's STS-87 Space Shuttle Columbia mission 1997; died aboard STS-107 Columbia re-entry disaster 1 Feb 2003. SUNITA WILLIAMS (Indian origin, American; mother Bonnie, father Deepak Pandya) — went to ISS in 2006 + 2012 (127 + 195 days); 2024 Boeing Starliner 1st crewed test (stranded on ISS due to thruster issues, returning via SpaceX Crew-9 in 2025). Rakesh Sharma remains INDIA's ONLY cosmonaut with Indian rocket-flown designation still pending (Gaganyaan). described India as 'Saare Jahan Se Achcha' to PM Indira Gandhi.

cards.front:
The FATHER of INDIAN SPACE PROGRAMME, who founded ISRO, is:

(A) A.P.J. Abdul Kalam
(B) DR. VIKRAM SARABHAI (1919-71)
(C) Homi J. Bhabha
(D) Satish Dhawan
cards.back:
(B) DR. VIKRAM SARABHAI (1919-71)

Science, Tech & Defence — DR VIKRAM SARABHAI (12 Aug 1919 – 30 Dec 1971) — 'FATHER of INDIAN SPACE PROGRAMME'; founder + first chairman of ISRO. BORN Ahmedabad (Sarabhai business family; wife Mrinalini Sarabhai was classical dancer; daughter Mallika Sarabhai dancer + activist). Studied at Gujarat College + CAMBRIDGE (PhD in cosmic ray physics under Sir C.V. Raman). RETURN to India 1947. KEY INSTITUTIONS FOUNDED: (1) PHYSICAL RESEARCH LABORATORY (PRL), Ahmedabad (1947) — India's first research institute for cosmic rays + space physics. (2) ISRO (15 Aug 1969) — superseded INCOSPAR (1962, founded by him as well). (3) THUMBA EQUATORIAL ROCKET LAUNCHING STATION (TERLS), Kerala — 1963 (near Thiruvananthapuram; geomagnetic equator passes through it). (4) INDIAN INSTITUTE OF MANAGEMENT (IIM) AHMEDABAD — 1961 (co-founded with Kasturbhai Lalbhai, first IIM). (5) Nehru Foundation for Development. (6) ATIRA (Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association). (7) Centre for Environmental Planning + Technology (CEPT). (8) PHYSICAL RESEARCH LABORATORY. VISION: Sarabhai famously argued India should NOT spend on ROCKETS while poor — BUT his counter was: 'There is no ambiguity of purpose. We do not have the fantasy of competing with the economically advanced nations... we must be SECOND TO NONE in the application of advanced technologies to the real problems of man + society.' Championed SATELLITE TELEVISION for education + rural broadcasting — led to the SITE experiment (Satellite Instructional Television Experiment 1975-76 with NASA's ATS-6, covering 2,400 villages). PROJECTS initiated: Aryabhata satellite, SLV-3 rocket (guided Dr. Kalam's development), ISRO-NASA cooperation, INSAT concept. SUCCEEDED Dr. Homi Bhabha as Chairman of AEC (1966) after Bhabha's death in a plane crash — also oversaw Atomic Energy. DIED 30 DEC 1971 at Kovalam, Kerala (unexpected sudden death, aged 52). Sarabhai was PADMA BHUSHAN 1966; PADMA VIBHUSHAN 1972 (posthumous). ICBM-scale impact on Indian science. VIKRAM LANDER of Chandrayaan-2 + 3 named after him. VSSC (Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre), Trivandrum (ISRO's rocket development centre) named after him. SUCCESSORS: (1) M.G.K. Menon (1971-72); (2) Prof. SATISH DHAWAN (1972-84) — built ISRO into professional organisation; SHAR renamed after him. (3) Prof. U.R. Rao (1984-94). (4) Dr. K. Kasturirangan (1994-2003). (5) G. Madhavan Nair (2003-09). (6) K. Radhakrishnan (2009-14). (7) A.S. Kiran Kumar (2015-18). (8) K. Sivan (2018-22). (9) S. Somanath (2022-). first ISRO Chairman; established PRL Ahmedabad 1947; TERLS Thumba 1963; 'Space City' Bengaluru named partly for him.

cards.front:

The President is elected by an Electoral College consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament AND elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (including the NCT of Delhi and the UT of Puducherry). 2. The value of the vote of an MLA depends on the population of the state (as per the 1971 Census, by the 84th Amendment). 3. A person cannot be elected President unless they are qualified to be elected to the Lok Sabha. 4. The President can be removed only by impeachment for 'violation of the Constitution' under Article 61. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 1 and 4 only
(D) 2 and 3 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Science, Tech & Defence — All four correct. Electoral College: elected MPs of both Houses + elected MLAs (nominated members are EXCLUDED). 1971 Census frozen value by 84th Amendment (2001). Qualifications mirror LS member qualifications + 35 age. Article 61 lays down the impeachment procedure, requiring a ¼-member notice, 14-day notice, and a 2/3-of-the-total-membership majority in each House.

cards.front:
Which of the following provisions was NOT introduced by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) establishing Panchayati Raj?

(A) Reservation of seats for SCs and STs in proportion to their population
(B) Minimum 33% reservation for women
(C) Five-year tenure for panchayats and holding elections within 6 months of dissolution

cards.front:
A state government passes a law on a subject in the CONCURRENT LIST that conflicts with an existing Central law on the same subject. The state law was passed AFTER receiving the President's assent. Which of the following is TRUE?

(A) The state law is void because Central law always prevails on Concurrent List subjects.
(B) The state law prevails in that state, except to the extent Parliament subsequently amends or repeals it (Article 254(2) exception).
(C) The state law needs ratification by Rajya Sabha to be valid.
(D) The state law is void because concurrent subjects can only be legislated on by Parliament.
cards.back:
(B) The state law prevails in that state, except to the extent Parliament subsequently amends or repeals it (Article 254(2) exception).

Science, Tech & Defence — Under Article 254(1), if a state law on a Concurrent subject conflicts with Central law, the Central law prevails. BUT Article 254(2) creates an exception — if the state law has been reserved for and received the PRESIDENT's ASSENT, it prevails in that state. Parliament can however still over-ride later by amendment/repeal.

cards.option2: The state law needs ratification by Rajya Sabha to be valid.
cards.option3: The state law is void because concurrent subjects can only be legislated on by Parliament.
cards.storedExplanation: Under Article 254(1), if a state law on a Concurrent subject conflicts with Central law, the Central law prevails. Which of the following is NOT a 'money bill' under Article 110?

(A) Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax.
(B) Declaration of any expenditure as 'charged on the Consolidated Fund'.

cards.front:
The doctrine of 'Colourable Legislation' means:

(A) A law that discriminates on the basis of colour or race.
(B) A legislation which, though appearing to be within the competence of a legislature, in substance encroaches on a field reserved for another legislature.
(C) A special Presidential decree during Emergency.
(D) A law passed by a state subject to central approval.
cards.back:
(B) A legislation which, though appearing to be within the competence of a legislature, in substance encroaches on a field reserved for another legislature.

Science, Tech & Defence — 'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.' Classic phrasing in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo vs State of Orissa (1953). The legislature cannot dress up a law that is actually outside its competence as one within its competence by clever drafting. Used to strike down state laws that trespass on Union List fields, or vice versa.
